In baptism, confirmation, the laying on of hands, receiving the gift of the Holy Ghost, temple ordinances, the sacrament, patriarchal blessings, family history work, missionary service—the Church provides repeated opportunities to receive divine provision and make sacred commitments. When our lives fail to bear good fruit (love, peace, long-suffering, gentleness, goodness—Galatians 5:22-23), the question of verse 4 becomes personal. Is the problem God's provision or our response? Have we been 'pruned,' or are we resisting the owner's hand? The verse calls us to abandon excuses and accept accountability.

text_kjv: And now go to; I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and break down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down:

commentary.narrative:
The verdict falls. The rhetorical questions end, and God's decision is announced with terrible finality. 'And now, let me tell you what I am about to do to my vineyard.' The transition from interrogation to declaration marks the shift from courtroom to execution of judgment. What follows is the reversal of all the care lavished in verses 1-2. The hedge and wall that protected the vineyard are not merely neglected but actively removed. God withdraws his protection.

The removal of two protective barriers—mesukah (hedge) and geder (stone wall)—is deliberate and complete. A vineyard without hedges and walls is exposed to every threat: wild animals, thieves, wind, and hostile armies. The hedges, made of thorny branches, would have been the first line of defense; the stone wall would have provided more substantial protection. Their removal exposes the vineyard completely to 'devouring' (eaten up) and 'trampling' (trodden down). The passive verbs indicate that the vineyard becomes subject to external forces beyond its control—precisely the experience of invasion, exile, and military occupation that Judah would face. This verse contains Isaiah's first explicit hint that God's protection will be withdrawn from Israel as judgment. The ancient audience would have understood this in concrete historical terms: the removal of protective barriers meant exposure to Assyrian invasion.

word_study.meaning: A hedge, typically made of thorny branches woven together, forming an outer barrier around agricultural property. The mesukah was the first line of defense against small animals and theft.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes: 'The outer protective barrier around a vineyard, typically made of thorny branches. Its removal signifies the withdrawal of divine protection.' This is not accidental damage but deliberate removal—God actively takes away the hedge, symbolizing the withdrawal of his covenantal protection.

word_study.meaning: A stone wall, a more substantial barrier than a hedge. The geder would provide protection against larger animals and organized attacks. In covenant contexts, walls often symbolize security and the boundary between the holy and the unholy.
word_study.significance: The breaking down of the wall echoes imagery throughout Isaiah and the prophetic books of the collapse of Jerusalem's defenses. Historically, this would be fulfilled in 586 BCE when Babylonian forces breached Jerusalem's walls.

word_study.meaning: To be eaten, to be devoured. The causative sense here emphasizes that the vineyard, now exposed, will be consumed by predators and invaders. Ba'ar can also mean 'to burn,' suggesting total destruction.
word_study.significance: The exposure of the vineyard is not merely damage but destruction—it will be consumed as if fire had swept through it. This foreshadows the devastation of invasion and exile.

word_study.meaning: To be trampled, to be trodden underfoot. The term emphasizes humiliation and defilement—the vineyard, which once stood elevated on a fertile hillside, will be degraded and destroyed.
word_study.significance: Mirmis appears often in Isaiah as an image of humiliation and judgment—the people will be trampled by invading armies (3:15; 10:6). The vineyard becomes a figure for the nation's military defeat.

cross_references.connection: The 'day of the LORD' will bring judgment on 'every one that is proud and lofty...and all the cedars of Lebanon, and all the oaks of Bashan.' The removal of protection signals God's judgment falling on the proud.

Jeremiah's lament over Jerusalem's fall: 'The LORD hath purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion: he hath stretched out a line, he hath not withdrawn his hand from destroying.' The same imagery of breached walls and exposure.
The psalmist asks, 'Why hast thou then broken down her hedges, so that all they which pass by the way do pluck her?' The breaking down of hedges is explicitly framed as removal of divine protection.

God says to Israel, 'Behold, I will hedge up thy way...she shall not find her paths...and she shall not find them.' God can restore or remove hedges—protection is always conditional on covenant faithfulness.

commentary.historical_context: The historical context of verse 5 is the Assyrian invasion of Judah in 701 BCE and the later Babylonian siege of 586 BCE. Isaiah would have witnessed (or prophesied about) the vulnerability of a walled city stripped of its defenses. The physical removal of hedges and walls describes the military reality of ancient siege warfare: the first objective was to isolate the city and breach its outer defenses. Archaeological evidence from the Judean hill country shows numerous vineyards with stone walls and terracing from the Iron Age. The image of these being destroyed and the land trampled by invading armies would have been devastatingly concrete to Isaiah's audience.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 5:3-4 warns the people of Ammonihah: 'Behold, if ye suppose that ye can escape the justice of God, ye shall not.' The removal of protection (the hedge and wall) is equivalent to the withdrawal of God's guidance and support that comes when people reject the covenant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 103:8-10 records God's warning through Joseph Smith: 'There are many called, but few are chosen.' The hedge and wall of divine protection are not automatic; they depend on obedience and worthiness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple walls and its priestly guardians functioned as the spiritual hedge and wall protecting Israel. When the temple would be destroyed (586 BCE, and again in 70 CE), the removal of this sacred space signified the withdrawal of God's protective presence from the covenant community.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ becomes the new hedge and wall for God's people. In John 10:11, Jesus says, 'I am the good shepherd...I am the door of the sheep.' He serves as protection for his flock. The removal of the vineyard's protection in Isaiah 5 is reversed in Christ's promise: 'I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand' (John 10:28). The vulnerability exposed in verse 5 becomes the condition that makes Christ's protective love necessary and precious.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members should understand that God's protection is conditional, not automatic. The hedge and wall of divine protection—felt as guidance, peace, providential care, and the blessings of the Church and its institutions—depend on faithfulness to the covenant. When individuals or communities violate the basic stipulations (to keep the commandments, to love God and neighbor, to bear good fruit), they lose the protective hedge. This is not arbitrary punishment but the natural consequence of abandoning the very relationship that provides protection. The verse invites us to examine: Am I maintaining the hedge and wall of covenant faithfulness, or am I exposing myself to every wind of temptation and doctrine by neglecting prayer, scripture study, temple attendance, and obedience to conscience?

text_kjv: And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.
text_kjv_alternate: And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 6 completes the reversal, moving from the removal of external protection (verse 5) to the actual devastation of the vineyard itself. Four catastrophes compound in rapid succession: (1) the vineyard is laid waste, transformed from a productive garden into desolate wilderness; (2) it will no longer be pruned or cultivated—the constant, expert labor that sustains a vineyard ceases; (3) thorns and briers overtake it, choking out the cultivated vines; (4) most shockingly, God commands the clouds to withhold rain. The last clause reveals the singer's true identity with devastating force. No mere human vineyard owner can command weather. Only God controls the rain. This is the moment when the entire poem's ambiguity collapses. What seemed to be a human love song sung by a sympathetic owner is suddenly revealed to be a divine oracle. The intimacy of the opening—the beloved's song about his beloved's vineyard—was never merely personal or domestic. It was God's song about his covenant relationship with Israel.

The sequence follows the logic of covenantal curse. Deuteronomy 28:23-24 warns Israel: 'the heaven that is over thy head shall be brass, and the earth that is under thee shall be iron. The LORD shall make the rain of thy land powder and dust.' Isaiah invokes this same curse language. The withholding of rain in a semi-arid climate is the ultimate agricultural judgment—it is not repair but death. The vineyard will not be restored; it will be abandoned to desolation.

word_study.meaning: I will set it as a waste, I will make it desolate. Batat is a Hapax legomenon (appears only once in the Bible), derived from a root meaning 'to desolate' or 'to make a waste.' It is a strong term for complete desolation.
word_study.significance: The use of such a specific, forceful term emphasizes the totality of the judgment. This is not partial damage but complete transformation of the vineyard from a place of cultivation to a place of desolation.

word_study.meaning: To prune, to cut back, to tend carefully. Zamer refers to the careful, skilled labor that sustains a vineyard's productivity. Pruning removes dead wood, shapes growth, and ensures that the plant's energy goes into fruit-bearing.
word_study.significance: The cessation of pruning signals the end of care and cultivation. No one will tend this vineyard; it will be abandoned. This is not merely judgment but the withdrawal of the owner's constant presence and attention.

word_study.meaning: To dig, to hoe, to cultivate the soil. The verb refers to the constant work of keeping soil loose and free from weeds. A vineyard requires annual digging to maintain its health.
word_study.significance: Like pruning, digging represents the owner's ongoing presence and care. The end of digging signals abandonment and the reclamation of the land by wilderness.

word_study.meaning: Thorns and briers. Shamir and shayit are often paired in Isaiah as a signature phrase for desolation. The terms may refer to specific thorny plants native to the Judean landscape that naturally colonize abandoned fields. These are not the deliberately planted thorns and thistles of Genesis 3:18 but the natural outcome of a field abandoned to wilderness.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes: 'A word-pair almost exclusive to Isaiah, appearing as a signature image of desolation. The terms may refer to specific thorny plants native to the Judean landscape.' This pairing appears in Isaiah 7:23-25, 9:17, 10:17, and 27:4. It becomes Isaiah's signature image for the desolate land that results from judgment.

word_study.meaning: I will command the clouds. The verb tsavah ('to command, to give orders') is the same verb used throughout the Old Testament for God's commands to creation. This is the language of divine authority over natural phenomena.
word_study.significance: The sudden invocation of God's command over weather is the theological turning point. The singer is revealed to be God, not a human owner. This move from narrative to divine first-person declaration is the climax of the entire passage. God alone commands the clouds; no human can.

cross_references.connection: Moses warns Israel: 'the heaven that is over thy head shall be brass, and the earth that is under thee shall be iron. The LORD shall make the rain of thy land powder and dust.' Isaiah invokes the covenant curse that God promised in Deuteronomy.

Isaiah returns to the same pair, shamir va-shayit: 'In that day, every place shall be...briers and thorns: and there shall be set therein all the land become briers and thorns.' The desolation described in 5:6 is repeated and expanded.

Elijah tells Ahab, 'There shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.' Only God's prophets can command rain and drought. Isaiah's command over clouds asserts his divine authority.

Jeremiah laments the drought: 'The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah concerning the dearth...the earth mourneth; for the corn is spoiled.' The withholding of rain is God's judgment on Israel's covenant failure.

Jesus explicitly quotes Isaiah 5's vineyard passage and announces: 'Therefore say I unto you, The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof...he that falleth on this stone shall be broken: but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder.' The breaking of the vineyard is the removal of the kingdom.

commentary.historical_context: Verse 6 reflects the geography and climate of Judea. The region is semi-arid, with annual rainfall concentrated in winter (November-March). Vineyards depend absolutely on this rainfall; a year without rain would indeed devastate crops. The thorny plants that invade abandoned fields (shamir va-shayit) are real plants native to the Levant—species like wild briars and thistles that naturally colonize uncultivated land. Archaeological surveys show that when settlements were abandoned during periods of conflict or foreign invasion, the land rapidly reverted to thorny scrubland. Isaiah's image is not fanciful but grounded in the genuine experience of Judean land and climate. The withholding of rain is the ultimate judgment in an agricultural society; it is also, historically, the experience of prolonged drought that can accompany invasion and the collapse of irrigation systems.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob 5:38-47 contains extensive parallels about the withholding of nourishment from corrupt branches: 'What could I have done more for my vineyard? Behold, I knew that all the fruit of the vineyard, save it were these, had become corrupted...and notwithstanding all these things, I have not caused that my vineyard should perish' (Jacob 5:42-44). Unlike Isaiah, Jacob's account emphasizes God's repeated mercy and the possibility of grafting and restoration through the Restoration.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 82:7-8 extends the theme of covenant judgment: 'Wherefore, I, the Lord, in the beginning desired to warn you; but ye received not...if you will repent and return unto me, I will receive you, that you may have place in my house.' The Restoration reaffirms the pattern: judgment follows violation, but repentance opens the path to restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The withholding of rain in verse 6 is the inverse of the temple's blessing: the temple is the place where heaven opens and blessings flow down. The judgment of verse 6 represents the closure of heaven—the inability to access the ordinances and covenants that connect earth to heaven. The Restoration, through the restoration of the temple, reverses this closure.

commentary.christological_typology: The desolation of verse 6—the laying waste, the withholding of rain, the invasion of thorns—prefigures Christ's crucifixion and the spiritual desolation that follows the rejection of the vineyard owner's son. In Matthew 21, Jesus concludes the vineyard parable by saying the kingdom will be taken from Israel and given to another nation (Matthew 21:43). This is the bitter fruit of verse 6: the vineyard is destroyed. Yet Christ's death is not the end of the story. The withholding of rain becomes, in the gospel, the invitation to drink from the living waters that only Christ provides (John 4:14; John 7:37-39). The thorns and briers of judgment give way to the fruits of the Spirit through Christ's redemption. The desolate vineyard is transformed into the vineyard of the resurrected Lord, where all who believe are grafted in (Romans 11:17-24).
commentary.application: This final verse of the opening song compels reflection on the reality of covenant judgment. The withholding of rain represents the withdrawal of spiritual nourishment—the loss of inspiration, guidance, and the feeling of God's presence. This can happen personally when individuals neglect prayer and scripture study, creating a spiritual drought. It can happen communally when a people refuse to hear the prophets. The verse asks: Is my life yielding good fruit or thorns? Am I being pruned and tended, or am I abandoning my covenants to desolation? For Latter-day Saints, the verse emphasizes the precious nature of the temple, prophetic guidance, and the sacrament—these are the channels through which the 'rain' of heaven flows. When we lose access to or abandon these means of nourishment, we experience the spiritual equivalent of verse 6: withholding of rain, invasion of thorns, and desolation. Yet the passage also teaches that God is not arbitrary in judgment—he is responding to a failure to bear good fruit after lavishing care and provision. Repentance means returning to the practices of cultivation and inviting the owner's hand back into the vineyard.

text_kjv: For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

commentary.narrative:
This verse completes Isaiah's parable of the vineyard (5:1-7) by explicitly identifying the vineyard as Israel and Judah. The prophet moves from metaphor to reality: God's extensive care (plowing, clearing stones, planting choice vines) represents the covenant relationship and divine investment in His people. But the identification shifts the weight entirely onto the failure of Israel to produce the fruit God expected. The verse then delivers the devastating conclusion with a wordplay so precise it shocks the Hebrew ear: God looked for mishpat (justice) but found mispach (bloodshed); He looked for tsedaqah (righteousness) but found tse'aqah (a cry of anguish). The consonantal difference between these pairs — a single letter separates expectation from horror — makes the moral distance feel unbearable.

The wordplay is not decorative; it is the heart of the indictment. In English, 'justice' and 'oppression' sound unrelated, which dilutes the prophet's accusation. But in Hebrew, the near-identity of sound combined with the catastrophic difference in meaning conveys that Israel has perverted the very thing God expects of them. They have inverted justice into bloodshed, righteousness into cries of suffering. The TCR's rendering of tse'aqah as 'a cry of anguish' deepens the irony: this is the same word used for Israel's cry under Egyptian slavery (Exodus 3:7). God heard His people's oppression then and delivered them; now He hears the same cry rising from within His own people, directed at their own vulnerable members.

The identification of the vineyard as 'His pleasant plant' (literally, His 'plantings of delight' or 'plants of His delight') emphasizes that this judgment comes not from indifference but from thwarted love. God did not expect ordinary fruit; He expected the fruit of justice and righteousness — the covenant community living out its calling. Instead, the land of Israel became a place where the powerful devoured the vulnerable, where justice was perverted and the poor cried out.

word_study.meaning: A planted vineyard, representing an invested, cultivated relationship. In the Hebrew Bible, the vineyard often symbolizes Israel (Ps. 80:8-11; Jer. 2:21) because it requires constant care and is vulnerable to destruction.
word_study.significance: The metaphor carries the full weight of covenant: God's investment, expectation of fruitfulness, and anguish at betrayal.

word_study.meaning: Justice, judgment, or just decision. Encompasses both the legal process and its righteous outcome. Central to the Hebrew Bible's ethical vocabulary, mishpat is the protection and vindication of the vulnerable within the covenant community.
word_study.significance: This is the primary legal-ethical term in the covenant: God's expectation of Israel is that they practice mishpat — fair judgment that protects the weak. The term appears throughout the prophets as the measure of a covenant nation's faithfulness.

word_study.meaning: A rare word occurring only here, likely meaning 'bloodshed' or 'violence.' The TCR identifies it as a deliberate sound-play with mishpat, differing by a single consonant (ש vs. ח) and one vowel shift.
word_study.significance: The rarity of this word and its phonetic proximity to mishpat suggests Isaiah chose it deliberately. The wordplay conveys that what Israel has produced is not merely the absence of justice but its violent inversion — bloodshed masquerading as law.

word_study.meaning: Righteousness, right relationship, covenant faithfulness. Broader than mere legal correctness, tsedaqah implies active care for community well-being and restoration of right relationships.
word_study.significance: Paired with mishpat, tsedaqah represents the relational and ethical character God expects from His people. It is not abstract virtue but lived faithfulness within the covenant.

word_study.meaning: A cry of distress, lamentation, or anguish. Used throughout the Hebrew Bible for the cry of the oppressed (e.g., the Israelites' cry under Egyptian slavery in Exodus 3:7, 9; the cry of Abel's blood in Genesis 4:10).
word_study.significance: By using tse'aqah, Isaiah connects present-day injustice to the paradigmatic oppression of Egypt. The irony is shattering: the people whom God liberated from slavery have become slavemasters themselves, and their victims cry out in the same agony Israel once knew.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'a planting of his delights' or 'his plant of delight.' Sha'ashuim refers to that which brings joy or delight, particularly in intimate or beloved contexts.
word_study.significance: This phrase emphasizes God's personal investment and affection for Israel. The judgment is not the pronouncement of a distant deity but the grief of a lover betrayed — God tenderly planted what should have delighted Him, only to find corruption.

cross_references.connection: Uses the same vineyard metaphor to describe Israel's origins in Egypt and transplanting into Canaan, establishing the symbolic foundation for Isaiah's parable.
Similarly describes Israel as a 'noble vine' that has become a 'strange vine,' echoing Isaiah's indictment of degeneration from covenantal expectation.
Records Israel's cry (tse'aqah) under Egyptian slavery — the same word Isaiah uses to describe the cry of those oppressed by Israel itself, creating a devastating irony.
Abel's blood cries out (tse'aqah) from the ground, establishing a biblical pattern where oppression and violence speak directly to God, demanding redress.
References God's patience with His people before judgment, paralleling the patience implicit in Isaiah's vineyard: God gave every advantage, then waited for fruit.

commentary.historical_context: The vineyard metaphor in 7th-century Judah would resonate immediately with agrarian audiences. Vineyards were labor-intensive, long-term investments requiring multi-year patience before significant yields. Isaiah's audience would understand the owner's investment (removing stones, building a watchtower) and his reasonable expectation of return. The irony is that Israel produced 'wild grapes' — not merely inferior fruit but fruit of a different kind, suggesting perversion rather than mere failure. In the ancient Near Eastern context, the failure to produce expected fruit could symbolize both moral corruption and the breakdown of the feudal-covenant relationship between overlord and vassal. For Israel, the covenant with YHWH established their status as His special possession; their failure to produce justice was a violation of the foundational treaty.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 15:12-15, Nephi explains the meaning of the olive tree vision (paralleling Isaiah's vineyard) to his brothers, emphasizing that the tree represents the house of Israel and that branches that are broken off represent those scattered from the covenant people. Both Isaiah 5:7 and Nephi's explanation establish that Israel's unfaithfulness results in judgment, though in the Book of Mormon context, repentance and restoration remain possible through the gospel of Jesus Christ.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 86:1-11 applies Isaiah's vineyard metaphor directly to the Church in the latter days. The Lord is the owner of the vineyard (the Church); faithful members are the good grain; the 'tares' represent those who do not keep covenants. The passage reiterates Isaiah's central concern: the vineyard owner has every right to expect fruit from those He has planted and tended. The Doctrine and Covenants specifically invokes Isaiah's language to teach that even the restored Church faces the possibility of unfaithfulness and the resulting judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenant expectation Isaiah articulates — that God's people produce justice and righteousness — is central to temple worship. The temple endowment teaches that those who enter into covenants with God accept the obligation to live according to divine law and to become agents of justice and mercy in the world. Isaiah's indictment of Israel for producing bloodshed and cries of anguish instead of justice speaks directly to the covenant violation of failing to live as God's people in daily life beyond the temple walls.

commentary.christological_typology: The vineyard owner's disappointment and the resulting judgment prefigure Jesus's own indictment of Israel's leaders in Matthew 21:33-41 (the parable of the wicked husbandmen), where Christ directly applies the vineyard parable to His rejection by the religious authorities. The 'fruit' God expects — justice, mercy, and faithfulness — is ultimately produced through Christ's redeeming sacrifice and the transformation of the human heart that follows. Christ Himself is both the true vine (John 15:1-5) and the suffering servant who bears the consequences of Israel's injustice (Isaiah 53), making Isaiah 5:7 a shadow of the central mystery of redemption: God's people, having failed to produce the fruit of righteousness, are restored only through Christ's perfect fulfillment of the law and His atonement for covenant violations.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern covenant members with the same measure Isaiah applied to ancient Israel: Does our baptismal and temple covenant produce justice and righteousness in our daily lives? The wordplay between mishpat (justice) and mispach (bloodshed) asks whether our actions—in business, family, community, and politics—serve the vulnerable or exploit them. A believer who loves Christ but practices injustice toward the powerless has, in Isaiah's language, produced bloodshed instead of justice. The verse challenges us to examine where we have rationalized the subtle inversion of covenant values: Has our pursuit of wealth trampled the poor? Has our religious practice become detached from the ethical demands of discipleship? The anguish Isaiah describes is not abstract judgment but God's personal grief at watching those He loves betray the very purpose for which they were chosen.

text_kjv: Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

commentary.narrative:
The first of six woe oracles (5:8-23) opens with a direct indictment of the wealthy who are consolidating land ownership by absorbing the properties of the poor and middle class. In the ancient Israelite economy, land was not merely a commodity but the basis of family inheritance and tribal identity. The Torah established mechanisms to prevent the permanent alienation of land: the sabbatical year, the jubilee year (Leviticus 25), and the law of redemption ensured that land remained within families and that debts could not reduce an Israelite to permanent servitude. Those who 'join house to house' and 'add field to field' are systematically dismantling this covenant economic structure.

The oracle opens with hoy (הוֹי), a word that carries dual significance: it is simultaneously a funeral cry for the dead and a prophetic curse upon the living. By addressing the living oppressors with a funeral dirge, Isaiah pronounces their doom as already sealed. The verb 'join' (מַגִּיע, maggia) conveys not gradual accumulation but aggressive annexation. The phrase 'until there is no space left' implies that the consolidation continues until no one else can exist — a vision of monopoly so complete that it becomes grotesque. The concluding irony is cutting: those who sought to 'dwell alone in the land' through wealth will indeed dwell alone, but in a desolation they did not anticipate.

This woe directly violates the foundational covenant law. Leviticus 25:23-24 declares that the land belongs to God and that Israelites are merely stewards: 'The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine...and ye shall grant a redemption for the land.' By absorbing ancestral lands, the wealthy were not merely accumulating property; they were denying the next generation their covenant inheritance and erasing the family structures that held Israelite society together. Isaiah's indictment represents a prophetic defense of the covenant's economic justice.

word_study.meaning: An interjection functioning as both a lament for the dead (cf. 1 Kings 13:30; Jeremiah 22:18) and as a prophetic denunciation or curse. The word creates an emotional register of doom and funeral grief.
word_study.significance: By addressing the living oppressors with a funeral cry, Isaiah merges two registers: he simultaneously mourns their fate (as though already dead) and announces their judgment as inevitable. The use of hoy for six successive oracles (vv. 8, 11, 18, 20, 21, 22) creates a rhythmic pronouncement of doom, like tolling a bell.

word_study.meaning: To join, connect, or attach. In this context, it carries a sense of aggressive annexation or forced combination. The parallel verb in the second line is 'lay field to field,' which similarly conveys accumulation and consolidation.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes not honest purchase but the aggressive elimination of boundaries. The land-grabber is not buying property through normal commerce but annexing it by force or legal manipulation, erasing the separation between one family's inheritance and another's.

word_study.meaning: Bayit (house) can refer to a physical dwelling but in land-tenure contexts refers to household property and the family's fixed assets. Sadeh (field) refers to agricultural land. Together, they represent the totality of family inheritance.
word_study.significance: Isaiah specifies both dwellings and agricultural land because both were essential to family survival and identity. To eliminate both was to erase entire families from the land, turning what should have been an eternal inheritance into disposable property.

word_study.meaning: Alone, solitary, isolated. In the context of land ownership, it suggests possession without community.
word_study.significance: The irony is devastating: those who sought to stand alone in wealth and power will stand alone in desolation. The prophecy suggests that greed eventually isolates and destroys the greedy, leaving them surrounded by emptiness rather than by the community they should have stewarded.

cross_references.connection: Establishes the Torah's foundational principle that the land belongs to God and must not be sold permanently; every jubilee year (50th year) returns it to original owners, preventing exactly the consolidation Isaiah condemns.
Curses those who remove a neighbor's landmark, reflecting the Torah's legal protection of family land boundaries and inheritance rights that the woe-oracle targets.

Narrates Ahab and Jezebel's seizure of Naboth's vineyard, a historical example of the land-grabbing condemned in Isaiah 5:8; Elijah pronounces judgment on the royal couple, paralleling Isaiah's prophetic denunciation.
A contemporary prophecy condemning those who 'devise iniquity' and covet fields and houses, stripping families of their inheritance — echoing Isaiah's concern with systematic economic injustice.

Modern revelation reaffirms the principle that all things are God's and that stewardship (not ownership) defines humanity's relation to land and property, echoing the covenant principle Isaiah invokes.

commentary.historical_context: In 8th-century Judah, economic pressures and foreign tribute obligations created opportunities for land consolidation by the wealthy. Archaeological evidence (though not from Isaiah's exact era) indicates that in Iron Age Levantine societies, economic inequality intensified around the time of Assyrian expansion and increased taxation. Large landowners could afford to pay tribute; small farmers could not. Debt slavery and loss of ancestral land became mechanisms through which the powerful absorbed the holdings of the vulnerable. The result was a radical restructuring of society: a small elite owned vast tracts while displaced peasants became tenant farmers or slaves. The jubilee laws in Leviticus 25 suggest that even in the ideal form, the land-concentration problem was persistent enough to require structural safeguards. By Isaiah's era, it appears these safeguards had been systematically ignored. The 'no place left' phrase may reflect an actual crisis of landlessness in 8th-century Judah.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon extensively critiques economic injustice rooted in land concentration and exploitation. In Alma 34:28-29, Amulek warns against inequality and the hoarding of wealth while the poor suffer. In 4 Nephi 1:24-27, the decline of Nephite civilization begins when 'some were lifted up unto pride, and others were exceedingly humble; thus the Church began to be broken up.' The shift includes those who began 'to set their hearts upon their riches' and to separate from the poor. Isaiah's concern with systematic land-grabbing and its destabilizing effect on covenant community parallels the Nephite pattern of corruption through economic inequality.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 78:5-6 establishes that 'it is my purpose to provide for my saints' and commands the Saints to be equal in earthly things. The early Restoration emphasized that economic justice is a covenant principle, not optional virtue. The United Order (D&C 82, 92, 104) attempted to institutionalize the kind of equitable land and property distribution that the Torah's jubilee laws and Isaiah's indictment of land-concentration suggest God expects of His covenant people.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The law of consecration, central to the temple covenant in the Restoration, directly addresses the issue Isaiah raises: the oath to consecrate one's 'properties, and labors' to God implies that one's wealth and land are stewardship, not absolute possession, and that this stewardship must benefit the community, especially the poor. The woe against those who consolidate land at the expense of others is fundamentally a violation of the law of consecration.

commentary.christological_typology: The consolidation of land at the expense of the vulnerable prefigures the systems of oppression and injustice that will culminate in Christ's crucifixion. Matthew 23:14 records Jesus condemning the Pharisees for 'devouring widows' houses,' directly echoing the language of those who consume the vulnerable through legal and economic means. Christ's teaching that 'the last shall be first' and His identification with 'the least of these' (Matthew 25:31-46) represent a direct inversion of the wealth-consolidation ethic Isaiah condemns. In the kingdom of God that Christ establishes, access to inheritance and provision is restored to the marginalized, undoing the Isaianic injustice through redemption.
commentary.application: For modern members of the Church, this verse challenges the relationship between wealth accumulation and covenant faithfulness. Do our financial practices protect or exploit the vulnerable? Do we acquire property and consolidate resources in ways that displace or marginalize others, or do we steward with awareness of our obligation to the community? The principle is not that wealth is evil, but that it must never be pursued through systematic injustice or at the expense of others' covenant inheritance. The verse also invites examination of systemic injustice: participation in economic structures that extract wealth from the poor while enriching the already-wealthy may constitute participation in the very sin Isaiah condemns. Finally, the irony of the final clause — 'that they may be placed alone' — warns that greed ultimately isolates. Those who build isolated wealth without community, without justice, without conscience, find themselves truly alone: abandoned by God and abandoned by society.

text_kjv: In mine ears said the LORD of hosts, Of a truth many houses shall be desolate, even great and fair, without inhabitant.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah introduces this verse with a direct claim to prophetic audition: 'In mine ears said the LORD of hosts.' This formula asserts that the prophet has heard the divine judgment directly from God and is now transmitting it to his audience. The word 'ears' is significant — it emphasizes sensory immediacy and the reality of prophetic experience. Isaiah is not speculating or interpreting events; he is reporting what God has declared to him.

The judgment itself is poetic symmetry applied as punishment: those who accumulated 'many houses' through land-grabbing will see those very houses stand empty and desolate. The Hebrew word for 'desolate' (שַׁמָּה, shammah) implies not merely abandonment but ruin and devastation. The emphasis on 'great and fair' underscores that even the most impressive architectural achievements cannot save the wicked from judgment. Beauty, scale, and value mean nothing when judgment falls. The cruelty of the irony is pointed: the wealth-grabber sought permanence and status through property accumulation; instead, the houses become monuments to emptiness and loss.

This verse connects cause and effect. The land-grabber removed poor families from their inheritance by absorbing their properties; now the land-grabber's own magnificent houses will be emptied of inhabitants. The judgment is not arbitrary but a precise reversal of the crime. The houses, meant to display power and permanence, become ruins. Historically, this likely refers to the devastation of Judah during Assyrian siege and conquest: the grand estates of the wealthy would be burned or abandoned during military assault, and the wealthy themselves would be exiled, killed, or impoverished. But on the level of the oracle itself, the judgment is presented as God's direct reversal of covenant violation.

The formula 'of a truth' (אִם־לֹא אִם, ki im-lo) emphasizes certainty. This is not a conditional threat but an assured declaration. The judgment is already fixed in God's purpose.

word_study.meaning: The ears; often used metaphorically for the capacity to hear, listen, and obey. In prophetic contexts, 'in mine ears' emphasizes the immediacy and sensory reality of divine communication.
word_study.significance: The prophet claims direct auditory experience of God's word, establishing the basis for his authority to pronounce judgment. This is not interpretation but transmission of divine speech.

word_study.meaning: Desolation, ruin, devastation. Often used to describe land laid waste, cities destroyed, and populations dispersed. In covenantal contexts, desolation is the covenant curse—what happens when God withdraws His protection and blessing.
word_study.significance: The term carries weight beyond mere emptiness. Shammah suggests the active destruction or abandonment of what was once valued, implying divine judgment and the reversal of blessing.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'from the absence of one dwelling' or 'with no one inhabiting.' Yoshev (the one who dwells, inhabits) is the active agent; the phrase emphasizes emptiness through the absence of that agent.
word_study.significance: Houses exist to house people; without inhabitants, they are monuments to absence. The phrase stresses that judgment does not merely damage property but removes the people who gave it meaning and purpose.

cross_references.connection: The covenant curse for Israel's disobedience: God will lay waste cities, make the land desolate, and scatter the people so that 'your enemies...shall be astonished at you.' Isaiah 5:9 applies this pattern of covenantal judgment.
Lists the curses for covenant violation, including the siege of cities and the loss of harvests; Isaiah invokes the same covenantal judgment framework.

Jeremiah similarly threatens the Judean royal house that if they practice justice, their houses will flourish; if they do not, the palace itself will become desolate—the same connection between covenant faithfulness and the fate of dwellings.

Chronicles the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem (the historical context in which Isaiah likely prophesied) and God's deliverance; many Judean houses were indeed destroyed or left empty during the Assyrian threat.
Modern revelation warns that those who reject God's word and continue in darkness will face consequences, establishing the principle that judgment follows covenant rejection.

commentary.historical_context: The 8th century BCE was a period of Assyrian imperial expansion under Sargon II and Sennacherib. Judah and Israel faced increasing military pressure and demands for tribute. The wealthy, who had consolidated land and resources, would have constructed the grand houses Isaiah references. Archaeological evidence from Iron Age Judah shows both palatial estates of the elite and evidence of later destruction layers from Assyrian campaigns. When Assyrian armies besieged Judean cities, homes were burned, families displaced, and the survivors often exiled. The desolation Isaiah predicts was not merely prophetic metaphor; it became historical reality during the late 8th century. The 'great and fair houses' that had demonstrated the owner's power and permanence became smoking ruins. This historical backdrop makes Isaiah's oracle not merely a threat but a commentary on imminent events.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains numerous instances of prosperity leading to spiritual corruption and resulting desolation. In Helaman 13, the prophet Samuel the Lamanite warns the Nephites of coming destruction: 'Behold, I have seen the great wickedness of the people...And they have become proud, and haughty, and have persecuted your prophets...therefore the Lord hath sent me that I might show unto you that ye must repent, or that ye must perish' (Helaman 13:1-2). The cycle of wealth-induced corruption leading to desolation repeats throughout the Nephite record, paralleling Isaiah's pattern.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:39 states, 'And the residue shall be organized in its fellows in all these things, and shall be the strength of my people.' The principle that God desires His people to prosper but not to abandon justice and mercy runs through modern revelation. When prosperity is built on exploitation, desolation is the remedy. D&C 56:16-17 declares that the poor and rich are commanded to work together in righteousness, or judgment follows.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes the promise of refuge and protection for those who keep covenants faithfully (D&C 109:25-26). Conversely, those who break covenants forfeit that protection. Houses built on covenant faithfulness stand secure; houses built on injustice, regardless of their grandeur, ultimately become desolate. This principle extends to the spiritual house—the temple community built on principle—which endures, while structures built on falsehood crumble.

commentary.christological_typology: The desolation of houses built on unrighteousness prefigures the judgment Christ will pronounce on the religious establishment that rejected Him. In Matthew 23:37-39, Jesus laments over Jerusalem: 'O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets...how often would I have gathered thy children together...and ye would not!...Behold, your house is left unto you desolate.' The 'house' is simultaneously the temple and the whole religious and political structure built on injustice rather than righteousness. In Christ's economy, only that which is built on His foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11) will endure; all else will be shaken and removed (Hebrews 12:26-28). Isaiah's oracle points to the ultimate truth: that human structures, however impressive, cannot stand against God's judgment unless built on justice and truth.
commentary.application: This verse warns that material prosperity without moral foundation is fragile and subject to judgment. It challenges modern believers to examine whether their possessions are held in justice and used to bless others, or accumulated through exploitation and selfishness. The assurance that even 'great and fair' achievements will become desolate if rooted in unrighteousness should prompt honest reflection: Do my financial practices honor the vulnerable? Are my possessions a means to serve others or a tool to elevate myself above them? The verse also offers a corrective to the prosperity gospel or the assumption that wealth signals God's approval. Isaiah insists that blessing follows covenant faithfulness, and judgment follows covenant violation—not the reverse. Finally, the statement 'In mine ears said the LORD' reminds modern listeners that God's word, transmitted through prophets, carries objective authority. When prophets warn against injustice, they speak with the weight of divine authority, and ignoring their warnings invites the consequences Isaiah describes.

text_kjv: Yea, ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath, and the seed of an homer shall yield an ephah.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 10 extends the judgment announced in verse 9 into the agricultural sphere, turning the land itself against those who violated covenant law. The specific measurements make the curse concrete and quantifiable: a bath (approximately six gallons) from ten acres of vineyard represents catastrophic agricultural failure; a homer of seed (roughly six bushels) yielding only an ephah (about half a bushel) represents a tenfold loss. These are not merely poor harvests; they are economic collapse. A farmer who planted a homer of seed could expect significant yield under normal conditions; instead, he recovers barely enough to avoid starvation for one season.

The principle invoked is fundamental to ancient covenantal religion: the land itself obeys the God of covenant. When the people are faithful, the land flourishes; when they are unfaithful, the land withholds its blessing. This is not merely environmental consequence but theological principle—the land is responsive to covenant faithfulness and violation. Leviticus 26:4-5 promises abundant harvest for covenant obedience; verses 19-20 pronounce agricultural failure for disobedience. Isaiah invokes this same pattern. The curse operates not through abstract consequence but through the deliberate refusal of the land to provide. The landowner will see the vines flourish (suggesting no natural disaster has occurred) but will find at harvest that productivity has become virtually nil. This is more mysterious and more terrible than crop failure from drought or plague; it is nature's judgment executed through invisible means.

The specificity of the measurements also reflects the legal-economic precision of ancient Israelite society. Every farmer would have known how many acres were required to feed a family, what seed-to-harvest ratio was necessary to survive the year. Isaiah's audience would have immediately grasped the devastation he was describing: these yields would starve the wealthy land-grabber. The curse operates with brutal logic: you sought to absorb the land of others and live in splendor; instead, the land you seized will not sustain you. The judgment is not that crops fail but that the perpetrator of injustice will literally starve in the midst of land they claimed to own.

word_study.meaning: A Hebrew unit of liquid measure, equivalent to approximately six gallons or 22 liters. Used for measuring wine, oil, and other liquids. One bath was also equal to an ephah in dry measure (Ezekiel 4:11).
word_study.significance: The bath was a standard measure known to all Israelites; Isaiah uses it to specify the precise nature of the judgment. One bath from ten acres was absurdly low, making the prophecy quantifiably concrete.

word_study.meaning: A Hebrew unit of dry measure, equivalent to roughly 11 bushels or 390 liters. The largest dry measure in the Hebrew system, used for measuring grain and seed. Derived from 'hamor' (donkey), as it was the load a donkey could carry.
word_study.significance: A homer of seed represents significant investment and expectation of substantial return. A tenfold reduction in yield would render the seed-to-harvest ratio catastrophic and unsustainable.

word_study.meaning: A Hebrew unit of dry measure, roughly equivalent to 3.7 liters or one-tenth of a homer. A smaller, more practical measure for grain and flour.
word_study.significance: One ephah from a homer represents a tenfold loss—a complete economic catastrophe. The farmer recovers only 10% of what he planted, making agricultural production unsustainable.

word_study.meaning: To make, do, produce, or accomplish. In agricultural contexts, it refers to what the land produces or yields.
word_study.significance: The verb is straightforward: the land will produce these paltry amounts. The passive voice (the land 'shall yield') emphasizes that this is not the farmer's choice but the land's judgment.

cross_references.connection: The foundational covenantal promise: faithful obedience yields abundant harvests; covenant violation brings barren fields. Isaiah applies this same pattern to the specific sin of land-grabbing.

Lists agricultural curses for covenant disobedience: 'Thou shalt carry much seed out into the field, and shalt gather but little in; for the locusts shall consume it...thy vines and thy fig trees shall the caterpillar consume.' Isaiah's language echoes this curse tradition.
A later prophet uses similar language: 'Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough.' The agricultural curse for covenant neglect recurs throughout the prophetic tradition.
Amos, a contemporary of Isaiah, likewise condemns those who 'oppress the poor, and crush the needy' and warns of consequence through agricultural failure and loss of estate.
Modern revelation affirms that God controls the elements and will withhold blessing when His people break covenants, echoing the principle Isaiah invokes.

commentary.historical_context: The measurements Isaiah uses (bath, homer, ephah) would have been familiar to 8th-century Judean farmers and merchants. Agriculture was the basis of Judean economy; most people understood the relationship between seed sown, acres planted, and harvest yield. In a pre-industrial agricultural economy, a tenfold reduction in yield from seed was not merely unfortunate; it was catastrophic. A farmer might survive one bad year through stored grain, but sustained low yields would lead to bankruptcy and loss of land. The threat Isaiah makes is therefore not abstract or decorative—it describes a realistic economic nightmare for agrarian society. The covenant curse language (drawing from Deuteronomy and Leviticus) was also familiar from Torah reading and recitation. Isaiah's audience would recognize that he was invoking the classical patterns of judgment for covenant violation, raising the stakes by applying those patterns to their own day.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 37:24-30, Alma warns the young man Helaman about the consequences of breaking covenants: those who abandon the commandments will experience spiritual famine as well as material hardship. The Book of Mormon pattern is that spiritual disobedience produces material consequence. In 4 Nephi 1:24-26, prosperity leads to inequality and pride; then 'there began to be some contentions...which gave an exceedingly great many afflictions unto those who did not belong to the church of God.' Injustice produces famine, both spiritual and literal.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:36 states that God speaks to prepare His people for judgments coming upon the earth, and that those who break covenants will experience deprivation. The principle Isaiah articulates—that unfaithful stewardship of the land will result in the land's refusal to provide—reflects the broader Restoration principle that God expects faithful stewardship and will not bless those who exploit others.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The law of consecration requires that stewards use their property (including land) to sustain the poor and advance God's kingdom. One who accumulates land for private aggrandizement while others lack, violates this law. The consequence Isaiah describes—that such accumulated land will not sustain the violator—reflects the principle that God does not bless unrighteous accumulation. The temple endowment teaches that we are responsible before God for how we use what He has entrusted to us.

commentary.christological_typology: The curse that the land will not provide for those who violated covenant law prefigures the deeper truth that separation from Christ (the true vine and the source of all sustenance) results in spiritual famine and death. John 6:35 records Jesus saying, 'I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger.' The principle Isaiah articulates—that covenant violation severs the flow of blessing from the source of provision—applies most fully in Christ. Those who reject Christ, who is the source of eternal life, will experience the ultimate deprivation: separation from God and the inability to sustain the soul. Isaiah's agricultural curse is a shadow of this spiritual reality.
commentary.application: This verse addresses modern believers whose economic decisions may involve exploitation of others or unjust accumulation of resources. The principle is not that all loss or financial hardship is punishment for injustice, but that God sees and eventually judges the systematic violation of covenant principles. Those who build wealth through practices that harm the vulnerable should consider whether they are inviting the curse Isaiah describes. More broadly, the verse challenges the modern assumption that financial success is inevitable reward for cleverness or hard work. Isaiah insists that genuine provision—that which sustains life and flourishes over time—flows only through covenant faithfulness. Injustice may produce short-term wealth, but it severs the connection between labor and sustainable yield. Finally, the specificity of the measurements (the exact reduction of crops) suggests that Isaiah is speaking to a real economic crisis his audience was experiencing or would soon experience. The application is not merely spiritual but concrete: injustice destabilizes society and economies, producing poverty, famine, and collapse—not because God capriciously punishes, but because violation of justice is inherently destructive.

text_kjv: Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!

commentary.narrative:
The second woe oracle shifts from the exploitation of the land to the corruption of the will through alcohol. Those condemned in this verse organize their entire existence around intoxication: they rise early not to work or pray but to pursue drink, and they continue into the evening until wine inflames them. The structure of the indictment is devastating: the verb 'rise early' (שׁוּקַם, shakam) normally suggests diligence and readiness (in other contexts, it is positive to rise early to serve God). But here, rising early is perverted into the service of drink. The verb 'pursue' or 'follow' (רָדַף, radaf) typically describes hunting prey or pursuing enemies; applied to alcohol, it conveys obsessive, almost predatory hunger. The parallel phrase 'linger late' (מְאַחֲרֵי, me'aharê) suggests that the drinker remains until evening falls, organizing the full arc of the day around intoxication.

The problem Isaiah identifies is not merely individual vice (excessive drinking) but a systematic perversion of values and priorities. These people have made alcohol the organizing principle of their lives. They have inverted the proper order: instead of working, serving others, or seeking God, they pursue pleasure with the intensity and dedication that should be directed toward covenant faithfulness. The phrase 'till wine inflame them' uses a verb (יַדְלִיקֵם, yadliquem) that literally means to kindle, set ablaze, or light up. Wine inflames them—it becomes an inner fire that consumes their rational capacity. They are literally and figuratively burned by their pursuit.

In the context of the six woes (5:8-23), this oracle against drunkenness follows immediately after the oracle against land-grabbing. The connection is significant: greed and indulgence are paired as complementary evils. The wealthy who seized land spent their ill-gotten gains on luxury and intoxication, losing the capacity for moral judgment and covenant faithfulness. Drunkenness is not merely a personal moral failing in this oracle; it is a symptom of systemic injustice and a sign that the wealthy have detached themselves from the community and from God. They 'lift themselves up early' in self-service rather than in service to others or obedience to God.

word_study.meaning: To rise early, to wake early. In other contexts, it is a virtue (e.g., Abraham rising early to do God's will in Genesis 19:27). Here it is inverted—the early rising is in service to a vice rather than a virtue.
word_study.significance: The perversion of what should be a positive quality (diligence) into service of a destructive habit illustrates the comprehensive inversion of values in the condemned.

word_study.meaning: To pursue, chase, follow after. Often used for hunting or pursuing enemies. When applied to drink, it conveys obsessive, relentless craving and the intensity of the hunt.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests that the pursuit of drink has become the driving force of the person's existence, as consuming as the hunt is for the hunter. It is not casual drinking but compulsive pursuit.

word_study.meaning: Strong drink, fermented beverages other than grape wine. Could include beer, date wine, or other intoxicants. The Nazirite vow (Numbers 6:3) prohibits both yayin (wine) and shekar, indicating they were distinct intoxicating categories.
word_study.significance: By mentioning both 'strong drink' and 'wine' (yayin), Isaiah suggests an exhaustive indulgence in whatever intoxicants are available. The condemned are not selective; they pursue all forms of alcohol.

word_study.meaning: To kindle, set ablaze, light up. Literally, wine becomes a fire within them. The verb creates an image of intoxication as an inner conflagration that consumes rationality and moral capacity.
word_study.significance: This verb is visceral: it conveys the physical and spiritual consumption that intoxication represents. The person is not merely drinking; they are being consumed by fire.

word_study.meaning: To delay, linger, remain late. Suggests prolongation and persistence—the drinking does not stop but continues through the day until evening.
word_study.significance: The combination of rising early and lingering late creates the image of a full day organized around intoxication, suggesting compulsion and loss of self-control.

cross_references.connection: Paul's injunction 'be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit' directly invokes the principle Isaiah establishes: the person filled with alcohol is a person not filled with God's Spirit, and the two conditions are mutually exclusive.

Warns that 'wine is a mocker: strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise.' Proverbs repeatedly emphasizes that intoxication undermines wisdom and judgment, aligning with Isaiah's concern.

Eli misinterprets Hannah's prayer, accusing her of drunkenness; the text contrasts genuine spiritual seeking with drunken confusion, establishing the principle that alcohol obscures spiritual perception.

The Nazirite vow includes prohibition of wine and strong drink as part of separation unto God. Isaiah's condemnation of those who make drink their pursuit echoes the Nazirite principle that covenant dedication requires detachment from intoxicants.

The Word of Wisdom teaches that wine (except for sacramental use) and strong drink are not for the human body, establishing a modern Latter-day Saint principle that aligns with Isaiah's ethical concern about intoxication.

commentary.historical_context: In 8th-century Judah, wine was a staple beverage (water was often unsafe), but drunkenness was recognized as a vice. The biblical warnings against excessive drinking (Proverbs, later books of the Bible) suggest it was a genuine social problem, especially among the elite who had access to abundant wine and free time to consume it. Archaeological evidence from Iron Age Levantine sites shows wine-making and storage facilities, indicating significant wine production and trade. The wealthy, who had the resources to purchase or produce wine in quantity, would have been most susceptible to habitual intoxication. In the context of Isaiah's indictment of the wealthy (the land-grabbers of v. 8), linking them to drunkenness is both socially accurate and theologically pointed: those who built wealth through injustice often squandered it through vice. The pairing of greed and intoxication as twin corruptions appears in other ancient sources and likely reflects actual patterns of behavior among the elite.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon similarly condemns drunkenness and the use of intoxicating drinks as signs of spiritual and social corruption. In Alma 1:32, the wealthy Zoramites 'did wear costly apparel...their hearts were set upon their riches' and they were 'lifted up in pride.' In the context of their pride, the text emphasizes their indulgence. In 4 Nephi 1:24-26, the decline of Nephite civilization is marked by both economic inequality and the pursuit of 'wine, and strong drink, and all manner of fine apparel.' Drunkenness and injustice appear as symptoms of the same spiritual deterioration.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 89 (the Word of Wisdom) directly addresses the problem of intoxicating substances and establishes that abstinence from alcohol is part of LDS covenant practice. The revelation frames the use of 'wine and strong drink' as incompatible with spiritual preparation and reception of God's guidance. D&C 29:49 warns against those who commit 'these things' (which includes various sins), suggesting that violation of the principle of temperance is part of the pattern of covenant breaking.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple recommend interview includes questions about the use of alcohol and harmful substances. Covenant members agree to abstain from alcohol as part of their temple commitment. Isaiah's indictment of those who make drink their pursuit resonates with the temple principle that the body is a sacred vessel dedicated to God, not an instrument of self-indulgence. The law of consecration, central to temple covenant, implicitly requires that one's resources (including time and attention) be dedicated to God's work, not to personal intoxication.

commentary.christological_typology: The intoxication that clouds judgment and separates a person from spiritual awareness prefigures the condition of those who reject the light of Christ. In John 12:40, Jesus applies Isaiah's words about blindness and deafness (Isaiah 6:10) to those who reject Him, suggesting that rejection of truth results in a kind of spiritual intoxication—a state in which one cannot perceive spiritual reality. The 'fire' that wine kindles in the drunken person parallels the spiritual fire that consumes those who substitute earthly pleasures for communion with God. Christ alone provides the true spiritual nourishment and clarity; intoxication (whether literal or spiritual) is separation from that source. In Revelation 14:10, the cup of God's wrath that the wicked drink parallels Isaiah's oracle: the very drink they pursued becomes their judgment.
commentary.application: For modern members, this verse addresses the use of alcohol and other intoxicating substances, established as forbidden in D&C 89. But beyond the specific prohibition of alcohol, the verse invites examination of whatever takes the place of God as the organizing principle of one's life. Is there any habit, pleasure, or pursuit that has become compulsive, that claims early rising and late evening, that 'inflames' you and clouds your judgment? The principle is not merely about substances but about the ordering of priorities: Those who organize their lives around self-gratification—whether through drink, consumption, entertainment, or other pursuits—have inverted the proper hierarchy. The verse challenges believers to examine whether they rise early to serve God and others, or whether their days are organized around self-service. The warning against drunkenness is ultimately a warning against any condition that separates us from God's presence and guidance, that 'inflames' us with passions that overwhelm our better judgment, and that results in loss of awareness of God's work in our lives and in the world. The application is concrete: the pursuit of intoxication was destroying the moral capacity of Judea's elite; modern versions of this same pathology—whatever pursuits consume our time and corrupt our judgment—must likewise be abandoned.

text_kjv: And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts; but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

commentary.narrative:
The third woe oracle (implied through the same structure and connection to the preceding woes, though 'woe' is not explicitly stated here) shifts from drunkenness to a broader indictment of sensory indulgence and spiritual blindness. Isaiah catalogs five elements of excess: lyre, harp, tambourine, flute, and wine. The specific enumeration of instruments creates a sense of lavish sensory indulgence—a symphony of pleasure devoted to feasting. The problem Isaiah identifies, however, is not music or celebration per se, but the willful blindness that such pleasure enables. The wealthy are anesthetized by luxury; they have become incapable of perceiving God's work in the world.

The second half of the verse pivots to the central charge: 'they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.' The phrase 'work of the LORD' (po'al YHWH) refers to God's acts in history—both past deliverances (like the exodus) and present judgments. The wealthy revelers are oblivious to both. They do not perceive the divine activity shaping history around them; they are too absorbed in their feasting to notice that God is executing judgment. Historically, this was written in the context of Assyrian imperial expansion, when astute observers should have been seeing God's hand in the rise of this threatening power. Instead, the wealthy continued to feast, indifferent to the approaching catastrophe.

The moral and spiritual point is devastating: pleasure itself has become a barrier to perception of God. The instruments are not themselves sinful (the temple itself was filled with music and instruments), but they become corrupt when they become the sole focus of attention and when they distract from covenant responsibility. The wealthy have replaced awareness of God's presence and work with sensory experience. They have made the feast their god and become blind to the actual God who is at work in judgment and redemption. This third woe connects backward: the land-grabber (v. 8) accumulates wealth; the drinker (v. 11) then devours that wealth in intoxication; now the wealthy person hosts lavish feasts with musical accompaniment, all the while remaining willfully blind to the God whose judgment is approaching. The three woes form a narrative of spiritual deterioration: injustice, indulgence, and finally, complete spiritual blindness.

word_study.meaning: String instruments. Kinnor (harp/lyre) appears frequently in the Bible for music in worship, celebration, and lament. Navel (viol/harp) is another string instrument. The exact distinction between them is unclear from the biblical text, but both were associated with music-making in formal contexts.
word_study.significance: The pairing of multiple string instruments emphasizes musical sophistication and expense—these are not simple instruments but those requiring skilled musicians and significant resources.

word_study.meaning: A percussion instrument, likely a hand drum or tambourine. Used in worship (2 Samuel 6:5), celebration (Exodus 15:20), and sometimes in lament.
word_study.significance: The addition of percussion to the string instruments creates a full orchestra of pleasure, suggesting comprehensive sensory indulgence.

word_study.meaning: A wind instrument, likely a pipe or flute. Used in various contexts including celebration (1 Kings 1:40), mourning, and possibly ritual worship.
word_study.significance: The addition of a wind instrument completes the orchestra, involving multiple types of instruments and multiple skilled musicians playing together.

word_study.meaning: A feast, banquet, or drinking party. Often associated with celebration but also with excess and self-indulgence. The root suggests drinking (שׁתה, shatah).
word_study.significance: The word suggests not merely a meal but a prolonged celebration centered on consumption of food and drink, with entertainment provided by musicians.

word_study.term_english: work of the LORD / operation of his hands
word_study.term_original: פֹּעַל יְהוָה / מַעֲשֵׂה יָדָיו (po'al YHWH / ma'aseh yadav)
word_study.meaning: God's work, acts, or deeds. Po'al suggests active intervention; ma'aseh (works) encompasses creative and providential action. Yadav (his hands) emphasizes God's direct agency and power.
word_study.significance: These phrases refer to God's self-revelation through historical events. The wealthy ignore both God's past deliverances (establishing their obligation to Him) and His present judgments (approaching catastrophe). They are willfully blind to the divine narrative within which they live.

word_study.meaning: To regard, look upon, or see (both terms can mean literally or figuratively). The doubled command emphasizes the failure to perceive: they do not look and they do not see.
word_study.significance: The use of two verbs for perception (looking and seeing) emphasizes comprehensive spiritual blindness. They have eyes but do not see; they have ears but do not hear (echoing Isaiah 6:9-10).

cross_references.connection: Isaiah's commission includes the declaration that the people have ears but will not hear, and eyes but will not see. Isaiah 5:12 is the lived reality of this spiritual blindness: pleasure anesthetizes the capacity to perceive God's work.

Jesus's parable of the rich fool, who builds larger barns and says 'Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry,' only to be told by God, 'Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee.' The man, like Isaiah's revelers, is anesthetized by plenty and does not perceive God's approaching judgment.

Amos's contemporary prophecy: 'Woe to them that are at ease in Zion...That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches...That drink wine in bowls...but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph.' The parallel to Isaiah 5:12 is striking: the comfortable wealthy are spiritually blind to injustice and to God's coming judgment.

Contrasts the faithful who 'are glad in the work of thy hands' with those whose thoughts are too shallow to understand God's deeds. Isaiah invokes the same principle: spiritual perception requires attention and mindfulness.

Modern revelation teaches that those who seek to counsel God rather than hearken to His word will be humbled, and that God's work is done in His own way, not in the ways the proud devise. Isaiah's revelers are engaged in precisely this kind of refusal to acknowledge God's work.

commentary.historical_context: In 8th-century Judah, feasting with musical entertainment was a marker of elite status. Archaeological evidence from Iron Age Levantine sites shows that the wealthy commissioned and maintained professional musicians. The biblical text provides examples: at David's court (1 Samuel 16:16-23), musicians played for the king; in the accounts of Solomon's reign, the text emphasizes music and entertainment as symbols of prosperity and power. Isaiah's condemnation of those who feast with elaborate musical accompaniment reflects actual practice among the Judean elite. The context of his oracle is the Assyrian threat: astute political observers in the late 8th century would have recognized that Assyrian expansion represented both a military threat and evidence of God's activity in history (Assyria was the rod of God's anger, Isaiah 10:5). Those preoccupied with feasting were perhaps literally unable to perceive the historical forces shaping their world. The contrast between elaborate music and the silence of spiritual perception parallels the contrast between sensory feast and moral famine.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon describes a strikingly similar pattern in 4 Nephi 1:24-36. After a long period of peace and righteousness, the Nephites become 'lifted up in pride' and begin 'to set [their hearts] upon their riches and their fine things.' The text states they 'did not believe in those signs and wonders which had been shown them,' directly paralleling Isaiah's indictment that those absorbed in feasting 'regard not the work of the LORD.' The Nephite pattern of indulgence followed by spiritual blindness mirrors the progression Isaiah describes. Further, in Helaman 6:17-18, the Nephites become so consumed by 'pride and the vain things of the world' that they fail to recognize the infiltration of the Gadianton robbers—a literal blindness that follows spiritual blindness. The Book of Mormon's repeated invocation of Isaiah's patterns suggests the author understood these as timeless warnings.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 63:49-52 warns against those 'who receive these things and fail to live up to them' and who are 'overcome by the world,' suggesting that possession of truth combined with worldly preoccupation results in spiritual failure. The principle Isaiah establishes—that sensory indulgence and spiritual perception are often in tension—appears throughout Restoration doctrine. D&C 121:37 teaches that 'when we undertake to cover our sins or to gratify our pride, our vain ambition, or to exercise control or dominion or compulsion upon the souls of the children of men, in any degree of unrighteousness, behold, the heavens withdraw themselves.' The withdrawal of divine presence follows pursuit of worldly satisfaction.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: While the temple is filled with beauty, order, and in some traditions music and art, its purpose is focused worship of God and covenant-making, not self-indulgent pleasure. The temple experience is meant to heighten perception of God's work and to clarify the individual's relationship to God's eternal purposes. Ritual beauty serves revelation; it is never meant to substitute for it. The contrast Isaiah draws—between elaborate sensory experience and perception of God's work—challenges temple-goers to use the temple's beauty and order not as an end in themselves but as a means to deeper communion with God and clearer understanding of His will.

commentary.christological_typology: The willful blindness of those anesthetized by sensory pleasure parallels the spiritual blindness of those who reject Christ's revelation. In John 9:39-41, Jesus states, 'For judgment I am come into this world...If ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth.' The wealthy revelers of Isaiah's oracle declare (implicitly) that they see—they see their feast, their musicians, their prosperity—but they are blind to the God whose work is written across history. This is the sin Jesus condemns: the refusal to acknowledge truth when confronted with it. Christ is God's supreme act in history—the ultimate 'work of the LORD' and 'operation of his hands'—and rejection of Christ is the ultimate instance of the spiritual blindness Isaiah describes. Yet the Gospel offers recovery: Christ's atonement restores sight to the blind (Matthew 11:5; John 9:1-7), both literally and spiritually. Those who perceive in Him the work of God are healed.
commentary.application: This verse challenges modern disciples to examine whether spiritual indulgence or distraction has made them blind to God's work in their lives and in the world. Do entertainment, consumption, and pleasure so dominate attention that we are no longer aware of God's providence? Do we fail to perceive His guidance because we are too absorbed in immediate gratifications? The verse does not condemn beauty, music, or celebration but challenges the assumption that these can substitute for spiritual awareness or that they are proper ends in themselves. For Latter-day Saints, the challenge is particularly acute in a society of unprecedented material plenty and constant sensory stimulation. The application asks: Am I, like the ancient revelers, surrounded by beauty and pleasure yet blind to the Lord's work in my life? Am I so focused on entertainment and consumption that I miss the spiritual significance of events in my own family, my community, my nation? Have I become so comfortable that I ignore injustice or the suffering of others? The verse invites a practice of deliberate spiritual attention: setting aside time to perceive God's work, to read and study scripture and history through the lens of His activity, and to align my choices with His purposes rather than with the pleasures that surround me.
