Finally, the verse reminds us that true perception of God's work is incompatible with willful blindness. If we are not seeing God's hand, the first question is not 'Why has God hidden Himself?' but 'What am I choosing to look at instead?'

text_kjv: Therefore my people are gone into captivity, because they have no knowledge: and their honourable men are famished, and their multitude dried up with thirst.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah shifts from indictment to consequence. The opening word 'Therefore' (לָכֵ֛ן, laken) marks the pivot from the six woes to their fulfillment. The prophet employs the 'prophetic perfect' — using past tense to describe future events with such certainty that they are spoken as already accomplished in God's decree. Israel will go into exile. This is not a threat; it is a pronouncement of what is already decreed in heaven.

The cause of this catastrophe is starkly simple: 'lack of understanding' (מִבְּלִי־דָ֑עַת, mibli-da'at). But this is not mere ignorance or intellectual dullness. In Hebrew covenant language, da'at (knowledge) means covenantal knowledge — intimate awareness of God and his requirements, the binding relationship between the LORD and his people. What Israel has lost is not information but relationship. The pleasure-seeking elite of verse 12, who 'regard not the work of the LORD,' have severed themselves from the knowledge that sustains covenant life.

The consequence falls first on the nobles and the masses alike. The word translated 'honourable men' (מְתֵ֣י, metei) literally means 'men of' — men of position and rank. Yet they starve. The masses are 'dried up with thirst' (צִחֵ֥ה צָמָֽא, tsikhah tzama) — a doublet emphasizing total depletion. Those who feasted are now famished; those surrounded by abundance face drought. The poetic justice is searing: they refused to see the work of the LORD's hands (v. 12), and now they experience deprivation so complete that it strips away all status and leaves only raw human vulnerability.

word_study.term_english: gone into captivity / go into exile
word_study.meaning: The root galah carries a dual semantic range: (1) to be 'uncovered,' 'stripped,' 'exposed,' and (2) to 'go into exile,' to be 'carried away.' Both senses operate simultaneously in prophetic judgment. Israel is both exposed — stripped of protection and glory — and deported. The verb form here is the qal perfect, expressing certainty of future fulfillment.
word_study.significance: Exile is the ultimate covenant curse spelled out in Leviticus 26:33 and Deuteronomy 28:36. Isaiah uses the term that encompasses both the shame (being stripped bare) and the removal (captivity). The Dead Sea Scrolls reading at 1QIsaᵃ confirms the MT consonantal text here, maintaining the prophetic force of the term.

word_study.meaning: Knowledge in the covenantal sense — not mere information but intimate, relational awareness of God's character, will, and claims. To 'lack knowledge' is to have severed the inner cord that binds creature to Creator. The phrase 'mibli-da'at' (from lack of knowledge) emphasizes deprivation — the absence of what should sustain life.
word_study.significance: This echoes Hosea 4:6, 'My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.' In Isaiah's theology, to reject the knowledge of God is to reject covenant relationship, and covenant severance brings exile. Modern readers often miss this: the problem is not stupidity but willful refusal of God's claim on their lives.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'men of' (construct form of 'ish', meaning persons). When followed by a qualifier (here implied: men of honor, rank, position), it denotes the social elite. The Covenant Rendering's 'nobles' captures the social dimension more clearly than 'honourable men,' which can sound archaic in English.
word_study.significance: The contrast is intentional: the very persons whose status and wealth should insulate them from hunger and thirst are the first to fall. Their elevation in the social order cannot protect them from covenant judgment.

word_study.meaning: A poetic doublet — 'parched with thirst' or 'dried up with thirst.' Tsikhah refers to being dried out, scorched; tzama means thirst. The pairing creates emphasis through repetition of a single concept: complete dehydration, the literal opposite of the abundant water and wine they celebrated.
word_study.significance: The language echoes wilderness imagery — the desert that tests and refines. Those who refused to acknowledge God's work now experience abandonment in a wasteland of their own making.

cross_references.connection: The foundational covenant curse: 'I will scatter you among the heathen... and your land shall be desolate.' Isaiah's 'galah' (exile) is the enforcement of the covenant curse for covenant-breaking.

The specific curse of deportation: 'The LORD shall bring thee, and thy king... into a nation which neither thou nor thy fathers have known.' Exile is the ultimate loss of the land promised to Abraham.

The parallel diagnosis: 'My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee.' Isaiah and Hosea both identify covenant knowledge (da'at) as the vital cord.

The paradox of wealth: 'The rich man's wealth is his strong city' — yet here, honor and wealth prove powerless against covenant judgment. Material security cannot substitute for relationship with God.
The Book of Mormon preserves Isaiah's prophecy: Nephi quotes this chapter almost verbatim, applying Isaiah's indictment to both ancient Israel and the latter-day world. The warning is perennial.

commentary.historical_context: The threat of exile would have been visceral to Isaiah's 8th-century audience. The northern kingdom of Israel fell to Assyria in 722 BCE, and Judah faced the same fate. Ancient Near Eastern imperial practice involved the systematic deportation of conquered peoples — not merely to punish but to break cultural continuity and prevent rebellion. Exile meant loss of land, loss of access to the Temple and covenant sacrifices, loss of political identity. To an ancient Israelite, exile was not a distant hypothetical; it was the fate that had already befallen their northern cousins and now threatened Judah. Isaiah's 'prophetic perfect' — speaking of exile as though it had already occurred — frames it as an inevitable decree that could still be averted if the people repent.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi quotes Isaiah 5:13 in 2 Nephi 15:13, preserving the prophecy for latter-day Israel. In the Book of Mormon context, this warning applies to the covenant people in all ages — the Nephites, the Gentiles who receive the Book of Mormon, and the house of Israel in the last days. The pattern is eternal: covenant knowledge (da'at) is the foundation of stability; its loss brings captivity.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:11 warns: 'Therefore, I have sent forth the fulness of my gospel by the hand of my servant Joseph Smith, Jun., in his hour and in his time.' The restoration of covenant knowledge through the Restoration is God's answer to the catastrophic loss of da'at that Isaiah describes. The Gospel Doctrine of the Restoration explicitly teaches that the keys and knowledge necessary for covenant relationship had been lost and were restored.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, the endowment communicates the knowledge (da'at in Hebrew terms) necessary for covenant life and exaltation. The loss Isaiah describes — severance from God's knowledge — is the antithesis of temple initiation. To enter the temple is to receive increased knowledge of God's character, will, and the path to his presence. To reject that knowledge, as Isaiah's people did, leads to captivity and separation from the sanctuary.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah's diagnosis of Israel's need — loss of covenantal knowledge — points to the solution that only Christ provides. Jesus is 'the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6); in him is contained all knowledge of God. The exile Isaiah pronounces is a type of the spiritual separation from God that all humanity experiences through sin. Christ's Atonement restores the severed relationship; his knowledge, imparted through the Spirit, is the antidote to the ignorance that brought Israel to ruin.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 13 is a piercing warning against the gradual erosion of spiritual knowledge. The phrase 'lack of knowledge' should trouble us: Are we maintaining active, living awareness of God's character and his requirements? Or are we allowing the demands of pleasure, comfort, and social status to subtly sever our covenant consciousness? The verse suggests that exile does not come suddenly but through the slow replacement of God-knowledge with other preoccupations. The antidote is deliberate cultivation of covenantal awareness — daily scripture study, sincere prayer, attendance at the temple, and willingness to see God's hand in all things. The 'honourable men' and 'multitude' who experience famine and thirst represent not merely ancient Judah but any community — or individual — that has substituted status and plenty for the knowledge of God that alone sustains.

text_kjv: Therefore hell hath enlarged herself, and opened her mouth without measure: and their glory, and their multitude, and their pomp, and he that rejoiceth, shall descend into it.

commentary.narrative:
The vision expands from the political and social plane to the cosmic. Isaiah personifies Sheol — the Hebrew abode of the dead — as a ravenous beast with an insatiable appetite. The word 'hell' in the KJV is a significant translation choice (and limitation). In Hebrew, Sheol (שְׁאוֹל) is not the later Christian concept of hell as a place of active punishment; it is the shadowy, diminished realm of the dead where all humans eventually descend, regardless of moral status. Here, Sheol becomes a living monster, its jaw unhinged, its hunger boundless.

Isaiah's personification is deliberately grotesque and terrifying. Sheol enlarges itself (הִרְחִ֤יבָה, hirchibbah — a qal perfect, suggesting the inevitable opening of death's maw), opens its mouth 'without measure' (לִבְלִי־חֹ֑ק, libli-chok), and swallows everything that humanity valued. The four items that descend — 'glory' (הֲדָרָ֧הּ, hadarah), 'multitude' (הֲמוֹנָ֛הּ, hamonah), 'pomp' (שְׁאוֹנָ֖הּ, she'onah), and 'he that rejoiceth' (עָלֵ֥ז, allez) — are not abstractions. They correspond directly to the sins enumerated in the preceding verses: the land-grabbers' estates, the drunken revelers, the self-indulgent elite who celebrate their own cleverness and strength.

What makes this verse theologically devastating is its reversal of all human hierarchy. Kings, nobles, commoners — all descend into the same shadowy realm. Death is the great leveler, and Sheol's hunger knows no distinction. The passage implies that covenant judgment does not merely bring political exile; it brings death itself. The people perish, and their glory — everything they built and celebrated — is consumed into silence.

word_study.meaning: The Hebrew abode of the dead — not a place of punishment in the Christian sense, but a shadowy underground realm where all humanity descends after death. Sheol is often conceived as a vast pit or grave, a place of diminished existence, silence, and forgetting. In the Hebrew Bible, Sheol is morally neutral (both righteous and wicked go there), though by the late Second Temple period, Jewish thought increasingly differentiated compartments within Sheol.
word_study.significance: The KJV's 'hell' is a problematic translation that imports Christian eschatology into an OT text. Sheol is better understood as 'the grave' or 'the realm of the dead.' In Isaiah's context, Sheol represents the ultimate consequence of covenant-breaking: not merely political exile but the extinction of the nation, the end of generational continuity, the silencing of the people's voice. To descend into Sheol is to cease to exist in any meaningful sense.

word_study.meaning: Qal perfect of rachab, meaning 'to widen,' 'to enlarge,' 'to make room.' The feminine form agrees with Sheol (grammatically feminine in Hebrew). The image is of Sheol stretching its jaws wider, expanding its capacity to receive the dead.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests that Sheol is not merely present but actively reaching, gaping — an agent of consumption rather than a passive receptacle. This personification transforms death from a natural inevitability into an active, hungry force.

word_study.meaning: Pa'ar means 'to open wide,' 'to gape.' Piyah is 'mouth.' Libli-chok is 'without measure,' 'without limit' — literally 'for no boundary.' The phrase combines the image of a beast's jaws opening beyond all natural limit, suggesting Sheol's insatiable and boundless hunger.
word_study.significance: The phrasing echoes imagery from ancient Near Eastern mythology of chaos monsters (like the Leviathan) whose mouths threaten to consume all creation. Isaiah appropriates this mythological language to describe the consequence of covenant-breaking: the chaos of death itself becomes the instrument of judgment.

word_study.term_original: הֲדָרָ֧הּ הֲמוֹנָ֛הּ שְׁאוֹנָ֖הּ עָלֵ֥ז (hadarah hamonah she'onah allez)
word_study.meaning: Hadarah = splendor, honor, majesty; hamonah = multitude, throng, abundance; she'onah = tumult, noise, riotous celebration; allez = those who revel, who are exultant. These four terms encapsulate the excess and self-celebration of the elite described in vv. 8-12.
word_study.significance: The specificity is crucial. Isaiah is not describing the descent of abstract humanity into death but the concrete descent of the unjust wealthy, the revelers, the proud. Their specific sins — their hoarding, their celebration, their noise — are what Sheol swallows. The moral order is preserved even in death: those who lived by excess experience final emptiness.

cross_references.connection: A parallel meditation on death's leveling power: 'Notwithstanding a man vain in his honour abideth not... Yet God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave.' The psalmist, like Isaiah, contrasts human pride with the reality of Sheol's claim on all.

Qohelet catalogs human achievement and celebration — wealth, wine, honor, works — only to conclude: 'All is vanity.' Isaiah's vision of Sheol swallowing these things directly illustrates the Preacher's diagnosis.

Nephi's vision includes the destruction of those who 'sought the lusts of the flesh and the things of the world.' Isaiah's Sheol imagery anticipates the final judgment of those who chose covenant-breaking.

The Book of Mormon teaches that death will come upon the transgressor, and all souls will be brought to a state of accountability. Sheol, in Isaiah's vision, is part of that accountability — the end of human pretense and pride.

The revelation on hell distinguishes between Sheol (the temporary state of all souls) and outer darkness (reserved for the sons of perdition). Isaiah's Sheol foreshadows the cosmic accountability that D&C clarifies.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern texts (Ugaritic, Akkadian, Egyptian) also personify death and the underworld as a devouring force. The underworld in these cultures is imagined as a mouth, a pit, a place of no return. Isaiah draws on this common mythological language but applies it specifically to covenant judgment. The threat would have resonated with his audience: death is not merely a natural process but a consequence, a judgment. The imagery also reflects the political reality of 8th-century warfare — invasion, conquest, and mass deportation often meant death for many. Sheol was not a distant abstraction; it was the concrete fate of those swallowed by empire.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon's understanding of Sheol and resurrection theology enriches Isaiah's vision. Alma 40 describes Sheol as a temporary state ('a state of the soul between death and the resurrection'), contrasting it with later Christian concepts of hell. Alma 40:13-14 teaches that 'a state of happiness or a state of misery' awaits in Sheol, implying that even the intermediate state carries moral consequences — a development that illuminates what Isaiah means by Sheol swallowing the proud.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:41-42 reveals that 'it came to pass that Adam, being tempted of the devil, and he hearkened unto the temptation, and transgressed the commandment... wherefore, he was shut out from the presence of the Lord.' The expulsion from God's presence — spiritual death — is the precursor to physical death and descent into Sheol. D&C 76 further clarifies the ultimate fate of the rebellious and covenant-breakers.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple language, to be 'taken from the presence of the Lord' (expelled from the temple, the place of God's presence) mirrors the descent into Sheol — a state of separation from the divine. The descent into Sheol is the ultimate consequence of rejecting the covenants and the knowledge of God that the temple conveys.

commentary.christological_typology: Sheol, in its devouring hunger, represents the cosmic consequence of sin — what Paul calls 'the sting of death' (1 Corinthians 15:55-57). Christ's Resurrection is the ultimate answer to Sheol's claim. By descending into Sheol (the realm of death) and rising again, Christ transforms death from a place of final silence into a place of passage. His Resurrection opens the way for all humanity to ascend from Sheol. Thus, what Isaiah presents as judgment — Sheol's irresistible consumption — Christ converts into redemption: death is no longer the end but a transition within a larger covenant narrative.
commentary.application: Verse 14 confronts modern members with the reality that earthly achievements, status, and celebrations are temporary. The 'glory, multitude, pomp, and revelers' that Isaiah describes parallel the modern pursuit of wealth, influence, social status, and pleasure — the things that capture contemporary attention and energy. The verse invites a penetrating question: What have I built my life around? What do I celebrate and pursue? If I am investing primarily in things that Sheol will swallow, am I truly living according to covenants? The verse does not counsel joylessness or asceticism, but it does counsel reorientation: invest in things of eternal significance — relationships, righteousness, service, spiritual knowledge — that transcend the grave. The fact that Isaiah emphasizes the undoing of human pride in this verse should prompt reflection on where we harbor subtle pride in our own accomplishments and status.

text_kjv: And the mean man shall be brought down, and the mighty man shall be humbled, and the eyes of the lofty shall be humbled:

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah's vision continues to widen, now encompassing a complete reversal of human hierarchy. The verb in the Hebrew is שַׁח (shach), meaning 'to bow,' 'to be brought low,' 'to be humiliated.' The action moves from passive consequence (in v. 13) to active humiliation — Israel's people do not merely experience scarcity; they are actively brought low. The leveling is total and inescapable.

The verse employs a triadic structure that encompasses humanity in its entirety: adam (אָדָ֖ם, 'humanity' in its general, collective sense), ish (אִ֑ישׁ, 'each individual person'), and 'the eyes of the lofty' (eyes of those who look down on others). No category escapes. The general term 'humanity' and the particular term 'each person' ensure that both the species and the individual are subject to the same humiliation. But Isaiah does not stop there; he specifically targets the lofty — those whose very gaze is elevated, who literally look down. Their eyes are cast down.

This verse is theologically significant because it presents humiliation not as an unfortunate byproduct of exile but as an essential and comprehensive transformation wrought by judgment. The people who exalted themselves (v. 11) are comprehensively brought low. What appears to be mere political consequence is in fact cosmic moral reordering. And critically, the verse anticipates Isaiah's great theme in chapter 2: the exaltation of God alone and the humiliation of all human pride.

word_study.meaning: Qal perfect, meaning 'to bow,' 'to be brought low,' 'to be humiliated.' The root conveys both the physical gesture of bowing (lowering one's body before someone of superior status) and the spiritual state of humility or shame. In this context, the lowering is involuntary — judgment, not willing submission.
word_study.significance: The verb is used throughout Isaiah for the reversal of human pride. In 2:11, 'the lofty looks of man shall be humbled.' In 5:15, the same comprehensive humbling occurs. The consistency of vocabulary underlines that this is a deliberate pattern: God's judgment always involves the reversal of human exaltation.

word_study.meaning: The term adam refers to humanity in general, the human species, or humankind as a collective. It is the same word used in Genesis 1-2 for human creation. In this context, it denotes the universal nature of the humbling — all humanity, not merely Israel's elite or a particular class.
word_study.significance: Isaiah's use of adam suggests that the humiliation reaches the level of creation itself — reversing the exaltation of humanity that began with creation. Those made in God's image are reminded, through judgment, of their dependence and creatureliness.

word_study.meaning: The term ish means 'man,' 'person,' or 'each individual.' It is more specific and particular than adam. While adam encompasses humanity generally, ish emphasizes the individual person. The pairing ensures that both the collective and the particular are subject to humbling.
word_study.significance: The progression from the general (humanity) to the particular (each person) emphasizes that humbling is not a statistical phenomenon affecting the majority but a universal transformation affecting every individual. No one escapes.

word_study.meaning: Einei = eyes; gvohim (from gavah) = high, lofty, exalted. The phrase 'eyes of the lofty' is a synecdoche — the eyes represent the proud gaze of those who look down on others. In the ancient world, as in modern society, to 'lift one's eyes' or to have 'high eyes' was a gesture and symbol of pride and superiority.
word_study.significance: Isaiah specifically targets the visual expression of pride. The lofty are not merely tall or powerful but are characterized by the arrogant gaze — the refusal to lower one's eyes in humility before God or in recognition of others' dignity. Their punishment involves the literal casting down of those eyes.

cross_references.connection: The fuller development of the theme: 'The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.' Verse 15 previews what Isaiah expands in chapter 2.
Among the things the Lord hates: 'A proud look.' Isaiah's targeting of 'the eyes of the lofty' directly addresses the proud gaze that Proverbs identifies as abominable to God.

The apostle echoes Isaiah: 'God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble... Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God.' The pattern Isaiah describes — the humbling of the proud and exaltation of the humble — becomes a foundation of NT ethics.
Nephi's quotation of Isaiah 2:11 in the Book of Mormon preserves the theme for latter-day Israel: the exaltation of God and humiliation of human pride is a perennial covenant principle.

Alma teaches that 'whosoever shall humble himself shall be exalted; and whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased.' The Book of Mormon makes explicit what Isaiah implies: humiliation and exaltation are moral laws of the cosmos.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern culture, the 'high look' or 'raised eyes' was a marker of royal authority, military superiority, and social dominance. Sumerian and Akkadian texts describe victorious kings with 'raised eyes' and defeated enemies with 'lowered eyes.' Isaiah's language would have resonated at both the literal and symbolic levels: to be brought low meant both a loss of military power and a loss of the visual dignity associated with status. The triadic structure (humanity, each person, the lofty) also reflects a deliberate pedagogical strategy in ancient wisdom literature: stating a concept generally, then in particulars, to emphasize universality and inevitability.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly teaches the law of exaltation and abasement that Isaiah articulates. Alma 32 develops this into a principle of spiritual growth: humility is the prerequisite for receiving God's word and being exalted. The Book of Mormon suggests that Isaiah's prophecy of humbling is not merely punishment but a necessary spiritual condition — one cannot receive truth and grace while maintaining pride. Verse 15's comprehensive humbling is thus both judgment and invitation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 112:14 teaches: 'Beware of pride, lest thou shouldst enter into temptation.' The humbling that Isaiah describes in verse 15 is what D&C warns the Saints to avoid by proactively adopting humility. In the latter-day context, the principle remains: those who humble themselves voluntarily (through repentance and covenant-making) avoid the involuntary humbling that comes through judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is a place where all who enter — regardless of status, wealth, or worldly position — are equal before God. The ritual dressing and undressing, the removal of worldly distinctions, the universal covenants taken by all — these symbolize the leveling described in verse 15. In the temple, all who covenant with God experience the humbling that Isaiah describes as the consequence of judgment. But in the temple, this humbling is redemptive and voluntary.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ embodies the reversal of this pattern. Though he 'thought it not robbery to be equal with God' (Philippians 2:6), he 'humbled himself, and became obedient unto death' (Philippians 2:8). His voluntary humiliation — not as punishment but as redemptive choice — becomes the pathway to his exaltation. The pattern Isaiah describes (humbling as consequence of pride and covenant-breaking) is transformed in Christ: humbling becomes the pathway to exaltation for those who follow him. His Incarnation and Atonement reverse the equation — willingness to be brought low becomes the way to be lifted up.
commentary.application: For modern members, verse 15 invites honest self-examination about hidden pride. The 'eyes of the lofty' represents not merely outward arrogance but the subtle, internal attitude that places ourselves above others or above God's requirements. Where do I look down on others? In what ways do I hold my gaze elevated, refusing to truly see those I consider beneath me? The verse suggests that such pride — whether manifested in dismissiveness toward the poor, condescension toward those of different backgrounds, or resistance to submitting to God's prophets — is subject to humbling. The application, however, is not fatalistic. If we voluntarily humble ourselves — seek to serve others, genuinely listen, acknowledge our dependence on God — we can avoid the involuntary humbling that Isaiah describes. The key is recognizing that exaltation comes through humility, not despite it.

text_kjv: But the LORD of hosts shall be exalted in judgment, and God that is holy shall be sanctified in righteousness.

commentary.narrative:
The vision pivots decisively. Verses 13-15 focus on the humbling of humans; verse 16 shifts to the exaltation of God. This is not a new topic but the obverse side of the same reality. When human pride is leveled, God is exalted. When humans experience humiliation, God's holiness is revealed and set apart (sanctified). The word 'But' (ו, vav conjunctive) marks the turning point — while humanity falls, the LORD rises.

Isaiah presents two parallel statements about God's exaltation: (1) 'the LORD of hosts shall be exalted in judgment' (משְׁפָּ֑ט, mishpat), and (2) 'God that is holy shall be sanctified in righteousness' (בִּצְדָקָֽה, bitsedaqah). The first highlights the mode: God is exalted through his judicial acts — through judgment. The second amplifies and clarifies: the 'Holy God' (הָאֵל הַקָּדוֹשׁ, ha'El haqqadosh) sanctifies himself, manifests his holiness, through righteous acts.

What makes this verse theologically crucial is its insistence that God's judgment is not arbitrary violence but the expression of justice and righteousness. The very qualities Israel lacked — mishpat (justice) and tsedaqah (righteousness) — are precisely what characterize God's act of judgment. God does not merely punish the wicked out of power or anger; he judges them out of justice. His judgment is an expression of his holiness. To see God's judgment is to see God's character — not his vengeance but his righteousness revealed.

word_study.meaning: YHWH (the covenant name of God) of hosts/armies. Tsebaot refers to the heavenly armies, the stars, the powers of the cosmos under God's command. The title emphasizes God's sovereignty over all cosmic forces and his role as commander of creation.
word_study.significance: Isaiah uses this title repeatedly to assert that God's authority over judgment is cosmic in scope — not merely political but extending to all creation. The 'hosts' are subject to God's command; thus his judgment will be executed with absolute certainty.

word_study.meaning: Qal perfect, meaning 'to be exalted,' 'to be high,' 'to be lifted up.' The root suggests elevation and separation — to stand above and apart. When God is 'exalted,' he is distinguished, set apart, revealed as supreme.
word_study.significance: The same root used for human exaltation in v. 11 ('exalt themselves') is now applied to God. What the wicked attempted — to exalt themselves — God accomplishes in truth. The reversal is complete: human self-exaltation is replaced by God's genuine exaltation.

word_study.meaning: Justice, judgment, the act of judging rightly. Mishpat encompasses both the process of justice and the outcome — a righteous verdict. In Isaiah and throughout the Hebrew Bible, mishpat is one of the pillars of God's character and the foundation of a just society.
word_study.significance: The irony of verse 16 is sharp: the people of verse 7 who 'wait for judgment' (mishpat) expecting vindication find that judgment itself becomes their undoing. This is because true mishpat is against injustice, and they are unjust. God's judgment is righteous; theirs was not.

word_study.meaning: The Holy God. Qadosh (holy) means 'set apart,' 'separated,' 'sanctified.' It indicates a state of being fundamentally different from and transcendent to the common and ordinary. God is holy — he is wholly other, distinct from all creation, without moral blemish or compromise.
word_study.significance: This is Isaiah's characteristic way of referring to God: not merely 'God' but 'the Holy One' or 'the Holy God.' For Isaiah, holiness is God's defining attribute — it encompasses both his transcendence and his moral perfection. Israel's failure to honor God's holiness (v. 12, 'regard not the work of the LORD') brings judgment that manifests God's holiness.

word_study.meaning: Nifal perfect of qadash, meaning 'to be sanctified,' 'to be set apart (as holy),' 'to show himself holy.' The nifal voice indicates that God's holiness is revealed, demonstrated, displayed — not hidden. When God judges righteously, his holiness becomes visible and evident.
word_study.significance: The theological subtlety is profound: God does not become holy through judgment; he becomes known as holy. His holiness is revealed in the righteous acts that constitute judgment. This connects to Isaiah's larger vision: judgment itself is an act of revelation, making visible the divine character that had been ignored or denied.

word_study.meaning: Righteousness, right action, vindication of the innocent, and condemnation of the guilty. Tsedaqah is both an abstract quality (right living) and a concrete action (setting things right). In the context of judgment, it means the restoration of justice by condemning the wicked.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that the very virtues Israel lacked — mishpat and tsedaqah (justice and righteousness) — are precisely what characterize God's judgment. God judges because he is righteous; the judgment itself is the manifestation of righteousness.

cross_references.connection: The seraphim cry, 'Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.' Isaiah's vision of God's holiness and majesty, which follows immediately after chapter 5, is the culmination of this verse's promise that God's holiness will be revealed through judgment.

A parallel hymn: 'The LORD reigneth... he is high above all the people... they celebrate thy great and terrible name; for it is holy. The king's strength also loveth judgment.' God's holiness and justice are inseparable, as Isaiah asserts in verse 16.

Paul applies this principle to Christ's Atonement: God 'to declare his righteousness... that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.' God's judgment through Christ reveals both his justice and his righteousness — the very connection Isaiah draws.

In the Doctrine and Covenants, the Saints are taught to 'prepare yourselves, and... sanctify yourselves... that your faith and diligence and prayers may turn away the wrath of God.' The revelation assumes the principle Isaiah articulates: God's judgment is an expression of his righteousness and holiness.

Jacob, commenting on Isaiah's prophecies, emphasizes: 'O the greatness of the mercy of our God, the Holy One of Israel!' The title and concept Isaiah uses in verse 16 become a refrain in the Book of Mormon, emphasizing God's holiness as the foundation of his righteous judgment.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, divine justice was a key legitimation of kingship. Hammurabi's Code, for example, is framed as an expression of the god Shamash's righteousness; the king enacts divine justice. Isaiah invokes a similar framework but radically reorients it: the true king is the LORD, and his justice will be revealed through the judgment that topples the human rulers who have perverted mishpat and tsedaqah. This is a profound challenge to the political ideology of Isaiah's time, which often assumed that human rulers (especially the Davidic kings of Judah) were the agents of divine justice. Isaiah insists that God himself, not human rulers, is the true upholder of justice.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes repeatedly that God's judgments are righteous and his justice cannot be denied. Alma 42:22-24 explains the mechanism: 'There is a law given, and a punishment affixed, and a repentance granted... thus the meaning of the law is fulfilled.' The judgment Isaiah describes in verse 16 is, in the Book of Mormon's theology, the manifestation of an eternal law of justice and righteousness. God does not judge capriciously but according to an eternal principle that has been announced.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:45-46 teaches that the power of the priesthood is exerted 'by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned; by kindness, and pure knowledge.' This describes how God's priesthood power — and by extension, God's judgment — operates through righteousness, not arbitrary power. The principle Isaiah articulates in verse 16 is made explicit in the Restoration: God's exaltation comes through righteousness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, God is represented as the judge who sees all, knows all, and judges all according to righteousness. The covenants taken in the temple place the participant under the judgment of God — not a fearful prospect if one is righteous, because God's judgment upholds and protects those who keep covenant. Verse 16's assertion that God is exalted through justice means that the temple covenant-making itself is an expression of God's justice and holiness revealed.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is God's ultimate manifestation of righteousness (tsedaqah) and justice (mishpat). The Apostle Paul writes that Christ was 'made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption' (1 Corinthians 1:30). In the Atonement, God's justice is satisfied (Christ pays the debt of sin) and God's righteousness is vindicated (Christ's perfect obedience fulfills the law). Through Christ, God is exalted and his holiness is revealed. Thus, what Isaiah describes as God's exaltation through judgment finds its ultimate expression in Christ's redemptive judgment — the judgment that condemns sin but vindicates the repentant.
commentary.application: For modern members, verse 16 offers both comfort and warning. The comfort: God judges from righteousness, not caprice or anger. The warning: that righteousness, not human status or wealth, is the basis of God's judgment. The application is twofold. First, seek to understand what righteousness (tsedaqah) and justice (mishpat) mean in God's economy. Do not substitute our cultural or personal definitions of what is right; rather, study the law and the prophets to align our understanding with God's. Second, recognize that submission to God's righteous judgment is actually freedom — freedom from the fear that unjust rulers or circumstances can ultimately harm us, because there is a God of justice above all earthly powers. The verse calls us to trust in God's righteousness and to work, in our own spheres, to manifest justice and righteousness in our dealings with others.

text_kjv: Then shall the lambs feed after their manner, and the waste places of the fat ones shall strangers eat.

commentary.narrative:
The vision returns to the concrete, pastoral plane. After the cosmic images of Sheol and divine judgment, Isaiah presents a deceptively simple tableau: lambs grazing, strangers eating in the ruins of wealthy estates. The word 'Then' (וְ, vav conjunctive, marking sequence) indicates that this is the historical consequence of the spiritual realities described in verses 13-16. The prophecy moves from the metaphysical to the physical — we see what judgment looks like in terms of property, land use, and social displacement.

The image is constructed as a deliberate inversion of the land-grabbing described in verse 8. The 'owners' who 'join house to house, and lay field to field, till there be no more room' are now dispossessed. Their 'fat' estates — carefully cultivated lands, vineyards, orchards — become sheep pasture. 'Strangers' (גָּרִ֥ים, garim — foreigners, the displaced, those without property rights) now feed on what the wealthy once controlled. The word 'feed' (יֹאכֵֽלוּ, yokhelu) applies equally to lambs and strangers — both consume the land the mighty once claimed as their own.

What makes this verse theologically significant is its refusal to allow moral judgment to remain abstract. Injustice has concrete, visible consequences. The social order that elevated the wealthy and marginalized the poor will be inverted. Those who dispossessed others will be dispossessed. The land that was privatized and monopolized will return to common use — even if that use is merely grazing lambs. The 'waste places' (מְחִ֖ים, mechim) are not merely empty; they are the ruins of the mansions described in verse 9.

word_study.meaning: Rau (qal perfect of ra'ah) means 'to feed,' 'to graze,' 'to pasture.' Kvasim (plural of keves) means 'lambs' — the young of sheep, representing gentleness, innocence, and vulnerability. The verb describes the simple, natural activity of pastoral life.
word_study.significance: The use of lambs rather than other animals is significant: lambs do not represent strength or power but rather humble, innocent life. Where the proud once ruled, the meek now graze. This anticipates Matthew 5:5, 'Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.'

word_study.term_english: after their manner / as in their own pasture
word_study.meaning: Literally 'according to their word,' 'according to their speech/manner.' The phrase suggests that the lambs will graze naturally, as they do in their native pastures — unrestricted, belonging to the place. The Covenant Rendering's 'as in their own pasture' captures the sense of freedom and rightfulness.
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes that the grazing is natural and proper — not an invasion or aberration but a restoration of the land to its natural use. The lambs belong there in a way the dispossessed landowners no longer do.

word_study.meaning: Plural of michi or mechai, referring to desolation, ruins, waste places. The term appears elsewhere in Isaiah (e.g., 49:19) to describe land that has been destroyed or abandoned. Here it refers specifically to the ruins of the estates of the wealthy.
word_study.significance: The word emphasizes that the inversion is not merely a change of use but a destruction. The carefully maintained estates of the rich become wasteland — fitting punishment for those who consolidated wealth at others' expense.

word_study.meaning: The KJV's 'fat ones' is a difficult translation. The Covenant Rendering's 'wealthy' is more likely correct, interpreting the term as referring to the rich, the prosperous, those who 'grew fat' on their acquisitions. The metaphorical use of 'fat' to mean 'prosperous' or 'wealthy' is attested in other biblical texts.
word_study.significance: Whether the term refers to 'fat livestock' owned by the wealthy or to the wealthy themselves (who have become metaphorically 'fat' through accumulation), the sense is the same: those who prospered through injustice will lose their prosperity.

word_study.meaning: Plural of ger, meaning 'foreigners,' 'sojourners,' 'aliens' — those without property rights or social status, often dependent on the charity of landowners. In ancient Israel, resident aliens were a vulnerable population, frequently the subject of protective laws (Exodus 22:21, etc.).
word_study.significance: The use of 'strangers' to describe those who feed in the ruins suggests a complete social inversion. The marginalized, the propertyless, the vulnerable become the ones who have access to the land. The land passes from private ownership (and hoarding) to use by those without claims — almost a return to the idea that the land belongs to God and its use should be open to all.

cross_references.connection: A similar image of the land restored after judgment: 'Happy are ye that sow beside all waters, that send forth thither the feet of the ox and the ass.' The humbled land becomes a place of simple pastoral life.

The law of the Sabbath year: the land is to lie fallow, and the poor and the beasts of the field are to eat the produce. Isaiah's image of lambs and strangers eating in the waste places echoes this covenantal principle that the land is not to be monopolized.

A proverb on just land use: 'Much food is in the tillage of the poor: but there is that is destroyed for want of judgment.' Isaiah's vision shows this principle being enforced: the lands of the unjust are rendered waste.

A reversal of power: 'As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women.' Similarly, Isaiah's image of the dispossessors being dispossessed reflects the principle that judgment reverses the wrongdoer's own actions.

The Book of Mormon teaches: 'Behold, it has been made known unto me by an angel, that the spirits of all men, as soon as they are departed from this mortal body, yea, the spirits of all men are taken home to that God who gave them life.' The restoration of land to humble use in Isaiah 5:17 foreshadows the cosmic restoration where all injustice is made right.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient agrarian societies, land was the primary form of wealth and power. The consolidation of land — whether through purchase, foreclosure, or outright seizure — was a common form of economic injustice in the ancient world and in the ancient Near East. Archaeological evidence suggests that in pre-exilic Judah, land concentration was indeed a problem, with small farmers losing holdings to wealthy elites. When conquest and deportation came, the land left behind would indeed have been reclaimed by the landscape — returning to pasture or becoming overgrown. Invaders and settlers would use it as they saw fit, often reducing it to pastoral use. Thus, Isaiah's prophecy reflects not merely theological ideal but historical possibility: conquest would literally reverse the property relations that had characterized pre-exile Judean society.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains striking parallels to Isaiah's vision of land reversal. In Helaman 7-8, Nephi prophesies the ruin of the Nephites because of their wickedness and land concentration. In Mormon 2, Mormon records the fulfillment: the land that the Nephites had consolidated is overrun by the Lamanites, and the carefully built civilization reverts to a simpler, more dispersed state. Isaiah's prophecy in verse 17 finds its application in Book of Mormon history.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 38:39 teaches: 'And the rich shall hear all these things and shall repent and come forth and make themselves known unto the Lord.' The revelation suggests that judgment is designed to bring about a turning from unjust accumulation. The restoration of land to common use (as in v. 17) is not merely punishment but a pathway toward justice and covenant renewal.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaching on stewardship — that we hold the earth as a stewardship from God, not as absolute private property — is reflected in verse 17's vision of land being restored to common use. In Doctrine and Covenants 104:14-16, the Saints are taught: 'I, the Lord, have made the earth rich... and all things therein are mine.' The consolidation described in verse 8 represents a violation of stewardship principles. The restoration in verse 17 is the correction.

commentary.christological_typology: The image of lambs feeding on the ruins of the wealthy suggests a reversal that points to Christ's teaching in Matthew 5:3-12 — the Beatitudes, which proclaim that the poor, the meek, the hungry, and those persecuted for righteousness are blessed. Christ comes to overturn the social order that exalts the wealthy and humiliates the poor. His kingdom is one where the last shall be first and the first shall be last. The vision of lambs (associated with innocence and vulnerability) inheriting the land that the mighty once hoarded is Christological in its orientation toward justice and reversal.
commentary.application: For modern members, verse 17 raises questions about wealth, property, and stewardship. It challenges a culture of private accumulation and asks: Are we consolidating land (or resources, or wealth) in ways that dispossess others of basic security and opportunity? Are we exercising stewardship or hoarding? The verse does not suggest that private property is inherently wrong, but it does suggest that when property consolidation becomes a means of oppressing others, it invites judgment. Conversely, the verse invites reflection on how the Church's law of consecration and stewardship — the principle that the earth and all things belong to God and we are stewards, not owners — represents a pathway toward justice. The verse also speaks to the notion of 'waste places' — areas of society that become neglected because they are no longer profitable or interesting to the wealthy. Isaiah suggests that such places will be reclaimed, not for the wealthy, but for the vulnerable. The application for members today is to consider: What 'waste places' exist in our communities? Whom are we leaving behind in our pursuit of prosperity?

text_kjv: Woe unto them that draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as it were with a cart rope:

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah introduces the third and most powerful woe oracle of the chapter. The opening 'Woe unto them' (הוֹי, hoi) marks this as a judicial pronouncement — not a curse, but a solemn warning of destruction. The image is visceral and deliberate: the people of Judah are pictured as creatures bound to a rope, hauling their own transgression behind them like oxen yoked to a plow or a cart. But here is the terrible irony: they are not being forced. They are voluntarily bound to their sin.

The phrase 'draw iniquity with cords of deceit' (מֹשְׁכֵ֥י הֶעָוֺ֖ן בְּחַבְלֵ֣י הַשָּׁ֑וְא) presents sin as something actively hauled, pulled, dragged forward. The word חַבְלֵ֣י (chavlei, 'cords') suggests thin, deliberate restraints — cords of their own making, spun from deceit (shav). Isaiah then escalates the image: 'and sin as with cart ropes' (וַכַּעֲב֥וֹת הָעֲגָלָ֖ה חַטָּאָֽה). Where the first line speaks of individual iniquities drawn by thin cords, the second line speaks of sin itself — the entire complex of transgression — being hauled with the thick, heavy ropes used for carts and plows.

The progression is from 'cords of deceit' to 'cart ropes.' What began as thin self-deceptions has become thick, heavy bondage. The image suggests that sin operates through a process: first, one entertains a lie (a cord of deceit), binding oneself loosely; then, as the lie is embraced and acted upon repeatedly, the bondage thickens and strengthens until one is yoked to sin itself like an ox to a cart. The people do not recognize that they are enslaved; they experience their sin-hauling as normal, as their mode of life. Yet they are deeply, powerfully bound.

This oracle reveals a fundamental truth about sin that the other woes hint at but do not make explicit: sin is self-imposed slavery. The sinners are the ones who have bound themselves with their own cords. They are simultaneously victims and perpetrators — victims of their own deceptions, perpetrators of the lies that bind them.

word_study.meaning: An interjection expressing lamentation, warning, or condemnation. It is often translated 'woe' and marks a prophetic pronouncement of doom or warning. In Isaiah 5, the word introduces six distinct oracles (vv. 8, 11, 18, 20, 21, 22), each naming a specific transgression.
word_study.significance: The repeated use of hoi (six times in Isaiah 5) creates a rhythmic, liturgical effect — almost like a funeral dirge or a series of condemnations. Each woe is a distinct warning, but together they form a comprehensive indictment of the society.

word_study.meaning: Qal participle of mashak, meaning 'to draw,' 'to drag,' 'to pull.' The participle form suggests ongoing, habitual action — the people continuously, constantly draw/drag. They are characterized by this action.
word_study.significance: The use of the participle (rather than a simple verb) suggests that this is not a single transgression but a persistent way of life. The people are defined by their dragging of sin.

word_study.meaning: Iniquity, transgression, wickedness, the violation of covenant law. Avon encompasses both the act of transgression and the state of guilt resulting from it. It is the comprehensive term for covenant-breaking.
word_study.significance: Isaiah uses avon to describe the complex of injustices catalogued in the previous verses — the land-grabbing, the drunkenness, the pride, the mockery of God. These are not isolated sins but expressions of a single, pervasive iniquity against the covenant.

word_study.meaning: Plural of chevel, meaning 'rope,' 'cord,' 'line.' Chavlei specifically refers to cords or ropes, often used for binding or securing. The word can also mean 'allotment' or 'portion' (as in 'a measured rope marking a boundary'), but here it means literal cords binding.
word_study.significance: The image of cords is crucial: they suggest restraint, bondage, but also deliberate construction. These are not chains imposed from outside but cords people have spun themselves.

word_study.meaning: Vanity, emptiness, falsehood, deception. Shav refers to that which is false, without substance, insubstantial. In ethical contexts, it means the lies and deceptions that people embrace instead of truth and covenant reality.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'cords of deceit' captures the meaning better than 'cords of vanity.' Isaiah is saying that the binding agent — what holds people to their sin — is deceit. They believe lies about themselves, about God, about the world, and these lies bind them.

word_study.meaning: Sin, transgression, that which misses the mark (the fundamental meaning of the root). Chattaah is distinct from avon (iniquity) in that it emphasizes the missing of the target — the failure to conform to God's standard — rather than the guilt or state of corruption resulting from transgression.
word_study.significance: By the second line, Isaiah has shifted from 'iniquity' (avon) to 'sin' (chattaah) — from the guilt-state to the act of missing the mark. The escalation suggests that what began as specific transgressions (iniquity) has become a comprehensive, ongoing pattern of missing the mark (sin).

word_study.meaning: Avot (plural of av, 'rope,' 'cord,' but also 'power,' 'strength' when used metaphorically) haa'agalah (of the cart). This refers specifically to the thick, heavy ropes used to harness and control large, powerful animals like oxen yoked to a cart or plow. These are not delicate cords but heavy restraints.
word_study.significance: The progression from chavlei (thin cords of deceit) to avot (thick cart ropes) is key. What began as a subtle lie has become an overwhelming, heavy bondage. The image captures how sin, once embraced, becomes increasingly burdensome and inescapable.

cross_references.connection: Jesus teaches: 'Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.' Isaiah's image of being bound with ropes of sin anticipates Christ's teaching that sin is a form of slavery from which only truth can liberate us.

Paul echoes the principle: 'Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness?' The binding to sin that Isaiah describes is, in Paul's terms, yielding oneself as a servant to sin.

Peter warns: 'While they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption: for of whom a man is overcome, of the same is he brought in bondage.' The false prophets and teachers who had deceived Isaiah's people with lies are the agents who spin the 'cords of deceit.'

Lehi teaches: 'Wherefore, men are free... to choose liberty and eternal life, through the great Mediator of all men, or to choose captivity and death, according to the captivity and power of the devil.' The choice to be bound by 'cords of deceit' is explicitly a choice for captivity, the alternative to the liberty Christ offers.

Alma teaches: 'Therefore, my son, see that you are merciful unto your brethren; deal justly, judge righteously, and do good continually.' The antidote to the self-imposed bondage Isaiah describes is to 'deal justly' — to break free from the cords of deceit by embracing truth and justice.

commentary.historical_context: The concept of sin as bondage was common in both biblical and ancient Near Eastern literature. The idea that transgression enslaves the transgressor (rather than liberation or empowerment being the result) reflects ancient wisdom traditions. The specific image of hauling — dragging iniquity like a cart — would have resonated with an agrarian audience for whom the sight of oxen, bound and laboring under heavy loads, was daily. Isaiah invokes this familiar image to drive home the point: those who pursue transgression are not free agents but beasts of burden, bound to the very sins they embrace. The phrase 'cords of deceit' suggests false prophets, false doctrine, false hope — the lies told (perhaps by false prophets or by the elites themselves) that convinced people that their transgressions were acceptable or even virtuous.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly develops the theme of sin as bondage. In Mosiah 23:12-13, King Noah's people are warned about becoming 'servants unto sin,' yet they reject the warning. By Mosiah 24, they are explicitly in bondage — not merely spiritually but politically and militarily, as a consequence of their spiritual bondage. The Book of Mormon shows how the 'cords of deceit' (the false doctrines that Noah's priests taught) led to actual, tangible oppression and bondage. Isaiah's metaphorical image becomes literal history in the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:14-15 teaches: 'And I declare unto them things which have been written before them... that they are obligated to believe all the scriptures, all the Lord's words, which he hath given them.' The Lord's message through the Restoration is that truth, revealed through scripture and prophets, is the antidote to the 'cords of deceit.' Those who embrace the revealed word are freed from self-imposed bondage; those who reject it bind themselves with the cords of their own deceptions.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, initiates pass through different rooms and states, ultimately ascending to the highest state — the celestial room, which represents the presence of God and ultimate freedom/exaltation. The descent through the world (the telestial and terrestrial rooms) can be understood as the progressive binding that Isaiah describes: each transgression, each deception embraced, tightens the cords. The temple experience, by contrast, is a pathway to loosening those cords through covenant-making and alignment with divine truth.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is, in the language of John 8:34-36, the liberator from sin's bondage: 'If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.' Where Isaiah shows people bound with 'cords of deceit' of their own making, Christ offers liberation — not through law alone but through truth ('ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free'). The Atonement is the ultimate severing of sin's bonds. Christ breaks the cords that bind people to their transgressions by taking upon himself the consequences and offering forgiveness. His Resurrection is the ultimate proof that sin's bondage has been overcome.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 18 is a searching indictment of self-deception and self-imposed bondage. The verse asks: What lies are binding me? What false beliefs about myself, my circumstances, or my potential keep me enslaved? Where have I made a covenant (even unknowingly) with deception, accepting a lie as truth? The verse suggests that sin often works not through obvious coercion but through subtle deception — 'cords of vanity' that feel light at first but thicken over time. The application is threefold: (1) Awareness — recognize when you are beginning to embrace a deception or rationalization that serves a selfish interest; (2) Resistance — refuse the initial binding cord before it becomes a cart rope; and (3) Liberation — if you find yourself bound by patterns of sin and deception, seek through repentance, faith in Christ, and honest self-examination to break the cords. The verse also warns against complacency: those who 'draw iniquity' may not recognize their bondage. Regular repentance, scriptural study, and honest conversation with trusted mentors or Church leaders are means to break cycles of self-deception.

text_kjv: That say, Let him make speed, and hasten his work, that we may see it: and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw nigh and come, that we may know it!

commentary.narrative: Isaiah's second woe oracle shifts from economic injustice to spiritual defiance. These mockers are not atheists; they acknowledge God's existence and invoke his titles deliberately. Their taunt reveals the hardness that precedes judgment: 'Let him hurry! Let him speed up his work so we can see it!' This is brazen contempt dressed as a dare. They are essentially challenging God to make good on his threats—a challenge born from confidence in their own power and a refusal to believe that divine judgment will actually reach them. The repetition of 'let him...let the...come' creates a rhythmic mockery, as if they are mimicking God's word back at him in derision.
commentary.narrative_continued: The theological depth lies in what their mockery reveals: they understand that God's judgment is real and threatened, but they bet that either (1) God lacks the power to execute it, or (2) it will never touch them. This is not ignorance but willful rebellion. By invoking 'the counsel of the Holy One of Israel'—Isaiah's signature title for God, used over 25 times in the book—they knowingly invoke the very holiness that will destroy them. The irony is crushing: their own words will become prophecy when, in just a few verses, God's judgment arrives on the 'distant nation' (v. 26-30). Their mockery will be answered not by argumentation but by invasion.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: In the historical context of Isaiah's ministry (roughly 740–700 BCE), Jerusalem had experienced decades of relative stability and economic prosperity under King Uzziah (ruled c. 792–740 BCE). This prosperity bred complacency and a false sense of security. The mockers here are the wealthy, powerful, and influential—those with the most to lose. They have convinced themselves that power and wealth are proof of God's favor, not warnings of judgment. Their taunt is the voice of a nation that has forgotten the covenant and imagines itself immune to accountability.

word_study.meaning: To hurry, to act quickly. Yemaher emphasizes speed; yachisha conveys urgency and swiftness. The two verbs together create an intensified demand for immediate action.
word_study.significance: The repetition (speed, speed up) mimics the rhythm of a taunt, suggesting breathless mockery. These are not respectful requests but sarcastic demands, as if the mockers are stamping their feet like impatient children.

word_study.meaning: Counsel, plan, purpose—God's intentional will and design. In Hebrew thought, atzat is not mere advice but divine purpose unfolding according to plan.
word_study.significance: The mockers demand to 'see' and 'know' God's atzat, as if faith could be replaced by empirical observation. This reflects a fundamental spiritual blindness: the demand for proof replaces trust in the covenant.

word_study.meaning: Isaiah's characteristic title for God, emphasizing both transcendent holiness (separation from all that is profane or common) and covenant relationship with Israel specifically. Qedosh appears in Isaiah more than 25 times and rarely elsewhere in Scripture.
word_study.significance: The title itself represents the dynamic tension at the heart of Israel's covenant: God is absolutely holy (set apart, other), yet bound to Israel by covenant oath. The mockers invoke this title knowingly, making their defiance all the more audacious. They are mocking the very God who has chosen them.

cross_references.connection: Do not be wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and depart from evil.' The refusal to fear God and the self-sufficiency evident in Isaiah 5:19 stand in direct contradiction to Proverbs' core wisdom.

Knowing this first, that there shall come in the last days scoffers... saying, Where is the promise of his coming?' The New Testament echoes Isaiah's portrait of mockers who challenge God to prove his word.

Verily I say, let all things be done in order... he who doeth not anything until he is commanded, and receiveth a commandment with doubtful heart, and keepeth it not.' The mockers of Isaiah 5:19 exhibit the inverse: they reject God's clear word and demand proof on their own terms.
Korihor's taunt against God ('when ye see these things ye cannot deny them; therefore why talk ye about this book?') parallels the mockers' demand for immediate, visible proof in Isaiah 5:19.

commentary.historical_context: The prosperity of Uzziah's reign (c. 792–740 BCE) had made Judah wealthy and militarily strong. Archaeological evidence suggests significant building activity and economic expansion during this period. However, 2 Chronicles 26:16 records that 'when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction.' Isaiah's contemporaries, especially the merchant class and nobility, had grown accustomed to success and power. They had begun to treat God's covenant as a guarantee rather than a call to obedience. The mockers in verse 19 are confident precisely because they have never experienced consequences—and they believe they never will. Their taunt reflects the spiritual condition of a nation that has confused prosperity with righteousness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly warns against this same spirit of defiance. In 2 Nephi 28:14-15, Jacob records: 'They wear stiff necks and high heads; yea, even the rich and the learned, the wise and the honorable; but they are all laid low in the dust.' The mockers of Isaiah 5:19 are the spiritual ancestors of Laman and Lemuel, who demanded signs and challenged God's power on their own terms (1 Nephi 17:50).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 63:58 states: 'They who believe not shall not dwell in his glory.' The mockers of Isaiah 5:19 believe God exists but refuse to believe he will act. This is a faith problem, not an intellectual one—precisely the kind of lukewarmness condemned in D&C 63:54.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenant between God and Israel is renewed repeatedly in the temple. The mockers have broken this covenant mentally before they break it behaviorally—they have already rejected God's word in their hearts.

commentary.christological_typology: The mockers' demand for visible proof of God's power and counsel prefigures the later demand for a sign from Jesus in Matthew 12:38-39 ('we would see a sign from thee'). Christ's answer—that no sign will be given except the sign of Jonah (resurrection)—echoes Isaiah's refusal to perform on demand. Both the mockers of Isaiah and the sign-seekers of Matthew assume that faith follows proof; Scripture insists the reverse is true.
commentary.application: The spirit of verse 19 remains dangerously alive in modern life. It appears whenever we demand that God prove himself according to our timeline and expectations, whenever we assume our prosperity or success is proof of God's favor (or his irrelevance), and whenever we privately mock the warnings of Scripture while outwardly maintaining propriety. The verse calls us to examine our hearts: Are we trusting God's word, or are we testing God? Are we living by faith, or by the demand for visible proof? The mockers' fate—destruction by a distant army they could not foresee—teaches that those who refuse to hear God's counsel through his prophets will eventually be forced to see it through judgment.

text_kjv: Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!

commentary.narrative: The fourth woe oracle pronounces judgment on those who have inverted the moral categories themselves. This is not mere hypocrisy (saying one thing while doing another) but a deeper corruption: the systematic reversal of the very standards by which behavior is judged. Isaiah presents three pairs—evil/good, darkness/light, bitter/sweet—that cover the moral, perceptual, and sensory dimensions of human experience. When someone 'calls evil good,' they are not merely excusing wickedness; they are redefining the words themselves. This is more than propaganda; it is a collapse of the common language that allows society to function. When light becomes darkness in the collective speech of a people, the foundations of justice, beauty, and truth have been shaken.
commentary.narrative_continued: The repetition of the formula 'put X for Y' creates a hammering effect, driving home the totality of the corruption. There is no neutral ground. Every faculty by which humans comprehend reality—moral reasoning, visual perception, sensory experience—has been perverted. This is the logical conclusion of the arrogance displayed in verse 21 ('wise in their own eyes'): when you trust only yourself as the arbiter of value, you will eventually call evil good simply because you have decreed it so. The woe is pronounced not because God is arbitrary or temperamental, but because the mockers have cut themselves off from the only source of stable meaning: God's revealed word.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: Historically, this inversion of moral categories appears whenever a society attempts to justify systematic exploitation or oppression. In Isaiah's time, the wealthy were redefining 'righteousness' as wealth accumulation and 'justice' as the securing of advantage. The prophetic voice of Isaiah refuses this redefinition. He insists that 'evil' and 'good' are not negotiable, that 'light' and 'darkness' are not subjective categories, and that the 'bitter' taste of injustice cannot be repackaged as 'sweet.' The woe is a blast against relativism masquerading as sophistication.

word_study.meaning: To say, to speak, to declare. In this context, the verb carries the weight of performative speech—not merely opinion but authoritative declaration that shapes reality and behavior.
word_study.significance: The mockers are not passive thinkers but active speakers who reshape language itself. Their words are a form of power, and they wield this power to overturn moral reality.

word_study.meaning: Evil, wickedness, harm, badness—both moral wickedness and harmful consequences. Ra is the fundamental term for all that is contrary to God's order and covenant.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that ra encompasses moral and experiential badness. In Isaiah's woe, 'calling ra good' represents the ultimate corruption of moral reasoning—treating destructive behavior as beneficial.

word_study.meaning: Good, beautiful, beneficial—that which is in harmony with God's order, covenant, and design. Tov describes both moral goodness and functional excellence.
word_study.significance: The reversal of tov and ra is catastrophic because these terms are the fundamental moral vocabulary of Scripture. When they are inverted, the entire moral language collapses.

word_study.meaning: Darkness (choshek) = absence of light, blindness, confusion, judgment; Light (or) = clarity, truth, God's presence, blessing. These are not merely physical phenomena but metaphors for spiritual and moral reality.
word_study.significance: In Isaiah (and throughout Scripture), light and darkness are cosmic categories representing the conflict between God's order and rebellion against it. To call darkness light is to reverse the entire moral universe.

word_study.meaning: Bitter (mar) = harsh, unpleasant, mournful; Sweet (matok) = pleasant, delightful, satisfying. These terms cover sensory and emotional experience.
word_study.significance: The inclusion of sensory language (bitter/sweet) alongside moral (evil/good) and perceptual (darkness/light) categories suggests total corruption: no dimension of human experience remains trustworthy.

cross_references.connection: All the words of my mouth are in righteousness; there is nothing froward or perverse in them.' Wisdom's speech is the opposite of the mockers' inversion—truth and clarity rather than reversal and confusion.
Ye who turn judgment to wormwood, and leave off righteousness in the earth.' Amos names the same inversion: the twisting of justice (mishpat) into its opposite.

Woe unto you that call evil good, and good evil, that put darkness for light, and light for darkness, that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!' The Book of Mormon reproduces Isaiah's woe verbatim, emphasizing its timeless relevance to all God's people.
That wicked one cometh and taketh away light and truth through disobedience.' The reversal of light and darkness is not morally neutral—it is the work of Satan himself.

And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.' The New Testament echoes the choice between light and darkness as fundamental to the human condition.

commentary.historical_context: In the 8th century BCE ancient Near East, the manipulation of language was a tool of political power. Royal inscriptions from Assyria and Babylon frequently redefined reality through official language: defeats were called victories, conquests were portrayed as merciful acts. Isaiah's contemporaries in Jerusalem were engaged in a similar game—redefining justice and righteousness to serve their economic interests. The wealthy were calling their exploitation of the poor 'righteousness,' their oppression 'justice,' their greed 'blessing.' Isaiah's woe exposes this linguistic tyranny. In the context of verse 7 (the vineyard produces wild grapes when justice and righteousness are expected), verse 20 names what has happened: the very categories of judgment have been perverted. The society no longer knows how to recognize justice when it appears, nor can it see its own injustice.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 15:20 reproduces this woe in its entirety. The Book of Mormon's preservation of Isaiah's words in the New World context underscores the principle that these woes are not historical museum pieces but timeless warnings for all covenant peoples. Nephi and his descendants faced the same temptation to invert moral categories.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:29-33 describes the conditions of the latter days using language strikingly similar to Isaiah's woe: 'And there shall be men standing in that generation, that will not pass until they shall see an overflowing scourge; for a desolating sickness shall cover the land... And again, another angel shall sound his trump, saying: That great church, the mother of abominations, that made all nations drink of the wine of the wrath of her fornication, that church is the whore of all the earth.' The inversion of moral categories is precisely what characterizes Babylon/the great church.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, light and darkness, good and evil, are presented as ultimate cosmic categories. The veil itself represents the boundary between light (the celestial room) and relative darkness (the terrestrial/telestial). The mockers of Isaiah 5:20 have rejected this cosmic order.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus is the Light of the world (John 8:12), and his presence forces a crisis of moral vision: 'Now is the judgment of this world' (John 12:31). His coming makes it impossible to call darkness light or light darkness—his light reveals all things. The woe of Isaiah 5:20 prefigures the judgment that Christ's coming will execute: the inversion will be exposed and reversed.
commentary.application: This verse speaks powerfully to modern covenant members. In what ways has contemporary culture inverted moral categories? How do we distinguish between God's definitions of good/evil and the culture's? The temptation to call evil good appears in countless forms: redefining sexual morality as 'freedom,' treating the pursuit of wealth as 'success,' describing the abandonment of faith as 'enlightenment,' or calling the rejection of God's word 'tolerance.' The woe is not directed at those who make occasional errors in judgment but at those who systematically overturn the categories themselves—who have made a religion of the reversal. The challenge for modern believers is to cultivate the moral vision to see truly, to call things by their right names, and to resist the constant pressure to adopt the world's linguistic tyranny. We must ask: Are we calling good what God calls good? Are we seeing light as light?

text_kjv: Woe unto them that are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight!

commentary.narrative: The fifth woe oracle is the briefest and sharpest of the collection, and its brevity is itself a rhetorical weapon. No elaboration is needed. The indictment is complete in itself: self-sufficiency in wisdom is its own condemnation. Those who are 'wise in their own eyes'—who have made themselves the arbiter of truth and righteousness—stand under woe. The parallel phrase 'prudent in their own sight' (understanding only from their own perspective) reinforces the isolation of such people. They have cut themselves off from the only source of genuine wisdom: the fear of the LORD and submission to his revealed word.
commentary.narrative_continued: This woe is the logical culmination of verses 19-20. The mockers of verse 19 dare God to act because they trust their own judgment. The inverted moral categories of verse 20 are possible only for those who have enthroned themselves as judges. Verse 21 names the root sin: self-referential wisdom. In Hebrew thought, true wisdom (chokmah) is not the accumulation of knowledge or clever thinking but rather the fear of God and alignment with his order. The person 'wise in their own eyes' has abandoned this foundation and replaced it with ego. They have become a law unto themselves.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The historical background makes this woe even more pointed. The wealthy, educated elite of 8th-century Jerusalem prided themselves on their sophistication, their diplomatic skill, their economic acumen. They had 'figured out' how to prosper in a competitive world. They were the smart ones—they knew which alliances to make, which judges to bribe, which laws to exploit. They had no use for the warnings of an old prophet who spoke of covenant faithfulness and justice for the poor. Their 'wisdom' was precisely their blindness, their strength precisely their weakness. Isaiah's woe announces that genuine foolishness masquerades as wisdom when it refuses submission to God.

word_study.meaning: Wise, skillful, prudent—one who possesses chokmah (wisdom). In Hebrew thought, true wisdom is not mere intelligence but the integration of knowledge, fear of God, and practical righteousness.
word_study.significance: The word itself is not condemned; wisdom is a divine gift. What is condemned is wisdom that isolates itself from its source—wisdom that becomes self-serving and arrogant.

word_study.term_english: in their own eyes / in their own sight
word_study.meaning: The repetition of 'in their eyes' and 'before their face' emphasizes that they see only themselves. They have become the center of reference, the measure of all things.
word_study.significance: The redundancy is not accidental; it drives home the isolation and self-enclosure of self-referential wisdom. There is no external standard, no transcendent measure—only the self.

word_study.meaning: Understanding, perceptive, prudent—one who demonstrates binah (understanding). Often used of practical intelligence and discernment.
word_study.significance: Here, navon represents the corruption of legitimate understanding into prideful self-sufficiency. The person who should use discernment to align with God's will instead uses it to justify their own desires.
