cross_references.connection: Be not wise in thine own eyes: fear the LORD, and depart from evil.' This proverb is the exact antidote to Isaiah's woe—true wisdom begins with fear of God, not confidence in self.
Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him.' Proverbs diagnoses the spiritual death of self-referential wisdom even more starkly than Isaiah.

Be of the same mind one toward another. Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits.' Paul applies Isaiah's warning to the church, showing its continuing relevance.
Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men.' Paul inverts the mockers' wisdom: what appears foolish to human pride is actually divine wisdom.

commentary.historical_context: The political and intellectual elite of Jerusalem in Isaiah's time were products of the royal court and merchant class. They had been educated in diplomacy, economics, and statecraft. They prided themselves on their ability to 'read the times' and navigate the complex politics of the ancient Near East. Assyria was expanding; Egypt was declining; smaller nations had to be clever to survive. In this context, Isaiah's insistence on covenant faithfulness and justice for the poor seemed naive, even dangerous. The 'wise ones' believed their survival depended on pragmatism, not piety. Yet Isaiah announces that their very cleverness—their refusal to listen to prophetic warning, their trust in their own judgment—is the thing that will destroy them. Genuine wisdom, he insists, means submission to God's revealed will, even when that seems economically inefficient or diplomatically unwise.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 9:28 records Jacob's warning: 'O that cunning plan of the evil one! O the vainness, and the frailties, and the foolishness of men! When they are learned they think they are wise, and they hearken not unto the counsel of God, for they set it aside, supposing they know of themselves.' This passage directly echoes Isaiah's fifth woe and applies it to the Book of Mormon community.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:27-28 states: 'Hearken to the voice of the Lord your God, while I speak unto you; for no one can deny my word... therefore, prepare ye for the coming of the Bridegroom.' The invitation to listen to God's voice stands in direct opposition to the self-sufficiency condemned in Isaiah 5:21.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple endowment, the figure of Lucifer represents pride and self-sufficiency—the belief that one can progress through one's own wisdom rather than submission to God's plan. Isaiah's woe speaks to this same temptation.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ embodies true wisdom not by intellectual superiority but by perfect submission to the Father's will. In the wilderness temptations (Matthew 4), Christ rejects the use of his own power and wisdom apart from the Father's instruction. He models the alternative to the mockers' self-sufficiency: 'I can of mine own self do nothing' (John 5:30).
commentary.application: This verse confronts a temptation that runs deep in Western culture and even in LDS culture: the deification of human reason and the dismissal of revealed truth as antiquated or restrictive. We see this in the impulse to 'spiritualize away' commandments we find inconvenient, to interpret our own desires as the Holy Ghost, to trust our judgment over the counsel of living prophets. The verse calls us to radical humility: to recognize that genuine wisdom means submission to God, that our insights and understanding are only valuable when they align with revealed truth, and that the person most dangerous to their own salvation is the one who is 'wise in their own eyes.' How do we check ourselves? By asking: Am I listening to the voice of God through his prophets, or only to the voice in my own head? Am I willing to be taught, or do I only seek to confirm what I already believe?

text_kjv: Woe unto them that are mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink:

commentary.narrative: The sixth woe oracle drips with caustic irony. Isaiah inverts the language of martial valor and transforms it into a portrait of pathetic excess. The mockers who would be heroes in battle have instead become 'heroes' at the banquet table. The terms 'mighty' (gibborim) and 'men of strength' (anshei-chayil) are normally reserved for warriors of exceptional prowess—David's elite warriors are called gibborim in 2 Samuel 23. Here, Isaiah applies this military vocabulary to drinking prowess, creating an effect of bitter sarcasm. These are not insignificant drunks but powerful people who have redirected their strength and capacity from defense of the nation to personal indulgence. The sarcasm carries a sharp political edge: at precisely the moment when Israel needs military strength to face the approaching Assyrian threat (vv. 26-30), its 'heroes' are incapacitated by drink.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verse is also an indictment of a specific cultural sin: the abuse of wine and alcohol as an escape from responsibility. Drunkenness appears throughout Scripture as a sign of moral collapse (Noah in Genesis 9:21, the sons of Eli in 1 Samuel 2:12, the leaders in Ephesians 5:18). Here, Isaiah connects the drunkenness to the broader pattern of woe oracles: greed (v. 8), oppression (v. 11-12), and defiance (v. 19) all lead to the anesthetic of drink. The 'heroes' who drink themselves senseless are simultaneously avoiding the moral reckoning their actions deserve and rendering themselves useless for any genuine defense of the nation. Yet verse 23 will reveal that their drinking is merely the surface symptom of a deeper corruption: they are corrupt judges who sell verdicts for bribes.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The Covenant Rendering captures this irony perfectly: 'Woe to those who are heroes at drinking wine, / champions at mixing strong drink!' The parallel structure emphasizes that the mockers have made drinking an art form, a skill developed with the same discipline that a real warrior brings to combat. This is not casual excess but cultivated vice. The social setting is likely the banquets of the wealthy, where Jerusalem's elite gathered to celebrate their prosperity and power. Amos provides a parallel denunciation: 'That chant to the sound of the viol, and invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David; That drink wine in bowls' (Amos 6:5-6). The luxurious setting makes the judgment more cutting: these are not the desperate poor driven to drink by misery, but the wealthy using alcohol to anesthetize their consciences while their nation slides toward judgment.

word_study.meaning: Heroes, mighty ones, warriors—men of exceptional strength, valor, and martial prowess. The plural form suggests a class: the mighty men of David's army are called gibborim (2 Samuel 23:8-39). In war, a gibbor is a warrior who turns the tide of battle.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that applying gibbor to drinking prowess is bitterly ironic. These men have the capacity and strength for genuine heroism but have squandered it on indulgence. The woe is not against drinking itself but against the perversion of strength.

word_study.term_english: men of strength / men of valor
word_study.meaning: Men of valor, men of substance—those who possess chayil (strength, capacity, often military strength). In biblical usage, anshei-chayil are the capable, the powerful, those who get things done.
word_study.significance: The phrase appears in military contexts (1 Samuel 14:52) and commercial contexts (describing wealthy merchants). Here it describes those with power and capacity who have directed that power toward personal gratification rather than public good.

word_study.meaning: Yayin is fermented grape wine; shekar is strong drink—beer, mead, or other fermented beverages with high alcohol content. The two terms together cover the full range of intoxicating drinks.
word_study.significance: The distinction between wine and strong drink is important in biblical law (Leviticus 10:9 forbids priests to drink either before entering the sanctuary). Here, the mockers pursue both varieties with equal vigor, suggesting total commitment to intoxication.

word_study.meaning: To mix, blend, pour—often used of wine preparation. The verb suggests skill and deliberation: someone carefully mixing drinks to achieve the perfect potency.
word_study.significance: The use of masak (rather than a simpler verb for 'drink') suggests that these 'heroes' approach their drinking with the same craftsmanship a vintner brings to wine-making. This is not desperate gulping but ritualized excess.

cross_references.connection: And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit.' Paul inverts the path of Isaiah's mockers: not wine but the Holy Ghost should fill the believer's life.

That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall; That chant to the sound of the viol... That drink wine in bowls.' Amos condemns the same pattern: luxurious living by the wealthy while the nation faces judgment.

Wine is a mocker: strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise.' Wisdom literature warns that alcohol itself is a deceiver, which aligns with Isaiah's judgment on those who trust in its effects.

That inasmuch as any man drinketh wine or strong drink among you, it is not good, neither meet in the sight of your Father... In consequence of evils and designs which do and will exist in the hearts of conspiring men.' The Word of Wisdom applies Isaiah's warning directly to the Latter-day Saint community.

commentary.historical_context: Archaeology confirms that wine was abundant in 8th-century Judah and that banqueting was a central feature of elite social life. The wealthy had vineyards (Isaiah itself mentions them), and wine served both as a commodity for trade and as a status marker for the upper classes. Banquets were venues for political power plays, business deals, and displays of magnificence. They also served as escapes—places where the pressures of maintaining wealth and power could be temporarily forgotten. Isaiah's condemnation of the drinking 'heroes' sits within the broader context of Assyrian expansion and political crisis. In roughly 740 BCE, Tiglath-Pileser III began systematically reducing the smaller kingdoms of the Levant, including Israel. Judah faced genuine military threat, yet its leaders were responding not with repentance or military readiness but with increased indulgence. The irony Isaiah emphasizes is temporal: the 'heroes at drinking' will soon face a real army (vv. 26-30), and their drunkenness will leave them defenseless.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 5:53 condemns those who 'rob the poor because they are rich' and engage in drunkenness and carousing. The Book of Mormon applies Isaiah's pattern to Nephite society: the coupling of oppression, pride, and excess.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 89 (the Word of Wisdom) explicitly connects abstinence from wine and strong drink to spiritual clarity and preparation for the endowment and temple ordinances. The revelation makes Isaiah's woe contemporary for LDS believers.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Word of Wisdom is given as a preparation for temple worship and covenant-making. The mockers of Isaiah 5:22 are precisely those rendered unfit for the temple—their bodies and minds clouded by intoxication, their covenants dissolved in wine.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus' first public miracle (John 2) involved turning water into wine at a wedding—affirming wine's legitimate place in covenant celebration. Yet throughout his ministry, Jesus warns against drunkenness and excess (Luke 21:34). The contrast is instructive: wine in moderation and in its proper context (covenant celebration) is blessed; wine used as an escape from responsibility and a mask for moral collapse is condemned. Christ himself models restraint and clear-eyed awareness, standing in direct opposition to the drunken 'heroes' of Isaiah.
commentary.application: For modern believers, this verse speaks to more than just alcohol (though that is included). It addresses any habit or behavior that turns strength into weakness, that clouds judgment, that allows us to escape the moral challenges of our time. Drunkenness on wine is obvious; but drunkenness on entertainment, social media, shopping, career advancement, or even spiritual bypassing (using religion to avoid genuine growth) are more subtle forms of the same vice. The verse asks: Are we using our strength and capacity for genuine good—for protection of the vulnerable, for building Zion, for raising righteous families? Or are we 'mighty' only at indulgence and escape? The deeper question: What am I anesthetizing myself from feeling? What moral reckoning am I avoiding? The 'heroes' of verse 22 are about to discover that their drunkenness cannot protect them from judgment. Modern covenants call us to clarity, sobriety, and readiness—not to be found intoxicated when the Lord comes.

text_kjv: Which justify the wicked for reward, and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him!

commentary.narrative: Verse 23 completes and deepens the sixth woe by revealing its full scope. The 'heroes at drinking wine' are also corrupt judges who sell verdicts for bribes. This verse strips away any pretense: what looks like mere indulgence is actually the symptom of a judicial system rotted at its core. The mockers have weaponized their authority. They 'justify the wicked'—they acquit the guilty in exchange for a bribe (shoched). They 'take away the righteousness of the righteous'—they strip the innocent of their legal rights and protections. This is not occasional corruption; the Hebrew verbs are masculine participles, indicating habitual, characteristic action. These are judges who have made a career of injustice.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Covenant Rendering captures the ruthlessness: 'who acquit the guilty for a bribe / and strip the innocent of their rights!' The Hebrew terms are precise: matsdikim ('acquitting,' from the root meaning 'to declare righteous') and tsidqat tsaddiqim ('the righteousness of the righteous'). The wordplay is devastating: those who should 'declare righteous' (make tsedaqah—justice—happen) instead 'declare guilty' the innocent. The very verb that should be associated with justice is inverted. This echoes verse 20's inversion of moral categories: the language of justice itself has been corrupted.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The connection to verse 7 is now unmistakable. In verse 7, the vineyard 'looked for judgment (mishpat) but behold oppression (mespach); for righteousness (tsedaqah) but behold a cry (tseaqah).' Here in verse 23, we see exactly how that has happened: the judges—the institution meant to guarantee justice and protect the righteous—have become instruments of oppression. The wealthy and powerful can sin with impunity because the judges they have bribed will declare them innocent. Meanwhile, the poor and vulnerable have their 'righteousness' stripped away: even if they are right, the corrupted court system denies them their due. This is the complete perversion of the covenant order, where God promised to defend the widow, the orphan, and the sojourner (Deuteronomy 10:18). Instead, the covenantal system itself has been weaponized against them.

word_study.meaning: To justify, acquit, declare righteous—from the root tsadiq (righteous). To pronounce someone not guilty or in the right.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that this verb is identical in form to the one that should describe God's righteous judgment. The corruption lies in applying this verb in the wrong direction: acquitting the guilty instead of acquitting the innocent.

word_study.meaning: Wicked, guilty, culpable—morally corrupt, deserving punishment. Throughout Scripture, rashaʿ is the opposite of tsadiq (righteous).
word_study.significance: In verse 23, the rashaʿ should face judgment but instead face acquittal—because they have bribed the judges.

word_study.meaning: Bribe, payment for corruption. Explicitly forbidden in the Torah (Exodus 23:8, Deuteronomy 16:19). A shochad perverts justice by substituting the judge's private interest for public duty.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that shochad is forbidden in Torah law and represents the complete betrayal of the judicial trust. By accepting bribes, judges have severed themselves from the covenant itself.

word_study.meaning: The righteousness (or rights/vindication) of the righteous. Tsidqah encompasses both moral virtue and the legal vindication/acquittal that should flow from righteousness. Tsaddiq is the righteous person—one who stands in right relationship with God and neighbor.
word_study.significance: The phrase connects directly to verse 7's lament: God sought tsedaqah but found mespach (oppression). Here, the tsaddiqim's tsidqah is actively stripped away by corrupted judges. They lose not only their property or safety but their very status as righteous persons in the community.

cross_references.connection: Thou shalt not wrest the judgment of thy poor in his cause... And thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous.' The Torah explicitly forbids what Isaiah's judges are doing—accepting bribes and distorting justice.

Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates... Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift.' Deuteronomy repeats the prohibition and adds the principle: justice must be equal and impartial.
A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment.' Wisdom literature names the same evil: bribery as the instrument of justice's perversion.

Ye have cast out the prophets, and sought all manner of ways to pervert the way of righteousness; and now ye are murderers, and ye seek to excuse yourselves.' The Book of Mormon diagnoses the same institutional corruption in Nephite society.

When a man is desirous to serve his country... he doth labor with all his might to do those things which he doth suppose to be just... But when a man is desirous of power... then cometh the evil day.' King Benjamin's address directly addresses the temptation of judicial corruption that Isaiah warns against.

commentary.historical_context: Judicial corruption was endemic in the ancient Near East. Egyptian, Assyrian, and Hittite sources all attest to the bribery of judges and the perversion of justice. In Israel and Judah, the system of local judges and city elders was vulnerable to precisely this kind of corruption because local judges were often wealthy landowners who had personal interests in the outcomes of cases. Samuel's own sons, we're told, 'turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment' (1 Samuel 8:3)—a sin that precipitated the demand for a king. In Isaiah's time (8th century BCE), the centralization of wealth and power meant that those with money could effectively purchase verdicts. The poor and vulnerable had no advocate in court. This was not occasional malfeasance but systematic injustice built into the structure of society. Archaeological evidence from the 8th century shows the gulf between rich and poor widening precisely during Isaiah's period, suggesting that such judicial corruption was real and consequential.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 11:20-22 records the case of Zeezrom, a lawyer who uses his skill to 'pervert the ways of righteousness' for gain. The Book of Mormon demonstrates how professional exploitation of the legal system corrupts society. Similarly, Helaman 7:5 laments: 'O that ye would repent! O that ye would repent and not bring more desolation upon the land.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 98:10 states: 'Therefore, renounce war and proclaim peace, and seek diligently to turn the hearts of the children of men, one to another, and to justfy the righteous and condemn the wicked.' This verse directly inverts Isaiah's judgment: true covenant order involves justifying the righteous and condemning the wicked.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, covenants are made to 'sacrifice all things for the kingdom of God' and to 'consecrate ourselves to the building up of the kingdom of God.' This stands in absolute opposition to the corrupt judges' consecration to private gain at the expense of justice.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus stands trial before corrupt judges (Matthew 26-27) who 'justify the wicked' (Pilate, Herod) by acquitting them while 'stripping the righteous' of their rights (Jesus is condemned despite Pilate declaring him innocent). Yet Jesus' apparent defeat becomes his victory: his death and resurrection reverse all corrupted verdicts and establish his redemptive justice for all people. He becomes the ultimate Judge who will set all things right.
commentary.application: This verse speaks to institutional integrity in ways that go far beyond ancient Judah. Modern believers encounter versions of this temptation: professionals (lawyers, judges, executives) who rationalize corruption as 'how business works,' or who accept pressure to compromise justice for financial advantage. The verse also speaks to more subtle forms: the tendency to judge based on personal relationships rather than objective truth, or to punish those we dislike while excusing those we favor. On a personal level: Do I compromise truth for advantage? Do I apply different standards to different people based on how they affect my interests? Do I shade evidence when it suits me? The deeper principle: Justice is not a commodity. Truth is not negotiable. The righteous deserve vindication and protection; the wicked deserve accountability. When we corrupt these categories—when we pretend evil is good or that might makes right—we are participating in the same institutional collapse that Isaiah condemns. The challenge for modern covenant members is to cultivate radical honesty, to defend the weak, and to insist that our professional and institutional commitments remain aligned with divine justice.

text_kjv: Therefore as the fire devoureth the stubble, and the flame consumeth the chaff, so their root shall be as rottenness, and their blossom shall go up as dust: because they have cast away the law of the LORD of hosts, and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel.

commentary.narrative: The sixth woe concludes with the sentence of judgment, and it is catastrophic and totalizing. Isaiah employs two images of destruction that cover both the instantaneous (fire) and the progressive (rot), both above-ground (blossom) and below-ground (root). Nothing will survive. The mockers will not recover, rebuild, or escape. Their destruction will be complete and irreversible. The imagery shifts from judicial metaphor to apocalyptic vision: what begins as a woe oracle (a pronouncement of disaster) culminates in prophetic vision of how that disaster will unfold.
commentary.narrative_continued: The cause is now stated with devastating clarity. The mockers have 'cast away the law of the LORD of hosts' (torah YHWH Tsebaot) and 'despised the word of the Holy One of Israel' (imrat Qedosh Yisra'el). The verbs are acts of deliberate contempt, not ignorance. Ma'asu means to reject, refuse, spurn—an active rejection. Ni'etsu means to despise, scorn, treat with contempt. These are choices, not accidents. The mockers have not merely failed to obey; they have actively turned away from God's instruction and made a deliberate show of their contempt. This is not the ignorance of verse 19 (not hearing) but the willful defiance of verse 20 (inverting all values) expressed now as explicit rejection of Torah itself.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The historical moment is critical. Isaiah's prophecy was delivered in the late 8th century BCE, and the mockers would live to see it fulfilled. In 701 BCE (a few decades after Isaiah's ministry began), Sennacherib's Assyrian army surrounded Jerusalem, and the northern kingdom of Israel had already been destroyed and depopulated by the Assyrians in 722 BCE. The 'distant nation' of verse 26-30 materialized. The root rotted. The blossom blew away as dust. Those who had mocked God's word, corrupted justice, and inverted moral values were swept away. The accuracy of Isaiah's prophecy was vindicated in real time, making this woe oracle not merely moral exhortation but genuine forecast of what would come to pass.

word_study.meaning: Esh (fire) is both literal fire and metaphor for judgment, destruction, purification. Lehabah (flame) is the visible expression of fire's power. Together they represent unstoppable destructive force.
word_study.significance: In Isaiah, fire frequently symbolizes God's judgment (cf. Isaiah 9:19, 10:17). The 'fire' that 'devours' the mockers is divine wrath made visible.

word_study.meaning: Stubble (kash) is the dry stalk left after grain harvest; chaff (chashash) is the husk separated from grain. Both are essentially valueless—leftover agricultural waste to be burned.
word_study.significance: The mockers are reduced to the status of post-harvest waste. Their elaborate complexity, their systems of injustice, their confident rhetoric—all are reduced to kindling.

word_study.meaning: Root (shoresh) is the foundation, the source of life and stability. Blossom (pirchah) is the visible flowering, the fruit-bearing potential. Together they represent the whole plant, from foundation to fruit.
word_study.significance: The progression from ground-level fire (instant destruction) to root-and-blossom imagery (complete systemic failure) suggests that the mockers' entire existence—foundation and aspiration—is undone.

word_study.meaning: Mak is rot, decay, decomposition—the natural process of corruption. Avak is dust, fine powder—what remains after all structure has dissolved.
word_study.significance: Mak suggests internal corruption; avak suggests external dispersal. The mockers will not be struck down in a moment but will rot from within and scatter to nothing.

word_study.meaning: To reject, refuse, spurn, treat with contempt. Ma'as is an active verb of deliberate rejection, not passive ignorance.
word_study.significance: The mockers have not passively failed to keep Torah; they have actively thrown it away. Their destruction is the inevitable consequence of this deliberate rejection.

word_study.meaning: To despise, scorn, treat with contempt or insult. Niʿatz implies a show of scorn—public, performative rejection.
word_study.significance: The mockers have made a spectacle of their contempt for God's word. Their public defiance is matched by public judgment.

word_study.meaning: Instruction, teaching, law—God's comprehensive revelation of his will and character. Torah includes narrative (God's acts), wisdom (counsel for living), and legal statutes.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering retains 'Torah' rather than 'law' to capture the full meaning: not merely legal code but God's entire covenantal instruction. By rejecting Torah, the mockers have rejected the totality of God's self-revelation.

word_study.meaning: Word, saying, utterance—a specific instance of speech. Imrat emphasizes the spoken, prophetic word.
word_study.significance: The mockers have despised not only written law (Torah) but the spoken word of the prophets. They have rejected both written and prophetic revelation.

word_study.meaning: Isaiah's signature title for God, appearing over 25 times in Isaiah and rarely elsewhere. It combines transcendent holiness (separation from all that is profane) with covenant particularity (bound to Israel).
word_study.significance: The phrase appears now for the third time in this chapter (v. 16, 19, 24), creating a inclusio (bookending structure) for the woe oracles. The mockers are rejecting the God who is both absolutely holy and covenantally bound to them.

cross_references.connection: And the light of Israel shall be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame: and it shall burn and devour his thorns and his briers in one day.' Isaiah repeats the image: God's fire consumes the rebellious growth on his vineyard.

For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts.' Malachi echoes Isaiah's final woe: the mockers and the wicked will be reduced to stubble.
If we suffer, we shall also reign with him: if we deny him, he also will deny us.' Paul applies the principle: rejection of God's word leads to being rejected by God.

And after they had dwindled in unbelief they became a dark, loathsome, and a filthy people, full of idleness and all manner of abominations.' The Book of Mormon shows how rejection of God's word (Torah) leads to total degeneration.

And the arm of the Lord shall be revealed; and the day cometh when they who have not heard his voice shall be obedient or utterly destroyed.' The D&C pronounces the same judgment: rejection of God's revealed word results in destruction.

commentary.historical_context: The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse with no theologically significant variants, suggesting it was copied with care and considered crucial by the Qumran community. The manuscript evidence confirms that this woe oracle, with its explicit judgment and specific imagery, was considered authoritative prophecy. Historically, Isaiah's words were vindicated by events. The northern kingdom of Israel was destroyed by Assyria in 722 BCE. Jerusalem survived Sennacherib's siege in 701 BCE (through what appeared to many as miraculous intervention: 2 Kings 19:35), but the city was eventually destroyed by Babylon in 586 BCE. The mockers of Isaiah 5 did indeed see their 'root become rottenness' and their 'blossom blow away as dust.' The accuracy of these predictions served to establish Isaiah as a true prophet and vindicated his message: rejection of Torah leads to destruction.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records repeated cycles of this same pattern: prosperity leading to pride, pride leading to rejection of prophetic warning and God's word (the equivalent of Torah), and rejection leading to destruction. Helaman 13 records Nephi's prophesy that Jerusalem's destruction will be replicated in the Nephite land if they do not repent—and it comes to pass within the century.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:38 states: 'Whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' The Lord binds his identity to his word spoken through prophets. Rejection of the servants' word is rejection of the Lord's word. D&C 133:50-51 describes the destruction that comes to those who reject the word: 'And another trump shall sound, which is the third trump; and then come the spirits of just men made perfect... And also the resurrection of the just.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, covenants are made to 'receive truth, wherever it comes from.' This stands in absolute opposition to the mockers' rejection of Torah. Temple worship involves the reception and embodiment of revealed truth; rejection of revealed truth separates one from temple blessings and their fruits.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ came as the embodiment of Torah—the living word (John 1:1, 14). His rejection by the Jewish leaders parallels the mockers' rejection of Isaiah's word. Yet where the mockers face destruction, Christ's rejection becomes redemptive: his death and resurrection reverse judgment, offer salvation to the repentant, and restore the covenant. The woe of Isaiah 5:24 is not the final word; the gospel of Christ offers a way of escape for those who repent and receive his word.
commentary.application: This final verse applies Isaiah's entire woe oracle to modern covenants with devastating force. The Latter-day Saints have been given unprecedented access to revealed truth: living prophets, continuing revelation, restored scripture, and temple covenants. The verse asks: Are we receiving this truth or casting it away? Are we honoring the word spoken through God's servants, or are we joining the mockers who despise it? The consequences Isaiah describes are not merely historical but eternal: those who reject God's law and despise his word will not merely face temporal judgment but will exclude themselves from his presence and glory. The verse offers a choice: Will we be like the 'heroes at drinking wine' who corrupt justice and mock God's word? Or will we be like those who 'fear the LORD, and depart from evil,' who listen to the prophetic voice, who honor covenants, and who stand in the light of God's truth? The destruction of the mockers, terrible as it is, is not inevitable for us—but only if we choose repentance, only if we choose to receive the law of the Lord and honor his word spoken through his servants.

text_kjv: Therefore is the anger of the LORD kindled against his people, and he hath stretched forth his hand against them, and hath smitten them: and the hills did tremble, and their carcases were torn in the midst of the streets. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks a catastrophic shift from indictment to execution. The six woe oracles of Isaiah 5:8-23 have catalogued Israel's moral failures—greed, drunkenness, pride, moral inversion, and rejection of God's word. Now the consequences arrive with devastating immediacy. The anger of the LORD is no longer threatened or restrained; it 'blazes' (The Covenant Rendering), an active, burning force. The imagery is visceral: God's hand, which once delivered Israel from Egypt, is now outstretched in judgment. The mountains themselves tremble—a sign of theophanic presence and cosmic upheaval. The phrase 'their carcases were torn in the midst of the streets' represents one of the ancient world's greatest horrors: exposure without burial. In ancient Near Eastern custom, denying proper burial was the ultimate dishonor, leaving the dead unprotected and their souls in liminal distress.

What makes this verse structurally crucial is its refrain: 'For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.' This refrain—*od yado netuyah*—becomes a leitmotif through Isaiah 9:12, 17, 21 and 10:4, creating a unified literary arc of judgment that continues and escalates. The repetition signals not a single judgment but an *ongoing process*. The hand remains extended; more strikes are coming. This is not vengeance concluded but judgment in motion.

word_study.meaning: To kindle, burn, become hot with anger. The root suggests a fire actively burning rather than a state of anger. It denotes divine wrath at its most active and dangerous.
word_study.significance: The verb moves from passive displeasure to active combustion. The Covenant Rendering's 'blazes' captures the incandescent quality. This is not irritation but divine fire.

word_study.meaning: To stretch out, extend the hand. In Exodus, God's outstretched hand delivers Israel from Egypt (Deut 4:34, 5:15). Here the same gesture becomes an instrument of judgment.
word_study.significance: The dual-use theology here is devastating. The very hand that saved Israel now strikes Israel. Covenant faithfulness reversed becomes covenant violation punished. The repetition of this phrase throughout 9:12-10:4 emphasizes that judgment is not momentary but relentless.

word_study.meaning: Corpse, carcass. Often used of animals, the application to human dead here is deliberately dehumanizing.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'corpses lay like refuse' emphasizes that these are not properly buried, not dignified, not mourned in the customary way. In the ancient Near East, this represented social and spiritual catastrophe.

word_study.term_english: his hand is still stretched out
word_study.meaning: Yet/still his hand is extended. The adverb *od* ('still, yet') implies continuation and incompleteness.
word_study.significance: This is the structural refrain of Isaiah 5-10. It appears in 9:12, 17, 21 and 10:4, binding these chapters into a single theological statement: judgment is ongoing, the hand has not been withdrawn, and more consequences are coming. The repetition prevents the reader from finding false comfort in any single judgment.

cross_references.connection: God stretches out his arm to deliver Israel from Egypt with 'mighty acts of judgment.' Here in Isaiah 5:25, the same gesture of the outstretched hand becomes an instrument of judgment against Israel itself.
The refrain 'his hand is stretched out still' is repeated exactly, confirming that Isaiah 5 and 9:8-10:4 form a unified arc of escalating judgment with no cessation.
Moses prophesies that God will 'raise up a nation against you from far, from the end of the earth'—a warning fulfilled in Isaiah 5:26-30 as that distant nation approaches in judgment.
Amos uses the refrain 'I will not turn away the punishment' in a series of oracles against nations, paralleling Isaiah's use of the refrain to signal unstoppable judgment.
'My arm is over all the earth' (says the Lord). Isaiah 5:25 demonstrates that arm raised both to save and to strike, according to the covenant responsiveness of God's people.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near Eastern world operated under a strict honor-shame system in which proper burial was fundamental to human dignity and peace of the soul. A corpse left exposed in the streets—*kasuchah beqerev chutsot* ('like refuse in the streets')—represented not merely death but erasure from society. The Assyrian and Babylonian siege practices Isaiah's audience would have witnessed or heard of included exactly this: heap the dead in public spaces as a terror tactic and a profound violation of religious obligation. The mountains trembling at divine judgment is theophanic language; earthquakes were understood as the earth responding to the presence and wrath of God. This verse depicts not just military defeat but cosmic disorder—the created order responding to broken covenant.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:27-28 presents a parallel vision of God's wrath 'stretched out' against those who reject covenant. The refrain of judgment continuing and 'his hand stretched out' echoes through Alma's lament over the Lamanites who have rejected the gospel message.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:14-20 speaks of God's judgments being poured out 'with fire and with his sword' upon the wicked. Isaiah 5:25 prefigures the doctrine that covenant rejection triggers divine judgment that is prolonged and comprehensive, not momentary.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The outstretched hand of God is central to temple ordinances, where the Lord's blessing is extended through priestly hands. Here, that same symbolic gesture becomes judgment—illustrating that covenants demand faithfulness or face consequences. The principle mirrors the temple vow: obedience brings blessing; disobedience invokes the judgment symbolized by the Lord's outstretched hand.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 5:25 prefigures the suffering Messiah in a counterintuitive way: just as the Lord's hand is stretched out in judgment against covenant-breaking Israel, so too will the Messiah's hands be stretched out—pierced—bearing the judgment that fallen humanity deserves (Isaiah 53:5-6). The hand extended to strike and the hand extended to save are unified in the Cross.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse presents an uncomfortable but necessary truth: covenant faithfulness is not optional. God's patience, though long-suffering, has limits. The refrain 'his hand is still stretched out' warns that judgment, once initiated, does not automatically reverse itself; we must return to covenant with intention and urgency. The exposure of Israel's dead in the streets—the loss of dignity—reflects a deeper spiritual loss that comes from rejecting God's instruction. We are called to examine where we have grieved the Spirit through moral compromise, and to remember that God's hand, extended toward us, requires our response.

text_kjv: And he will lift up an ensign to the nations from far, and will hiss unto them from the end of the earth: and, behold, they shall come with speed swiftly:

commentary.narrative: The perspective shifts dramatically in verse 26. No longer are we viewing the internal decay of Israel described in verses 8-23; now Isaiah pulls back to a geopolitical vista and shows God as the supreme military strategist. The 'distant nation' is not explicitly named—it could be Assyria, Babylon, or any empire that would later be used as God's instrument. But the *mechanism* is clear: God raises a signal flag (*nes*) and whistles (*sharaq*) for this nation as a shepherd whistles for dogs or a beekeeper summons swarms (cf. Isaiah 7:18). This is God summoning warriors as if they were animals responding to command. The whistling—an audacious image—reduces even mighty empires to obedient servants of divine purpose. They come 'with speed swiftly,' an emphatic doubling that conveys relentless momentum. The anonymity of the 'distant nation' is theologically important: it makes the judgment timeless and portable. Any empire can become the rod of God's judgment. This was profoundly meaningful to Isaiah's original audience facing Assyrian expansion, but it also speaks to every generation facing unexpected judgment.

word_study.meaning: A signal flag, pole, or banner raised on high ground to muster troops or give a visible command. In military contexts, the nes gathered scattered forces.
word_study.significance: In Isaiah, *nes* has dual theological force: here it signals judgment (5:26), but in 11:10 and 11:12 it becomes a banner of salvation around which the scattered remnant gathers. The same word, different purposes—a microcosm of God's dual role as judge and redeemer.

word_study.meaning: To hiss, whistle. Used of summoning bees (7:18), it is an onomatopoetic term that denotes a sharp, compelling sound.
word_study.significance: The verb reduces empires to animal status. God doesn't command them respectfully; he *whistles*. This is psychological dominance. No matter how mighty Assyria or Babylon, they respond to God's whistle like trained creatures. It strips human empires of their pretended autonomy.

word_study.meaning: From afar, from a distance. The preposition *mem* with the noun *rachok* (distance, remoteness).
word_study.significance: The distance is both geographical and theological. The army comes from beyond the horizon, beyond human control, from regions that seem remote. This emphasizes that God commands forces far beyond Israel's reach or vision.

word_study.term_english: from the end of the earth
word_study.meaning: From the edge or extremity of the land/earth. *Qetsev* denotes the boundary or limit, making this phrase hyperbolically distant.
word_study.significance: The phrasing emphasizes totality and remoteness. It is not a neighboring nation but one from the very margins of the known world. The imagery makes the judgment feel both inevitable and otherworldly.

cross_references.connection: God 'shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt.' The same verb *sharaq* is used, extending the image of God as one who commands distant forces with a whistle.

Moses warns Israel: 'The LORD shall bring a nation against thee from far, from the end of the earth...a nation whose tongue thou shalt not understand.' Isaiah 5:26 is the fulfillment of this Deuteronomic curse.
In the messianic future, the *nes* (ensign) becomes a banner of redemption around which the scattered remnant of Israel gathers. The same word that summons judgment (5:26) will summon salvation.
God summons kingdoms as 'a shepherd calls his flock.' The imagery of God as one who whistles and musters nations is developed further in Jeremiah's prophecies of Babylon.
The Lord declares that He 'shall raise up' nations to be 'a scourge unto my people.' Like Isaiah 5:26, this teaches that God uses worldly powers as instruments of judgment on covenant peoples.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near East operated on a network of competing empires. By Isaiah's time (8th century BCE), Assyria was the rising superpower, systematizing conquest in unprecedented ways: mass deportation, military efficiency, psychological terror. Isaiah's audience lived under the shadow of Assyrian expansion. The genius of Isaiah 5:26 is its claim that this terrifying, distant power is not autonomous—it is whistled forth by God like a trained animal. This was radical theology: it meant that Israel's devastation was not random or because Assyria was stronger, but because God had decided to use Assyria as a tool. Paradoxically, this was meant to be comforting: if God is commanding the army, then judgment, though severe, was purposeful and limited to his sovereign will, not Assyria's caprice.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 25:15 speaks of God gathering 'all nations in his own due time' for judgment. The principle of God as supreme orchestrator of history, commanding nations through his will, is central to Book of Mormon theology and resonates with Isaiah 5:26.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 87 (the prophecy on war) depicts God's will directing the movements of nations. Section 101:11-15 teaches that God 'raiseth up' nations as scourges and that ultimately all nations are subject to his purposes. Isaiah 5:26 is the archetype for this doctrine.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The raising of the ensign relates to the temple signal of gathering. In latter-day revelation, the Lord raises the 'ensign' or banner of the restored gospel from which all nations are called to gather. Isaiah 5:26's banner of judgment inverts into Isaiah 11:12's banner of salvation—both orchestrated by God's sovereign will.

commentary.christological_typology: The distant nation raised to execute judgment prefigures the Roman power that would later be raised to bring judgment on Jerusalem in 70 CE. But more deeply, Isaiah 5:26 foreshadows Christ's authority over all nations and powers. In Revelation, Christ alone holds the keys to summon and dismiss kingdoms. His outstretched hand (verse 25) and his whistled command (verse 26) are the prerogatives of divine sovereignty that find their ultimate fulfillment in the Messiah.
commentary.application: Modern readers may find in this verse both warning and assurance. Warning: the structures and powers of the world, however imposing, are subject to God's sovereign will and can be deployed as judgment against those who break covenant. Assurance: we are not subject to the blind forces of history; we live under God's purposeful governance. For covenant members, the application is urgent: do not trust in the arm of flesh or the stability of earthly powers. Do not assume your nation, your leader, or your circumstances are permanent. Seek first the kingdom of God, knowing that He commands all things and uses history to call His people to repentance.

text_kjv: None shall be weary nor stumble among them; none shall slumber nor sleep; neither shall the girdle of their loins be loosed, nor the latchet of their shoes be broken:

commentary.narrative: Isaiah's description of the approaching army reaches cinematic intensity. The fourfold negation—not weary, not stumbling, not slumbering, not sleeping—creates a relentless, almost inhuman cadence. This is an army that does not tire, does not falter, does not rest. The contrast to Israel's 'mighty men' in verse 22 (who 'are mighty to drink wine') could not be starker. While Israel's heroes stagger drunk, the enemy's soldiers maintain perfect discipline and readiness. The final details—the belt (girdle) remains fastened at the waist, the sandal-strap (*serok nealav*) does not tear—seem mundane but carry profound military meaning. Loose clothing or broken footwear meant vulnerability and the need to stop for repairs. An army that doesn't need to pause for such things can cover vast distances without rest. The entire verse describes an army that has transcended human limitation, an engine of judgment calibrated by God himself. The precision of Isaiah's description suggests an eyewitness or someone who understands military technology intimately. This may reflect Isaiah's observations during Assyrian military campaigns or his deep knowledge of military logistics.

word_study.meaning: Tired, exhausted, faint. Often describes the state of a warrior after battle or forced march.
word_study.significance: The negation of *ayef* is crucial: even after traveling 'from the end of the earth,' these soldiers are not exhausted. It is a superhuman characteristic that emphasizes that human fatigue does not apply to this army.

word_study.meaning: To stumble, fall, be weak. Used metaphorically for spiritual or moral failure (e.g., Isaiah 40:30).
word_study.significance: Not only are they not tired; they don't even stumble. Their footing is sure. This combines physical discipline with implied divine support—the roadway itself seems to cooperate with their advance.

word_study.meaning: Slumber (drowse, light sleep) and sleep (deep sleep). Together they cover all forms of rest.
word_study.significance: The two words together create an emphatic doubling: no rest whatsoever, neither dozing nor deep sleep. This is relentless vigilance and perpetual motion. The Dead Sea Scrolls variant (1QIsaᵃ) preserves the same consonantal text, confirming that this meaning was stable in transmission.

word_study.meaning: *Ezor* = belt or girdle; *chalaçav* = loins. The girdle held up armor and tunic.
word_study.significance: A loosened belt meant the soldier's kit was coming undone, a sign of disorder and the need to stop and retie. The girdle fastened meant the soldier was combat-ready, not stopping for maintenance. It is a small detail that conveys absolute preparedness.

word_study.meaning: *Serok* = strap or latchet; *ne'alav* = his sandals. The sandal-strap held the leather sandal to the foot.
word_study.significance: A broken strap meant stopping to repair or replace sandals—a delay that could cost lives in a forced march. The fact that none of the enemy's sandal-straps break is impossible without divine intervention. It underscores the supernatural readiness of this army.

cross_references.connection: Later, Isaiah teaches that those who wait upon the Lord 'shall renew their strength: they shall mount up with wings as eagles...they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.' The language echoes verse 27, but applied to God's covenant people rather than his instrument of judgment.

Moses describes Egypt as a land where you must work for water, but the land the Lord gives Israel is one 'the eyes of the LORD thy God are always upon it.' Isaiah 5:27's description of an indefatigable army inverts this blessing—when Israel fails, God's attention turns to instrumental judgment.

Joshua is commanded that the book of the law 'shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night,' suggesting constant vigilance and preparation. The enemy army in Isaiah 5:27 has this same relentless focus, but toward destruction rather than obedience.

Paul exhorts: 'Let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober.' The spiritual alertness Paul urges is contrasted with the false vigilance of Isaiah's invading army, which rests in no faith, only in military superiority.

The Lord speaks of those who will be 'armed with righteousness and with the power of God in great glory.' Isaiah 5:27's description of superhuman readiness in the enemy army is countered by D&C's promise of divine armor for the righteous.

commentary.historical_context: The Assyrian Empire was known for its military efficiency and the use of relay stations to move messages and troops across vast distances rapidly. The forced march along the royal road from Mesopotamia to the Levant could take weeks, yet Assyrian infantry and chariots were organized with what seemed to the ancient world like superhuman efficiency. Soldiers were rotated through relay stations to maintain alertness. Supplies were pre-positioned. Horses and infantry operated in synchronized rhythm. To Isaiah's contemporaries, the Assyrian war machine must have seemed almost inexplicable—not merely strong but relentless, tireless, perfectly coordinated. Isaiah's description of verse 27 reflects what his audience would have observed or heard of the Assyrian approach: an army that did not seem bound by normal human limitations.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 2:29-31 describes the Lamanite army approaching with similar relentlessness and organization. The Book of Mormon frequently employs military imagery to describe how God's judgments operate—not chaotically, but with terrible precision.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:21 speaks of judgments coming 'upon all nations with a just recompense.' The precision and relentlessness of Isaiah 5:27's army mirror the ordered, purposeful nature of God's judgments in latter-day revelation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment includes imagery of God's power to protect the faithful and to execute justice. Isaiah 5:27's description of an army that operates with divine precision but toward destructive ends emphasizes that God's power can be deployed in multiple directions—to save or to judge. The lesson for the temple participant is that alignment with God's law is not optional.

commentary.christological_typology: Paradoxically, Christ embodies both the tireless faithfulness of Isaiah 5:27's army and something far deeper. In Luke 22:41-44, Christ 'prayed more earnestly' in Gethsemane while 'his sweat was as it were great drops of blood'—not superhuman endurance that eliminates struggle, but endurance *through* weakness. Christ's fidelity to God's purpose is human (not angelic), yet absolute. In contrast to the emotionless, tireless army of verse 27, Christ's judgment (when He returns as judge) will be combined with mercy and a perfect understanding of human frailty.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 5:27 presents a spiritual paradox. On one hand, we are warned not to underestimate the relentlessness of worldly opposition to the gospel and to covenant living. Evil does not rest; temptation does not sleep; the forces arrayed against righteousness are tireless. On the other hand, we are called to a similar spiritual wakefulness and readiness—'watch and pray that ye enter not into temptation' (Matthew 26:41). The application is not to fear the enemy's readiness but to match it with our own: consistent repentance, constant vigilance in prayer, and the refusal to become spiritually lax. Our spiritual belt (readiness for battle) must be girded, our sandals (commitment to walk the covenant path) must be intact. Spiritual complacency is the antithesis of verse 27's message.

text_kjv: Whose arrows are sharp, and all their bows bent, their horses' hoofs shall be counted like flint, and their wheels like a whirlwind:

commentary.narrative: Verse 28 continues the catalog of military preparedness with almost cinematic precision. Every element of the army's arsenal is weaponized and ready. The arrows are not merely present but *sharpened*—already honed to a lethal edge. The bows are not merely carried but *bent* (strung and drawn), ready to release. This is an army not marching toward battle but already in a state of combat readiness, as if the battle has already begun. The comparison of horses' hooves to flint is brilliant natural observation: flint is one of the hardest, sharpest substances in the ancient world. Horses with hooves 'like flint' can traverse rocky terrain at speed without slowing or stumbling. The final image—chariot wheels 'like a whirlwind'—is both literal and metaphorical. Literally, chariot wheels spinning at speed create a dust storm and a sound like wind. Metaphorically, a whirlwind in biblical imagery often signals divine presence and power (Ezekiel 1:4; 2 Kings 2:11). Isaiah's language suggests that this army moves with a quality that seems almost divine, or at least divinely empowered. The precision of the description indicates that Isaiah may have witnessed Assyrian military parades or campaigns, or at minimum, studied them intently.

word_study.meaning: *Chetz* = arrow; *shanum* = to sharpen, whet. The adjective *shenumim* means sharpened, honed.
word_study.significance: The focus on sharpness emphasizes lethality. These are not blunt arrows for sport but honed for maximum penetration and destructive power. It speaks to preparation and intentionality.

word_study.meaning: *Qeshet* = bow; *darakh* = to tread, step on, and metaphorically to bend or draw. The adjective *derukh* means bent (in the sense of having been drawn back).
word_study.significance: Bows are not merely carried; they are actively drawn, strings taut, arrows nocked. The army is perpetually in the act of firing, not approaching to prepare for battle but moving through a state of perpetual engagement.

word_study.term_english: hoofs shall be counted like flint
word_study.term_original: פַּרְסוֹת סוּסָיו כַּצַּר נֶחְשָׁבוּ (parsot susaw kaçar nechshavu)
word_study.meaning: *Parsah* = hoof; *sus* = horse; *tzar* = flint (or flint-like hard stone); *nechshav* = reckoned, counted, valued as.
word_study.significance: The image is almost geological: the horses' hooves are not merely hard but are *valued/reckoned as* flint. This is poetic exaggeration that grounds itself in observation—cavalry horses worn by long campaigning do develop hardened hooves, and when flint is struck in ancient warfare (from chariots or cavalry), it creates sparks and fire. The Covenant Rendering's 'like flint' captures the comparison without the slightly awkward 'counted as' of the KJV.

word_study.meaning: *Galgal* = wheel; *sufa* = whirlwind, storm wind. The comparison is direct: wheels move with the speed and turbulence of a whirlwind.
word_study.significance: A whirlwind in Hebrew Bible often signals divine presence and power (2 Kings 2:11; Ezekiel 1:4; Nahum 1:3). To describe chariot wheels 'like a whirlwind' is to suggest that even the mechanical elements of the army partake of an almost divine power and speed. This poetic language makes the army seem not merely strong but supernaturally empowered.

cross_references.connection: Nahum prophesies the advance of an enemy army with similar military imagery: 'the shield of his mighty men is made red, the valiant men are in scarlet: the chariots shall be with flaming torches in the day of his preparation.' Like Isaiah 5:28, Nahum focuses on weaponry and mobility as signs of imminent destruction.

When the servant of Elisha sees the army surrounding them—'chariots...and a great host'—he is terrified. Yet Elisha's prayer opens his eyes to the greater spiritual reality. Isaiah 5:28's description of military might is countered by the doctrine that God's power transcends earthly armies.

The book of Job contains a magnificent description of the war horse: 'He mocketh at fear...he saith among the trumpets, Ha, ha; and he smelleth the battle afar off.' Isaiah 5:28's horses are similarly fierce and eager for war, functioning as instruments of judgment.

Jeremiah describes the approaching enemy: 'His horses are swifter than eagles...Woe unto us! for we are spoiled.' The language parallels Isaiah's description of superhuman military readiness and speed.

The Lord speaks of His power to protect Zion: 'Zion shall escape...by the brightness of my coming.' In contrast to Isaiah's invading army, the Lord's appearance is described with images of light and triumph, not merely military might.

commentary.historical_context: The Assyrian war machine was legendary in the ancient Near East for its technological sophistication. Chariots with reinforced wheels, elite cavalry units with composite bows (capable of firing at distance and with great force), and coordination between infantry and mobile units made Assyria nearly unstoppable on open ground. The composite bow—bows made of multiple materials (wood, horn, sinew) bent and held in tension—was a key Assyrian technology. These bows could penetrate armor that earlier weapons could not. Chariot wheels in Assyrian designs were more sophisticated than those of earlier cultures: they were lighter, more maneuverable, and capable of rapid movement. To an observer in the Levant, the approach of an Assyrian army must have seemed like a natural disaster—inevitable and overwhelming. Isaiah's precise description of arrows, bows, hooves, and wheels suggests that he was either present during Assyrian campaigns or deeply studied in military technology.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 3:26-27 describes the Lamanite military preparations: 'They...prepared themselves to come into the wilderness...And they did cut off the people of Amulon...and all those who had dissented from the church.' The Book of Mormon regularly employs military readiness as a metaphor for spiritual warfare preparation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 105:19 speaks of Zion's redemption in language that involves military struggle and eventual triumph. The weapons of the world (like those in Isaiah 5:28) are temporary and subject to God's larger purposes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony includes imagery of spiritual armor and preparation for battle—'loins girt about with truth' (Ephesians 6:14). While Isaiah's army girts itself for destruction, covenant members are girded for defense of their eternal covenants. The contrast illuminates the proper use of strength and preparation.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ as judge will come in power 'with the armies of heaven' (Revelation 19:14), yet His weapons are not arrows and chariots but truth, justice, and mercy. The contrast between Isaiah 5:28's purely destructive military power and Christ's redemptive power demonstrates a fundamental difference: worldly judgment is mechanical and impersonal; divine judgment is purposeful and redemptive, aimed at salvation even when appearing as judgment.
commentary.application: For covenant members, Isaiah 5:28 teaches vigilance without paranoia. The forces arrayed against the gospel—whether philosophical, cultural, political, or spiritual—are real and often sophisticated in their approach. They are 'bent bows' and 'sharp arrows,' strategically deployed. However, the application is not to fear but to recognize that these forces, however well-coordinated, remain subject to God's larger purposes. Our own preparation must not be military but spiritual: sharpened testimonies, sincere repentance, and prayers that are fervent and consistent. Like the enemy's readiness in verse 28, our spiritual readiness must be total and perpetual—not resting, not dull, not unprepared.

text_kjv: Their roaring shall be like a lion, they shall roar like young lions: yea, they shall roar, and lay hold of the prey, and shall carry it away safe, and none shall deliver it.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah shifts from the physical apparatus of war (weapons and horses) to the predatory nature of the invading army itself. The imagery becomes organic, even feral: the approaching soldiers are now lions, their sound a terrifying roar. The text uses two different Hebrew words for lion—*lavi'a* (lioness, mature lion) and *kephirim* (young lions in their prime). Together, they represent the full lethal capacity of a pride: the experienced huntress and the young males at peak strength. The progression of verbs in the verse creates an irresistible sequence: they roar (psychological terror), they seize the prey (physical conquest), they carry it away safely (successful conquest, no rescue possible). The final phrase—'none shall deliver'—is the theological crux. In Hebrew, *ein matsil* ('there is no rescuer, no deliverer') echoes the language of covenant unfaithfulness. Throughout the Prophets, only God is portrayed as the *matsil*, the deliverer. When Isaiah says there is none, he means that no human power, no other nation, no coalition of Israel's allies can prevent the devastation. This is not a roaring army; it is the roar of God's judgment made manifest in bestial fury.

word_study.meaning: A roar, growl, or sound of a wild animal (especially a lion). The verb *shaag* means to roar, growl; the noun form emphasizes the sound itself.
word_study.significance: The roar of a lion in the ancient Near East was perhaps the most terrifying sound in nature—it preceded the attack and paralyzed prey with fear. Isaiah uses this image to depict the psychological terror of the approaching army, not merely its physical threat.

word_study.meaning: Young lions, lions in their prime and at their most dangerous. Distinct from *lavi'a* (lioness or mature lion) or *ari* (lion generally).
word_study.significance: The specific choice of *kephirim* emphasizes peak physical power. These are not aging lions but those in the full strength of youth. Combined with the *lavi'a* mentioned first, the image covers the entire predatory capacity of the pride.

word_study.meaning: *Achaz* = to seize, grasp, hold; *teref* = prey, flesh, that which is torn or rended. The verb is intense and immediate—not gradual capture but sudden, violent seizure.
word_study.significance: The verb form suggests a completed action—the seizing is inevitable and final. Once the lion has prey in its grip, there is no escape. The theological meaning is that Israel, once seized by God's judgment, cannot reverse course.

word_study.meaning: To escape, to cause to escape, to deliver away. Here it means the lion carries off its kill without any threat of interference.
word_study.significance: The *palet* (escape) is secure and uncontested. No other power can retrieve or rescue the prey from the predator. This is theological language: when God's judgment falls, no human intervention can reverse it.

word_study.meaning: *Matsil* = deliverer, rescuer, one who saves. The negation *ein* makes this absolute: there is no deliverer.
word_study.significance: This phrase is theologically loaded. Throughout Scripture, God alone is 'the Deliverer' (*haMatzil*). To say 'there is no deliverer' is to say that all human sources of help—allies, leaders, military strength—are powerless. Only God has salvific power, and God has withdrawn His deliverance because Israel has rejected His law.

cross_references.connection: 'Lest he tear my soul like a lion, rending it in pieces, while there is none to deliver.' David uses identical language of predatory threat and the absence of human rescue, emphasizing that only God can deliver from such peril.

'The lion hath roared, who will not fear? The Lord GOD hath spoken, who can but prophesy?' Amos links the roar of the lion directly to God's voice and prophetic utterance—suggesting that the army's roar is, in truth, God's judgment voiced through history.

'Therefore I will be unto them as a lion: as a leopard by the way will I observe them: I will meet them as a bear that is bereaved of her whelps.' God Himself becomes the predator when His people reject covenant. Isaiah 5:29's lions are God's instruments, but the theology is Hosea's: God becomes the hunter.

'They gaped upon me with their mouths, as a ravening and a roaring lion.' The psalmist, in distress, uses the same lion imagery to describe those who oppose him, emphasizing the universal power of this metaphor for unstoppable threat.

'I, the Lord, stretched out the heavens, and built the earth...and all things came by me, and all things are sustained by me.' The principle that God alone sustains and can withdraw sustenance—allowing judgment to proceed unchecked—underlies Isaiah 5:29's theological message.

commentary.historical_context: The lion was a dominant predator in ancient Palestine and the Levant. Lions were known to hunt in coordinated prides, with males and females working together. The terror of a lion attack was absolute in the ancient world—there was no defense against a cornered or attacking lion except flight or hope for divine intervention. Hunting imagery in the ancient Near East was often used to describe both human warfare and divine judgment. An Assyrian relief from the palace of Ashurbanipal depicts the king hunting lions in controlled settings, suggesting that the ability to hunt lions was a mark of royal power and divine favor. Isaiah's use of lions as instruments of God's judgment would resonate powerfully with an audience familiar with both the terror of wild lions and the propaganda of Assyrian military might.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mormon 2:26-29 speaks of the Nephites falling into the hands of the Lamanites, unable to escape: 'And we were driven forth until we had come northward to the land of Jashon...and they...began to slay us.' The language of being seized and unable to escape parallels Isaiah's predatory imagery.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:17 speaks of Christ coming in judgment: 'Wherefore, I the Lord God will send forth flies upon the face of the earth.' While different imagery, the principle is the same: when God's people reject covenant, God sends instruments of judgment that cannot be resisted by human power alone.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony emphasizes covenant protection and the reality that those who break covenant lose that protection. Isaiah 5:29's lions represent the removal of divine shelter and the exposure of the covenant breaker to judgment. The lesson is that covenant is not peripheral to security but central to it.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is portrayed both as the Lion of Judah (Revelation 5:5) and as the gentle shepherd (John 10:11). In the final judgment, Christ will manifest both natures: He will judge with perfect justice (lion-like) yet offer mercy to the repentant. Isaiah 5:29's lions, in contrast, offer only destruction without redemption. The ultimate Lion of Judah will roar in judgment, but His roar will call the scattered sheep to gather (John 10:16), not drive them to destruction.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 5:29 presents a sobering reality: there are consequences to covenant rejection that cannot be averted by human means. We cannot negotiate, ally ourselves strategically, or outmaneuver God's judgment. The application is not paranoia but humility and urgency. If we have drifted from covenant faithfulness—in our families, our personal integrity, our generosity, our honesty—we must return *now*, not assuming that external security or political alliances or wealth will protect us. The promise is the obverse: those who remain in covenant have a Deliverer (*Matsil*) who is more powerful than all roaring lions. Our safety is not in earthly security but in faithfulness to God's law.

text_kjv: And in that day they shall roar against them like the roaring of the sea: and if one look unto the land, behold darkness and sorrow, and the light is darkened in the heavens thereof.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah 5 concludes not with a call to repentance or a promise of redemption, but with an image of total, utter darkness—the opposite of creation itself. The roaring of the distant nation is now compared to the roaring of the sea, which in biblical cosmology is a primordial force. The sea (*yam*) appears in Genesis 1:2 as part of the chaotic formlessness from which God creates order. Now, as judgment descends, that chaos is invoked—the ordered world is being un-created. The comparison of the army's roar to the sea's roar is not merely volume but evokes a sense of something unstoppable and vast, a force that violates the boundary between the ordered world and chaos. The second part of the verse shifts perspective: 'if one looks to the land, behold darkness.' This is not meteorological darkness but spiritual and moral darkness. The phrase echoes verse 20, where Isaiah condemned those who 'put darkness for light and light for darkness.' Now that moral inversion has consequences: literal darkness descends. The final image—'the light is darkened in the heavens thereof'—is a deliberate inversion of Genesis 1:3 ('Let there be light'). The creative word that brought forth light is now reversed, and darkness dominates. This is not merely military defeat; it is eschatological unraveling, a reversal of creation itself. The chapter ends without hope, without a word of redemption, painting a portrait of judgment so complete that even the cosmos seems to participate in the reversal.

word_study.meaning: *Nahama* = to roar, growl, murmur; *yam* = sea. The sea's roar is a specific, evocative sound—the surge of waves against the shore, a sound of primal power.
word_study.significance: In Hebrew cosmology, the sea represents chaos and the boundary between the ordered world and formlessness. To compare the army to the roaring sea is to invoke that primordial chaos. The army is not merely destructive; it represents the unraveling of order itself. The Covenant Rendering preserves this nuance: 'like the roaring of the sea.'

word_study.meaning: Darkness, obscurity, the absence of light. In biblical theology, darkness often represents evil, judgment, death, and spiritual alienation from God (who is light).
word_study.significance: The word *choshek* appears in verse 20 ('woe unto them that call evil good and good evil'—a moral inversion) and appears again in verse 30 (the consequences of that inversion). The connection is not accidental: moral darkness leads to literal darkness. This is a principle of judgment: you reap what you sow.

word_study.meaning: Distress, trouble, anguish, constriction. Often describes the pressure of enemies or the psychological state of those under siege.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering translates this as 'distress,' which captures the sense of being hemmed in, under pressure, with no escape. It is not merely sadness but the existential pressure of a world collapsing.

word_study.term_english: the light is darkened in the heavens
word_study.meaning: *Or* = light; *chashakh* = to grow dark, to be darkened (in passive voice); *arifim* = clouds, thick darkness, the heavens.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'light is darkened' is paradoxical: light by nature is not darkened; it is the absence of light that is darkness. Isaiah's phrasing suggests that the very source of light is being obscured or extinguished. This is a cosmic reversal. The world is not being conquered but un-created.

cross_references.connection: Genesis opens with darkness and formlessness ('the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep') until God says 'Let there be light.' Isaiah 5:30 reverses this movement: light fades, darkness dominates. Creation is being unmade by judgment.

'For the stars of heaven and the constellations thereof shall not give their light: the sun shall be darkened in his going forth, and the moon shall not cause her light to shine.' This eschatological darkening echoes Isaiah 5:30's cosmic reversal, suggesting a pattern of judgment that darkens the heavens.

The psalmist recalls God's power over the sea: 'Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength: thou brakest the heads of the dragons in the waters.' The sea that roars in Isaiah 5:30 is the same primal chaos that God established order over; now that order is violated.

'Woe unto you that desire the day of the LORD! to what end is it for you? the day of the LORD is darkness, and not light...even very dark, and no brightness in it.' Amos uses identical imagery of judgment bringing darkness instead of expected light, reinforcing this prophetic pattern.

'And the love of men shall wax cold, and iniquity shall abound...nevertheless, when the day cometh when the Son of Man shall come down in his glory.' The darkness of Isaiah 5:30 prefigures the darkness that will precede Christ's return—but His coming reverses it with light.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near Eastern world understood darkness literally and symbolically. Darkness meant vulnerability—predators hunted at night, enemies could attack unseen. Darkness also meant spiritual separation from the divine; the gods were associated with light, order, and the visible heavens. An eclipse, a dust storm obscuring the sky, or smoke from burning cities would have been understood not merely as meteorological phenomena but as cosmic disturbance, a sign that the order of things was violating. When Isaiah describes the light being 'darkened in the heavens,' his audience would have understood this both as literal (perhaps dust from invasion, or the smoke of burning crops and towns) and as spiritual (the withdrawal of divine order and favor). The roaring of the sea that drowns the warning of approach would have been understood by Levantine peoples (who lived on or near Mediterranean coasts) as an apocalyptic image: even nature itself is against you, and there is no escape.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 7:15 speaks of the weight of darkness that comes upon those who reject the gospel: 'And he shall go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith he will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people.' While Alma speaks of Christ bearing darkness, the principle is that those who reject God's redemption experience genuine darkness, a reversal of the light offered.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:21-22 speaks of the Lord 'coming down out of heaven, clothed in the brightness of his glory, to hear the cries of the saints and to answer their prayers...Wherefore, verily I say unto you, let the wicked take heed, for the day of the Lord cometh as a thief in the night.' The contrast is stark: while Isaiah 5:30 describes darkness descending on the covenant breaker, D&C promises light for the faithful.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment includes a symbolic journey from darkness to light, from ignorance to knowledge, from spiritual death to eternal life. Isaiah 5:30's movement from light to darkness represents the opposite journey—the consequence of covenant rejection. The temple teaches that the movement of the soul determines illumination; those who turn from God experience spiritual darkness.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ came as 'the light of the world' (John 8:12), and His resurrection reversed the darkness of the crucifixion. In Revelation 1:7, Christ's appearance is described with light imagery: 'Behold, he cometh with clouds; and every eye shall see him.' Significantly, Christ's judgment also brings light—it exposes all things (2 Timothy 1:10: 'Jesus Christ...hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel'). In contrast to Isaiah 5:30's darkness, Christ's judgment is accompanied by illumination. Those who come to Him move from darkness to light; those who reject Him experience His absence as darkness.
commentary.application: Isaiah 5:30, as the conclusion to a chapter of mounting judgment, serves as a warning about the cascading consequences of covenant rejection. The darkness described here is not arbitrary or temporary; it is the natural result of persistent refusal to obey God's law.
