Jeremiah also receives a commission to a people who will not listen: 'Thou therefore gird up thy loins, and arise, and speak unto them all that I command thee.' Like Isaiah, Jeremiah is called to prophesy even when rejection is assured.

The Lord tells Joseph Smith: 'Wherefore, I the Lord, knowing the calamity which should come upon the inhabitants of the earth, called upon my servant Joseph Smith.' Even in the Restoration, the principle holds: prophets are called to warn people who often will not heed.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern literature, divine commissions sometimes included success scenarios and sometimes included suffering and rejection. Isaiah's commission belongs to the second category. The prophet is not a success story in worldly terms; he is a 'sign and a wonder' (Isaiah 8:18) of judgment, not salvation. The judicial hardening Isaiah describes echoes ancient Near Eastern concepts of divine judgment: God confirms people in the condition they choose. In Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts, gods sometimes allow humans to proceed in their chosen folly to their own destruction. The model is not that God randomly hardens hearts but that He honors human choice by confirming it. The people have already chosen not to understand; Isaiah's mission is to make that choice irreversible through the word of God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi encounters the exact principle when he preaches to Israel. The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows that God's word can harden hearts as well as soften them (see Alma 24:30: 'they had become hardened in their hearts'). Abinadi explicitly quotes Isaiah 6:9 in Mosiah 12:26-28, applying it to King Noah's court. The Nephites understood that Isaiah's hardening commission applied not only to ancient Israel but to any people who reject the word of God. The principle is trans-historical: God sends prophets; some hear, some harden their hearts, and God honors that hardening.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 112:23 records the Lord telling Hyrum Smith: 'Therefore let your hearts be comforted; for all things shall work together for your good, and virtue shall go forth from you.' Yet earlier in D&C 1:30, the Lord acknowledges that some 'hearken to my voice' while others do not. The Restoration teaches that God sends His word; the people choose their response; God confirms their choice through His judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, the veil separates those who have made covenant (who can see) from those who have not (who cannot). Isaiah's commission to preach to those who cannot perceive illustrates the principle that spiritual blindness is not God's original intent but the result of human choice. Those who reject God's word progressively lose their capacity to see spiritual truth until the veil becomes absolute.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah's commission to preach to those who will not understand foreshadows Jesus's own experience. Jesus also performed signs and spoke parables to a people largely unable or unwilling to perceive Him. John 12:40 quotes Isaiah 6:10 directly to explain why 'they could not believe' in Jesus, even after seeing His miracles. Like Isaiah, Jesus was sent to judge as well as to save—His word became a sign of division (Luke 2:34). The hardening that Isaiah announces is the same hardening that will operate against Christ. Both messengers are rejected; both their rejections confirm people in spiritual blindness.
commentary.application: For modern believers, Isaiah's experience teaches humility about the limits of prophetic preaching and missionary work. Not all who hear will understand; not all who are taught will believe. The responsibility of the bearer of God's word is to deliver it faithfully, not to guarantee conversion. Isaiah volunteers for a mission in which failure, by worldly standards, is built in. Yet he goes anyway because his obedience is to God, not conditioned on results. For members called to teach, testify, or serve missions, the principle is clear: say what you are called to say with clarity and courage, and release the outcome to the Lord. The 'this people' language also warns against judgment: one does not determine who is in the hardened category and who is not. Isaiah teaches those he is sent to; God's Spirit discerns hearts. The commission is to preach, not to predetermine who will hear.

text_kjv: Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed.

commentary.narrative: The commission deepens into active hardening. Three imperatives—make the heart fat, make the ears heavy, shut the eyes—target the three organs of spiritual perception in Hebrew anthropology. The heart (lev) is the seat of understanding and decision-making. The ears receive revelation. The eyes perceive signs and wonders. All three must be sealed off. The purpose clause (pen—'lest') reveals the terrifying logic: the sealing-off is intended to prevent the very sequence of salvation: seeing, hearing, understanding, repenting (shuv—turning), being healed (rapa). Each step is blocked. Isaiah is not commissioned merely to witness rejection; he is commissioned to prevent conversion.
commentary.narrative_continued: The command to 'make the heart fat' (hashmen lev) is particularly vivid. A heart that is 'fattened' is coated over, insulated, incapable of receiving impressions. The image is of spiritual hardening as a physical coating. The Hebrew verb shaman ('to be fat') is used figuratively for the thickening and hardening of things—a heart weighed down by its own resistance. The people have already begun closing themselves; Isaiah's commission is to complete the process. This is judicial hardening in the fullest sense: God confirms in judgment what humans have already chosen in rebellion. It echoes Pharaoh in Exodus, where Pharaoh hardens his own heart first, and then God hardens it—not in arbitrary cruelty but in confirmation of human choice.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The healing clause ('and be healed,' rapa le) at the end is crucial. Healing in Hebrew prophetic theology is always spiritual healing—the restoration of a right relationship with God, the recovery of vision and hearing in spiritual matters. The command to prevent healing means preventing restoration, preventing the possibility of return. This is not temporary suspension of conversion but a sealing-off that may be permanent. The passage confronts the theological reality that humans can resist God so thoroughly that their resistance hardens into a condition of un-convertibility. This is the danger that haunts all of Isaiah's ministry: speaking to people who have already closed themselves off.

word_study.meaning: To make fat, to make thick, to coat over. The hifil form here is causative: 'cause to be fat.' Metaphorically, it means to render insensitive, to dull, to cover over with a barrier.
word_study.significance: The image of spiritual insensitivity as fatness or thickness is striking and tactile. A fat or greasy heart cannot be touched by the sharp edge of God's word. The Covenant Rendering chooses 'dull' to capture this sense of diminished sensitivity.

word_study.meaning: To make heavy, to weigh down, to burden. In the sense used here, it means to render heavy and sluggish—incapable of quick response.
word_study.significance: Heavy ears cannot leap up to hear the word of God. They are weighted down, sluggish, unresponsive. The verb kaved (heaviness, honor, weight) is used throughout Isaiah for the glory and weight of God's presence, but here it is inverted: the people's ears become heavy, incapable of responding to that glory.

word_study.term_original: שׁוּעַ (sha'a) or variants meaning 'seal, smear over, shut'
word_study.meaning: To shut, to close, to seal, to smear over. The image is of closing or coating the eyes so they cannot function.
word_study.significance: The three verbs—hashmen, hakbed, sha'a—progressively seal off the three channels of spiritual perception. The totality of sensory and intellectual shutdown is complete.

word_study.meaning: To turn, to return, to repent. The fundamental Hebrew verb for repentance and restoration of relationship with God.
word_study.significance: The entire arc of salvation is summarized in this clause: see → hear → understand → turn (shuv) → be healed. The blocking of shuv blocks the entire path of return to God. Shuv is not mere intellectual change but directional reversal—a complete 180-degree reorientation toward God.

word_study.meaning: To heal, to restore, to make whole. Used both physically and spiritually. Spiritual healing means the restoration of one's relationship with God.
word_study.significance: The healing Isaiah must prevent is restoration—the mending of the breach between God and people. By preventing vision, hearing, understanding, and repentance, Isaiah prevents healing. The hardened people remain in their spiritual sickness.

cross_references.connection: Pharaoh hardens his own heart; then God hardens it: 'And I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.' The judicial hardening of Isaiah parallels Pharaoh's hardening—it is confirmation in judgment, not arbitrary cruelty.

Paul cites both Exodus and Isaiah to explain the principle of hardening: 'Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth.' The hardening described in Isaiah is part of God's sovereign pattern across history.
The covenant curse of judicial blindness: 'The LORD shall smite thee with madness, and blindness, and astonishment of heart.' The hardening Isaiah announces fulfills the covenant curse for rebellion.

Alma teaches the principle of spiritual hardening: 'And thus he becomes a lesser and a lesser vessel, until his sins have overcometh his mercies, and then cometh the condemnation.' The Book of Mormon validates the principle that persistent rejection results in confirmed blindness.

The Lord warns of the danger of hardness: 'I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men.' The possibility of forgiveness remains open; hardening is the result of refusing to extend or receive forgiveness.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thinking, hardness of heart was understood as a condition that could become irreversible. The Egyptian Instruction of Ptahhotep warns against 'stiffening the neck.' Mesopotamian texts describe people who 'harden their ears' against the gods' word. Judicial hardening was seen as a response to persistent rebellion: the gods would confirm a person or nation in their chosen path until that path led to destruction. In Israelite thought, particularly reflected in the Deuteronomic history and the prophets, rejection of God's word led to a spiral of increasing blindness. The first refusal makes the second refusal easier; the second makes the third inevitable. By the time Isaiah's commission is executed, Israel's rebellion has already become systemic, and the hardening is the judicial recognition of that reality.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon shows hardening in real time. The people of Nephi repeatedly 'stiffen their necks' against prophetic warning until God removes His Spirit (Helaman 13:33). Korihor, the anti-Christ, is struck dumb—his mouth is sealed—because he persisted in rebellion (Alma 30:49-56). The pattern is consistent: persistent rejection hardens the heart; hardened hearts lose their capacity to perceive God's word; loss of perception becomes irreversible when the pattern continues. The Book of Mormon illustrates that hardening is not instantaneous but progressive.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:63-64 reveals the mechanism of spiritual death through rejection: 'Behold, I say unto you that the whole heavens and the earth are full of my glory; And all things whatsoever are upon the earth, in the seas, or in the heavens, are mine.' Yet those who reject this truth increasingly become blind to it. The Restoration teaches that hardening is the inverse of light—those who refuse light gradually descend into darkness that becomes self-perpetuating.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, the veil represents the barrier between the mundane and the divine. Isaiah's hardening command describes a people who have placed an impenetrable veil between themselves and God—not a veil they can pass through (as in the temple) but a veil from which they cannot escape. The difference is covenantal: those who enter into covenant can remove the veil; those who reject covenant are sealed behind it.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus enters the world as the embodiment of light and healing (rapa). His entire ministry is an invitation to see (perceive the signs), hear (receive His teaching), understand (discern His messianic identity), and turn (repent and be restored). The hardening that Isaiah announces is the same hardening that confronts Jesus: those who refuse to see will be confirmed in blindness; those who refuse to hear will become deaf to the Gospel. Yet Jesus comes not only as judge but as healer; His death provides the atonement that makes healing possible even for the most hardened (though they must choose to accept it).
commentary.application: The verse presents a sobering reality for modern believers: persistent rejection of spiritual truth hardens the heart in ways that become difficult to reverse. Every refusal to listen, every rejection of conviction from the Holy Ghost, every hardening against testimony makes the next refusal easier. The application is not fatalistic—the hardening is not random or predetermined—but urgent: one must not become like 'this people' through habitual rejection of God's word. For those bearing testimony, the verse explains why some remain unmoved even by powerful witness: they have already chosen not to hear, and that choice has become habit and then character. The mission is not to force conversion but to testify clearly, knowing that some have already sealed themselves off. The calling is to speak to those who can hear, not to despair over those who will not.

text_kjv: Then said I, Lord, how long? And he answered, Until the cities be wasted without inhabitant, and the houses without man, and the land be utterly desolate,

commentary.narrative: Isaiah's response to the commission is not acceptance but lament. 'How long?' (ad-matay) is the classic question of grief and bewilderment in Scripture. It does not protest the justice of the hardening but begs for its duration to be limited. Isaiah has just learned that his mission is to a people already closed against understanding, and his preaching will deepen that closure. Now he learns that the hardening will continue until total destruction. The answer is devastating: the commission will stand until cities are emptied, houses abandoned, and the land itself lies desolate—until the very infrastructure of human civilization has been unmade.
commentary.narrative_continued: The three-part destruction—cities without inhabitants, houses without people, land utterly desolate—reverses the three-part gift promised in Deuteronomy 6:10-11: 'The LORD thy God shall bring thee into the land which he sware unto thy fathers, and thou shalt possess great and goodly cities, which thou buildedst not, And houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not.' The covenant blessings were cities, houses, and cultivated land. The curse is the loss of all three. This is the language of covenant reversal—God will undo the gift because the people have broken the covenant. The desolation is not random catastrophe but the fulfillment of the covenant curses spelled out in Leviticus 26:31-35 and Deuteronomy 28:51-52.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: Isaiah's question is accepted by God; it receives a full answer. The prophet is not rebuked for asking but given the truth—the complete truth of the devastation his prophetic word will witness. The answer covers the entire span of Isaiah's ministry and beyond: from his time through the Assyrian exile (eighth century BCE) and the later Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem (sixth century BCE). Isaiah himself will not live to see the fullest fulfillment, but he is told that his word will stand against the people until the cities are emptied.

word_study.meaning: Until when? How long? A temporal question expressing bewilderment and grief. The phrase appears frequently in the Psalms and lament literature.
word_study.significance: Ad-matay is not defiance but desolation—not 'Why must this be?' but 'How much longer must this endure?' Isaiah has already accepted the justice of the hardening; he simply pleads for its term to be limited. The question expresses the heart of prophecy: speaking hard truth while grieving the consequences.

word_study.meaning: Devastated, laid waste, desolate, emptied. The state of having been destroyed or abandoned.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests not merely military defeat but complete depopulation and desolation. The cities are not conquered and resettled but emptied entirely.

word_study.meaning: Desolation, devastation, abandonment. The feminine noun emphasizes the state of being utterly forsaken and uninhabitable.
word_study.significance: The land itself is personified as a grieving widow, emptied of inhabitants, left alone. The desolation is total and final—it includes the land, not just the people.

cross_references.connection: The covenant curse: 'And I will make your cities waste, and bring your sanctuaries unto desolation... and your land shall be desolate.' Isaiah's answer echoes the specific covenant curses for covenant violation.

Another covenant curse: 'he shall besiege thee in all thy gates, until thy high and fenced walls come down, wherein thou trustedst, throughout all thy land.' The siege, the desolation, and the reversal of blessing are the covenant-curse pattern.

David's ad-matay: 'How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?' The question of the faithful in grief becomes Isaiah's question as a prophet witnessing judgment.

Jeremiah describes the same reversal—the land returning to formlessness: 'I beheld the earth, and, lo, it was without form, and void... the cities thereof were broken down.' The second major exile (Babylonian) fulfills what Isaiah prophesied.

Parallel covenant-curse language: 'And when your enemies are in your fields, they shall spill out your blood upon the earth.' Disobedience to covenant results in loss of the land—the same principle operates in all dispensations.

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah prophesied during the reign of King Uzziah (c. 740 BCE) and the rise of the Assyrian Empire under Sargon II and Sennacherib. The destruction he describes was fulfilled partially in 722 BCE when the northern kingdom of Israel fell to Assyria and again in 586 BCE when the southern kingdom of Judah fell to Babylon. Cities were indeed emptied, temples destroyed, populations deported. The desolation Isaiah witnessed or prophesied was not hypothetical but historically realized. The language of covenant reversal (emptied cities, abandoned houses, desolate land) would have been stark and recognizable to Isaiah's audience: they knew the covenant curses; they were aware that covenant violation led to such consequences.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records similar cycles of covenant-keeping and covenant-breaking resulting in prosperity or desolation (Helaman 4:24-26). When the Nephites and Lamanites turn from righteousness, their cities are emptied and laid waste (3 Nephi 8-9). The principle is consistent: covenant violation results in removal from the promised land. Mormon's record shows repeated cycles of this pattern throughout Nephite history. The 'how long?' lament appears throughout the Book of Mormon as righteous leaders grieve the hardness of their people's hearts.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 101:43-50 reveals that the principle of covenant and land continues in the Restoration. The 'promised land' of Zion is contingent on covenant obedience. The exodus of saints from Missouri, the desolation that follows their departure, and later restoration parallels the pattern: when covenant is broken, the land is emptied; when covenant is renewed, it is restored. D&C 121:33 states the principle: 'The rights of the priesthood are inseparably connected with the powers of heaven, and... the powers of heaven cannot be controlled nor handled only upon the principles of righteousness.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Isaiah's vision takes place in the temple, where covenant is centered. The hardening commission and the desolation that results represent the ultimate consequence of covenant violation—removal from the sanctuary, from the land, from God's presence. Those who break covenant are emptied from the land as the land is emptied of people.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah's lament ('How long?') foreshadows Jesus's own lament over Jerusalem: 'O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets... how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!' (Matthew 23:37). Both prophets speak judgment while grieving the judgment they must pronounce. Both witness the desolation of the city and the land. Christ's coming cannot prevent the hardening Isaiah describes; instead, Christ enters into it, carries it, and at last offers a healing beyond the physical restoration of cities and houses—a spiritual restoration through His atonement.
commentary.application: Isaiah's answer to 'How long?' teaches that divine judgment has both timeline and term. It is not random or eternal (verse 13 will hint at a 'tenth' that remains). The word of God will stand against a rebellious people until the consequences are utterly exhausted—until cities fall, people are exiled, and the land lies empty. But the term is set; it is not infinite. This gives both urgency and hope: urgency because the judgment is coming, hope because the judgment is limited. For modern believers, the principle applies to both individuals and nations: covenant violation leads to progressive spiritual desolation; the process can be reversed only by covenant renewal. The lament 'How long?' is appropriate for those witnessing injustice or the effects of sin, but it must be paired with willingness to continue speaking God's word faithfully, knowing that the timeline is in God's hands.

text_kjv: And the LORD have removed men far away, and there be a great forsaking in the midst of the land.

commentary.narrative: The final verse of Isaiah's commissioning vision completes the answer to 'How long?' The removal of people far away (richaq yehvah et-ha'adam) is the language of exile. God Himself—actively, personally—drives the people from the land. This is not invasion by foreign armies as an impersonal historical force but divine action: 'the LORD has sent the people far away.' The 'great forsaking' (azuvah) that follows is not just the physical absence of people but the sense of abandonment—the land itself is left orphaned, desolate, without inhabitants. The land mourns the loss of its people; the people mourn their separation from the land.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verse establishes a terrifying reality: covenant violation results in exile. God does not arbitrarily cast out His people, but when they persistently reject His word, He honors their choice by removing them from His presence—which is manifested in the land He gave them. The 'great forsaking' (rabba ha-azuvah) emphasizes the scale of the desolation. It is not a small or temporary abandonment but a sweeping, comprehensive emptying. Every house abandoned, every city emptied, the entire land left desolate. The covenant that began with a promise of land (Genesis 12:7) ends, when broken, with exile from the land.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The verb richaq ('sent far away') is in the hifil (causative) stem: God causes distance. This is not mere psychological separation but active removal. The people are not abandoned by God in the sense that God forgets them, but they are driven from His sanctuary, from His land, from His immediate presence in the temple. The covenant relationship, while not absolutely severed (as later prophecies show), is ruptured at its deepest level. Yet even here, at the nadir of judgment, the vision does not end in verse 12. Verse 13 will hint at restoration: a remnant will remain, a holy seed will survive. But first, the complete desolation must be witnessed and prophesied.

word_study.meaning: The Lord has caused distance / has sent far away. The hifil (causative) form makes God the active agent: He causes the removal, the distancing. Richaq in the hifil means to drive away, to remove to a distance, to exile.
word_study.significance: This is not circumstantial removal but divine action. God Himself orchestrates the exile. The active role of God in judgment emphasizes that exile is not meaningless suffering but covenant consequence. The distance is not arbitrary but just.

word_study.meaning: Abandonment, forsaking, the condition of being left desolate. The feminine noun emphasizes the land as a bereaved figure, emptied and alone.
word_study.significance: The land itself is personified in the forsaking. The earth grieves the departure of its inhabitants. In Hebrew thought, the land is not inert terrain but a covenanted entity that responds to the faithfulness or faithlessness of those who dwell on it (cf. Leviticus 18:28, where the land 'vomits out' those who defile it).

word_study.meaning: Much, great, many, abundant. The feminine adjective modifying azuvah ('forsaking') emphasizes the scale and extent of the desolation.
word_study.significance: The desolation is not partial or limited but comprehensive. The land is not partially forsaken but greatly, abundantly left alone.

cross_references.connection: The principle of covenant and land: 'That the land spue not you out also, when ye defile it, as it spued out the nations that were before you.' The land itself responds to covenant violation by rejecting its inhabitants.

The covenant curse of exile: 'I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day, that ye shall soon utterly perish from off the land whereunto ye go over Jordan to possess it... And the LORD shall scatter you among the nations.' The removal and scattering are covenant consequences.

The fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy in the Assyrian captivity: 'So was Israel carried away out of their own land to Assyria unto this day.' The northern kingdom's exile in 722 BCE realizes Isaiah's prophecy.

The Babylonian exile likewise fulfills the prophecy: 'And them that had escaped from the sword carried he away to Babylon.' The southern kingdom's exile in 586 BCE completes the desolation Isaiah foresaw.

The principle operates in the Restoration: 'Yea, let them repent of all their sins, and desire to keep my commandments, and I will receive them... But unto the wicked I say: Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from the house of Israel.' Covenant violation results in removal even in the latter days.

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah prophesied against the backdrop of the Assyrian Empire's expansion under Sargon II and Sennacherib in the eighth century BCE. The northern kingdom fell in 722 BCE; Judah narrowly escaped and then fell in 586 BCE to Babylon. The language of removal and exile was not theoretical for Isaiah's audience but an encroaching historical reality. The desolation he described—emptied cities, abandoned houses—would become literal in the archaeological record: excavations show destruction layers, abandoned settlements, and population shifts corresponding to these invasions. The principle of covenant curse fulfillment through military defeat and exile was well-established in Deuteronomic theology and understood by Isaiah's contemporaries.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon shows the same pattern cyclically: covenant violation leads to war, destruction, and removal from the promised land (see Helaman 4:24-26, 3 Nephi 8-9). When the Nephites break covenant, they are removed from their cities. The principle is consistent: the promised land is contingent on covenant keeping. The land itself responds to covenant violation by becoming a place of desolation. Later in Latter-day Saint history, saints would experience similar removal from promised lands (Ohio, Missouri, Illinois, Utah)—each time due to covenant violation or opposition to the covenant community.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 101:1-7 addresses the saints' exile from Jackson County, Missouri: 'Verily thus saith the Lord unto you who have assembled yourselves together to receive my words.' The revelation acknowledges that while Satan sought to destroy the saints through removal, God's purposes are not thwarted. The principle of removal as consequence of covenant violation operates in the Restoration as it did in Isaiah's time. D&C 64:34-37 reveals the deeper principle: forgiveness and covenant renewal restore what violation has lost.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Exile from the promised land is exile from the place of God's sanctuary. In Isaiah's time, this meant removal from the temple in Jerusalem, from the place of covenant renewal and atonement. The temple is the center of covenantal life; exile is separation from that center. In the Restoration, members who break covenant find themselves spiritually exiled even if physically present. The temple becomes inaccessible; the fullness of covenant blessing is withheld. Conversely, covenant faithfulness and renewal restore access to the temple and its blessings.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus experiences a form of exile when He is crucified outside the city, removed from the people who rejected Him. 'Behold, we go up to Jerusalem; and the Son of man shall be delivered unto the chief priests and unto the scribes; and they shall condemn him to death, And shall deliver him to the Gentiles' (Matthew 20:18-19). Yet Jesus's removal becomes redemptive: His separation from the presence of God the Father (the ultimate desolation) for the sake of all humanity effects universal reconciliation and the possibility of return from exile. The exile Isaiah describes is fulfilled not only in the Assyrian and Babylonian captivities but in the spiritual exile of humanity separated from God—an exile that Christ alone can reverse through His atonement.
commentary.application: Verse 12 soberly teaches that covenant violation has ultimate consequences: separation from God's presence and the land of promise. For modern believers, this does not mean that one lapse results in permanent exile but that persistent, unrepented covenant violation leads progressively away from God's presence. The verse calls for vigilance: if the ancient Israelites could be removed from the promised land despite their covenants with Abraham and Moses, no group of believers is guaranteed protection through heritage alone. Covenants must be renewed and kept daily. Conversely, the verse offers hope for those in spiritual exile: if exile came through covenant violation, return comes through covenant renewal. The land was repopulated when the exiles returned (Nehemiah, Ezra); individuals and communities can be restored when they turn from violation back to covenant. The application is urgent for those sensing spiritual distance from God: the remedy is not more effort or works but covenant renewal—seeking readmission to the sanctuary of God's presence through sincere repentance and renewed commitment.

text_kjv: But yet in it shall be a tenth, and it shall return, and shall be eaten: as a teil tree, and as an oak, whose substance is in them, when they cast their leaves: so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 6:13 closes the throne-room vision with a stunning reversal: after the prophet has been commissioned to proclaim destruction so total that cities are emptied and the land becomes a wasteland (verses 11–12), God now offers a word of hope. The passage balances unflinching judgment with qualified redemption. A tenth shall remain—a mercy, yet even this remnant 'shall return' (or be turned over, burned again). The language is neither comfortable nor triumphant; it is bracingly honest about judgment's severity. Yet even after this second burning, the metaphor shifts to forestry: a terebinth or oak tree, when felled, leaves behind a stump. That stump is living wood; it contains within itself the capacity to regenerate. This stump becomes the poem's theological pivot—it is 'the holy seed.'

The phrase 'holy seed' (zera qodesh in Hebrew) is the climax not just of verse 13 but of the entire chapter. It reconnects to the seraphim's cry of 'Holy, holy, holy' (verse 3), the very holiness that appeared to threaten destruction now becomes the character of the remnant itself. God's holiness both judges and redeems. The remnant is not a convenient escape clause or a generic survival of a fraction of the population; it is 'holy'—set apart by God for divine purposes, bearing God's character within it. This seed implies futurity: it will grow, will produce new life, will restore what judgment has decimated. The Covenant Rendering's translation—'the holy seed is its stump'—captures this better than the KJV's somewhat muddled 'whose substance is in them, when they cast their leaves.' The stump is the physical, material reality of hope rooted in judgment.

This verse stands as one of the most textually difficult in Isaiah, with variants in the Masoretic Text, the Septuagint, and the Dead Sea Scrolls (1QIsaᵃ). Yet across these traditions, the core promise remains identical: zera qodesh—the holy seed endures. The apparent compression and difficulty of the Hebrew grammar may even reflect the prophet's struggle to articulate what he has seen. How does one say that total devastation leaves behind a living root? The broken syntax mirrors the broken landscape, yet within that brokenness, life persists.

word_study.meaning: A tithe or a tenth part; a specific fraction denoting what remains. In the context of judgment, it emphasizes both severity (nine-tenths destroyed) and mercy (one-tenth preserved). The term echoes the language of agricultural tithe, suggesting that even the remnant belongs to God.
word_study.significance: The 'tenth' establishes the numerical foundation for remnant theology in Isaiah. It is not arbitrary but covenantal—God reserves a portion as sacred and belonging to Him.

word_study.meaning: To return, turn, turn back, or restore. In this context, the Niphal form (shall be turned/burned again) suggests passive transformation—the remnant itself will experience renewed judgment. The root shub is foundational in Isaiah, where repentance (return to God) and restoration (God's return to His people) interweave.
word_study.significance: The verb shub anchors remnant theology to covenant: judgment and restoration are cycles within God's faithfulness. The remnant does not escape judgment; it passes through it and is thereby refined (see Zechariah 13:9, where refining fire purifies the remnant).

word_study.meaning: To eat, consume, devour. In prophetic judgment language, it conveys destruction utterly—fire consumes the land. The KJV's 'eaten' may carry associations with consumption by exile or military conquest as well as literal burning.
word_study.significance: The image of being eaten/consumed emphasizes the totality of judgment. Even the remnant of the remnant experiences devastation. Yet as the stump remains beneath the consumed tree, life persists beneath apparent annihilation.

word_study.meaning: A terebinth tree, likely the turpentine tree (Pistacia), valued in the ancient Near East for its wood and resin. The KJV's 'teil tree' is archaic and obscure; modern translations prefer 'terebinth' or 'oak.' These are large, sturdy trees whose root systems are remarkably persistent after felling.
word_study.significance: The tree metaphor is not accidental. In Israelite imagination, trees symbolized stability, covenant (the oak at Mamre was a covenant site), and life force. That a felled tree's stump could regenerate was observable reality—these are not fantasies but botanical fact that Isaiah presses into theological service.

word_study.meaning: The stump or base of a tree left after felling; also can mean a standing stone or pillar. The root form means 'to stand' or 'to be set upright.' In The Covenant Rendering, it is rendered as 'stump,' emphasizing both its material reality and its living potential. The KJV's 'substance' is vaguer but not entirely wrong—the matsevet is the substantial part that remains.
word_study.significance: Matsevet carries covenantal weight in Hebrew Bible (Jacob's stone pillar at Bethel, Joshua's stones of remembrance). Here, the stump is both a natural remnant and a covenantal marker—God's faithfulness made visible in what persists through judgment.

word_study.meaning: 'Seed' (zera) denotes both offspring and future potential—what will grow and spread. 'Holy' (qodesh) means set apart, consecrated, belonging to God. Together, 'holy seed' refers to the remnant chosen and preserved by God, marked by God's own holiness. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this phrase identically, using the fuller spelling of qodesh (with waw), emphasizing its theological importance.
word_study.significance: This is the theological climax of Isaiah 6. The holiness that threatened Isaiah's life (verse 5: 'I am undone!') and the holiness that mandates desolation (verses 11–12) is now the character of the surviving remnant. God's holiness both judges and redeems. This seed will grow, will fill the earth, will become the foundation of restoration. Isaiah 11:1 will build directly on this promise: 'And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse.' The holy seed is not generic survival; it is God's preservation of His own purposes within His people.

cross_references.connection: The next major vision in Isaiah promises that 'there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse'—a direct fulfillment of the stump's regeneration promised here. The holy seed produces the Branch (Messiah).

Echoes the remnant principle: 'Two parts therein shall be cut off and die; but the third shall be left therein' (Zechariah 13:8), and that remnant 'shall call on my name, and I will hear them' (13:9). Both passages merge judgment with refinement.

Paul quotes Isaiah 10:22–23 to teach that 'a remnant according to the election of grace' survives (Romans 11:5). The holy seed becomes the theological foundation for Paul's argument about Israel's corporate salvation.

Speaks of believers being 'born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God which liveth and abideth for ever.' The language of 'seed' (sperma) and its eternal character draws on the zera qodesh theology of Isaiah.

The Lord promises the covenant people, 'I am in your midst,' and speaks of preservation and eventual restoration—echoing the stump theology where judgment coexists with divine faithfulness and the promise of renewal.

commentary.historical_context:
In the ancient Near East, the tree stump metaphor was not exotic. Assyrian records document widespread deforestation and the destruction of forests as part of military and administrative policy. Yet any farmer or shepherd would have observed that oak and terebinth trees, once felled, often regenerated from the living root system. This is not fantasy; it is ecological observation. Isaiah harnesses this ordinary fact to express an extraordinary theological claim: judgment is real and total, yet life persists in covenant.

The 'tenth' also carries historical weight. In the ancient world, tithing was a form of covenantal obligation and divine claim; by using this term for the remnant, Isaiah signals that the survivors belong to God, not to themselves. They are God's tenth—consecrated and preserved for His purposes. The deportation policies of the Assyrian Empire (which would occur after Isaiah's time) literally fulfilled this prophecy: the Northern Kingdom was destroyed, but a tenth (roughly, a fraction) was left in the land or taken into exile, forming the basis for later restoration under Cyrus the Persian and subsequent Jewish renewal.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly employs remnant theology. Nephi writes in 2 Nephi 25:15, 'I knew that the Lord God would consecrate my people'—echoing the 'holy seed' language. The entire Nephite/Lamanite division and reunification pattern reflects the logic of Isaiah 6:13: judgment and preservation, destruction and regeneration. Most directly, 3 Nephi 16:10–11 records Christ explaining that the gospel will come 'to a remnant of this people,' a direct application of zera qodesh.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:2 states, 'I have decreed in my heart, saith the Lord, that I will speak unto you at all times, in all places'—a covenantal promise that echoes the stump's endurance through judgment. D&C 35:24–25 teaches that even when the Church is judged, 'a few' are preserved 'for their righteousness.' The Restoration doctrine of the kingdom's latter-day growth from a small remnant (the Church restored in 1830) directly embodies the holy seed theology of Isaiah 6:13.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment teaches that humanity, though fallen and destined for judgment, carries within itself divine nature ('male and female created he them in the image of God,' Genesis 1:27). The stump bearing the holy seed parallels this: within the fallen, within the judged, persists what is sacred and capable of eternal growth. The sealing power—'that which is bound on earth shall be bound in heaven' (D&C 132:46)—ensures that the holy seed is not lost; family lines, covenantal bonds, endure through mortality and judgment.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 6:13 is fundamentally messianic prophecy, though indirectly. The 'holy seed' of verse 13 becomes the 'Rod out of the stem of Jesse' in Isaiah 11:1, a passage the early Church unanimously applied to Jesus Christ. The logic is this: if a stump can regenerate and produce new growth (11:1), then the holy seed must be capable of messianic manifestation. The stump, seemingly dead, holds within it the life force that will produce the Branch. Christ is the ultimate fulfillment of the remnant principle—He is the holy seed par excellence, bearing in Himself the holiness of God (Hebrews 1:3: 'the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person') and the future of humanity. In submitting to judgment (the crucifixion), He becomes the stump from which new life—resurrection, eternal life for believers—springs. The logic of Isaiah 6:13 reaches its climax in Christ: judgment and redemption are not opposites but chapters in a single story of covenantal faithfulness.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 6:13 offers a hardened realism about discipleship combined with an unshakeable hope. The verse does not promise that the righteous will be spared judgment or hardship. The 'tenth' that remains 'shall return' and 'be eaten'—meaning even the faithful remnant experiences tribulation, refinement, and loss. This is biblical and honest. Yet within that experience, life persists. The stump theology means this: whatever you face—personal tragedy, family loss, collective crisis, doubt, wilderness—you are not annihilated. The holy seed within you, your connection to God's covenantal purposes, remains. It cannot be consumed. It is capable of regeneration. In difficult seasons, when spiritual life feels burned away, the stump doctrine promises that roots remain and new growth is possible. Practically, this means: endure; trust the metaphor of the living root; know that covenant is not fragile but persistent; believe in resurrection—both literal and figurative. The holy seed is within you; let it grow.

text_kjv: And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah, that Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up toward Jerusalem to war against it, but could not prevail against it.

commentary.narrative:
This verse opens the Syro-Ephraimite crisis, one of the defining moments of Isaiah's ministry. The genealogy—Ahaz, son of Jotham, son of Uzziah—matters theologically: Uzziah is the king in whose death-year Isaiah received his throne-vision (6:1). That vision showed Isaiah the exalted Lord; now Isaiah must watch a descendant of that royal line face existential threat. The spiritual continuity of the dynasty is broken even as the genealogical line persists.

The historical situation was genuinely dire. In approximately 735 BCE, an anti-Assyrian coalition—led by Rezin of Aram (Syria) and Pekah of Israel (the northern kingdom, often called Ephraim after its dominant tribe)—sought to pressure Judah into joining their alliance against the Assyrian threat. When Ahaz refused, they moved to depose him and install a puppet ruler (v. 6). Yet notice the outcome: the text tells us immediately that they 'could not prevail against it.' The siege itself remains unnarrated—we never hear the battle. The suspense is not military but spiritual: how will Ahaz respond to God's call to faith?

The designation 'king of Syria' for Rezin reflects the Aramaic political structure; 'Syria' here means Aram, the Aramean kingdom north of Israel. The two-king coalition represents the northern powers against the southern Davidic dynasty. This is not a random territorial dispute but an assault on God's covenant with David (2 Samuel 7), which promised perpetual rule through David's line. God's response will protect the dynasty not because Ahaz deserves it but because the messianic promise is at stake.

word_study.meaning: to be able, to have power, to prevail; the root conveys both capacity and success. The negation lō' yakol means 'was not able' or 'could not overcome.' The Covenant Rendering's 'could not overpower it' captures the sense of military dominance that was unavailable to the coalition.
word_study.significance: The verb establishes the outcome before the narrative unfolds. Isaiah's audience knows the siege will fail. This allows the prophet to focus on the theological test: will Ahaz trust God's protection, or will fear drive him to human alliances (ultimately seeking Assyrian aid, which brings its own catastrophe)?

word_study.meaning: The name means 'my strength is Yah'—ironic for a king who was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:19-21). Uzziah's reign (c. 783–742 BCE) was marked by military strength and religious compromise; his final years saw him excluded from the temple.
word_study.significance: The genealogy reaches back to a king whose strength failed him. Ahaz inherits the name 'his father strengthened' (Jotham) from a line that began with divine strength but ended in disease and separation from the sanctuary. The pattern suggests spiritual decline even as royal power continued.

word_study.meaning: The dynasty, the royal line, the covenant house. In Hebrew thought, bet ('house') refers to both the physical building and the family line descending from an ancestor. The 'house of David' is the institution through which God's kingship is mediated to Israel.
word_study.significance: The threat is not merely to Ahaz as an individual but to the Davidic dynasty itself—which means it is a threat to God's own covenant promises. This explains why God responds with signs and promises in the next verses.

cross_references.connection: God's covenant with David, promising an eternal dynasty: 'thy throne shall be established for ever.' The Syro-Ephraimite crisis tests whether this covenant still holds.
The death of Uzziah marks the beginning of Isaiah's call vision. Ahaz, his great-grandson, now faces a crisis that will define whether the prophet's message of God's sovereign care is trustworthy.
The historical parallel account, showing that Ahaz ultimately sought Assyrian protection rather than trusting God—a choice that brought Assyrian domination and religious compromise.
An alternative historical narrative emphasizing Ahaz's unfaithfulness and idolatry during this crisis, offering a theologically critical perspective on his response.

commentary.historical_context: The Syro-Ephraimite War (c. 735 BCE) was a critical moment in Levantine geopolitics. Assyria under Tiglath-Pileser III was expanding westward and had begun tributary demands on the Aramean and Israeli kingdoms. An anti-Assyrian coalition formed, including Aram and Israel, seeking to pressure neighboring kingdoms into their alliance. When Ahaz refused, the coalition moved to overthrow him. Archaeologically, this event is corroborated by Assyrian records. The siege itself apparently failed—possibly due to Assyrian intervention elsewhere (Tiglath-Pileser was distracted by operations to the north), or simply because the city's fortifications held. The mention of the water aqueduct in v. 3 suggests Ahaz was conducting a military inspection of Jerusalem's crucial water supply, preparing for siege conditions. This is the same location (the upper pool) where an Assyrian general will later stand to threaten Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:17).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains numerous parallels to Ahaz's choice to seek human alliance rather than divine protection. Nephi warns against trusting in the arm of flesh (2 Nephi 4:34); the Nephite kings repeatedly face crises where trust in God is tested against fear-driven political maneuvering. The pattern of covenant people under threat, called to faith but tempted by worldly alliance, runs throughout the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 6:36 teaches 'fear not to do good,' a principle directly opposite to Ahaz's fearful response. D&C 38:30 promises 'if ye are prepared, ye shall not fear.' The crisis in Isaiah 7 becomes a case study in the consequences of unpreparedness and faithlessness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Davidic covenant, which God protects through this crisis, finds its ultimate expression in the temple order and in the messianic priesthood. Ahaz's failure to trust God is compounded by his later rejection of temple worship and adoption of pagan altar designs (2 Kings 16:10-16), showing how political faithlessness flows into spiritual corruption.

commentary.christological_typology: The protection of the Davidic dynasty in this crisis foreshadows God's protection of the messianic line. Though Ahaz himself will prove unfaithful, God preserves the dynasty through which the Messiah will come. The very next verses contain the Immanuel prophecy (v. 14), showing that even in the midst of human failure and political crisis, God's messianic promise remains intact and operative.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members face threats to faith that are functionally equivalent to Ahaz's crisis. We face pressures—from culture, from economic anxiety, from social pressure—that tempt us to seek protection in worldly alliances rather than trust in God's covenant promises. Ahaz's fear is understandable; his error is thinking that human strategy can substitute for faith. The question posed by Isaiah 7 is immediate and personal: when genuine threat comes, do we reach for God's word, or do we panic into the world's solutions?

text_kjv: And it was told the house of David, saying, Syria is confederate with Ephraim. And his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind.

commentary.narrative:
The news reaches the Davidic court that Aram and Ephraim (northern Israel) have formed a coalition—and the effect is immediate psychological collapse. The parallelism is striking: not just Ahaz's heart trembles, but the hearts of 'his people' as well. This is not individual fear but social panic. The report of 'confederation' (nāchāh, 'settling upon,' 'resting upon,' 'leaning into') conveys an active alliance, not a chance encounter. It is coordinated, intentional, and threatening.

The simile that follows is among the most vivid in Isaiah: their hearts shook 'like trees of the wood are moved with the wind.' In Hebrew thought, a tree in a wind is the image of helplessness—the tree has no choice, no agency, no control. The verb nua ('to shake, tremble, waver') describes involuntary motion. This is precisely the opposite of the steadfast faith Isaiah will demand in verse 4. The people are passively, helplessly trembling. They are not standing firm; they are not calling upon God; they are quaking.

Notice also that the message is directed to 'the house of David'—not just Ahaz personally but the entire royal institution. The threat is systemic. The Davidic covenant itself, which promised eternal rule, is now seemingly at risk. For the royal house and people of Judah, this moment feels like the end of everything they have been promised. Yet God's immediate response (v. 3) will reframe the crisis entirely: it is not about Ahaz's survival but about God's faithfulness to his own covenant.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'to rest upon,' 'to settle upon,' 'to lean into.' The root conveys the sense of settling into an alliance, placing weight upon, forming a union. The Covenant Rendering renders it 'has allied with,' capturing the sense of deliberate, resting union.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests not a temporary military alliance but a settled, intentional partnership. Aram and Ephraim are committed to this course. The use of nāchāh adds a note of finality—this is not wavering on their part. The irony is that while they settle confidently into alliance, Judah trembles without steadiness.

word_study.meaning: To shake, to tremble, to waver, to be moved involuntarily. The word describes passive, uncontrolled movement—the motion happens to the subject rather than being initiated by the subject. It is the motion of a tree moved by wind, not a tree bending at will.
word_study.significance: The choice of nua' is theologically important. Ahaz and his people are not making a deliberate choice; they are being tossed about by fear. This state of being moved by external forces stands in sharp contrast to the call to 'be still' and 'trust' in verse 4. Faith, by contrast, would be an active choice—a standing firm rather than a being shaken.

word_study.meaning: The dynasty, the royal institution, the lineage through which God's covenantal rule is mediated. In verse 2, 'the house of David' is the corporate entity receiving the news and experiencing the fear.
word_study.significance: The threat is institutional and covenantal. It is not merely that Ahaz personally is in danger; the very promise of eternal Davidic rule is being tested. This corporate dimension explains why God's response will be directed to the 'house of David' (v. 13) and will include the Immanuel sign—a promise of God's presence and protection for the dynasty, not just the individual king.

word_study.term_english: trees of the wood / forest trees
word_study.meaning: The trees of a forest, understood as a collective, vulnerable multitude subject to natural forces. In Hebrew imagery, a forest in wind is powerlessness and helplessness incarnate. The metaphor emphasizes that Judah's response is not a deliberate strategy but an involuntary panic.
word_study.significance: The simile levels the royal court with helpless vegetation. Normally, a king commands authority; here, Ahaz and his court are depicted as passive, subject to forces beyond their control. The irony—that a king positioned to rule is actually powerless—underscores the false crisis that fear creates. In reality, God is still sovereign; Ahaz just cannot see it yet.

cross_references.connection: The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion. Ahaz's trembling reflects the absence of faith; a righteous response would be boldness.

Isaiah later commands: 'Say ye not, A confederacy... neither fear ye their fear... Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself.' The same language of 'confederacy' appears; the remedy is to sanctify God rather than fear human alliance.
'The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?' A psalm expressing the opposite of Ahaz's response—confidence in God despite enemies and threats.

Nephi's injunction: 'O then, if I have seen so great things... why should my heart weep and my soul linger in the valley of sorrow?' The call to move from fear to faith based on God's proven faithfulness.

commentary.historical_context: The psychological reality of a siege threat in the ancient Near East cannot be overstated. A siege meant starvation, disease, and death. The combined forces of Aram and Israel represented the most powerful military powers in the Levant (apart from Assyria itself). From a purely military standpoint, Ahaz's fear was rational. However, Isaiah's point is that rational military calculation is precisely what faith transcends. The mention of the 'house of David' trembling together suggests that not only the king but his advisors, nobles, and people were seized by panic. This collective fear would soon translate into collective action—the decision to seek Assyrian protection, which would have far greater consequences than the original Syro-Ephraimite threat.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The collective trembling of the house of David parallels moments in the Book of Mormon when entire cities are seized by fear (e.g., Alma 2:28-29), and when the remedy is consistently a call to faith and remembrance of God's past deliverances (Alma 2:30). The pattern shows that fear is not an individual failing but a corporate spiritual condition requiring prophetic redirection.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:7-8 teaches that patience, faith, virtue, knowledge, temperance, patience, and godliness must characterize the faithful. Ahaz's trembling represents the absence of these virtues. D&C 68:6 promises that 'these words are not of men nor of man, but of me'—a reassurance that when God speaks through prophets, his word is more reliable than military calculations.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The house of David is covenanted to God as the dynasty through which temple worship and priesthood ordinances are administered. The threat to the Davidic house is thus a threat to the temple order itself. God's protection of the dynasty in this crisis preserves the institutional framework for covenant community.

commentary.christological_typology: Ahaz's trembling and helplessness foreshadow the human condition apart from Christ. The composite figure of Davidic kingship (which points to Christ as the ultimate king) is shown to be fragile, fearful, and subject to forces beyond its control—all things that the Messiah will not be. Christ's steadfastness in the face of opposition becomes a type of the trust that should characterize all believers.
commentary.application: The modern equivalent of Ahaz's trembling is the anxiety that comes from focusing on external threats while forgetting God's covenantal promises. Members of the Church often experience this: economic uncertainty, social hostility toward the faith, personal health crises. The response is not to deny the threat but to refuse to let the threat determine our spiritual posture. We are called to be 'bold as a lion' (Proverbs 28:1) in our faith, not to be trees shaking in the wind. This requires practicing what verse 4 demands: deliberate stillness, deliberate trust, deliberate refusal to let fear be our guide.

text_kjv: Then said the LORD unto Isaiah, Go forth now to meet Ahaz, thou, and Shearjashub thy son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field;

commentary.narrative:
God interrupts the narrative of fear with a command: Isaiah must go to Ahaz. But notice what God directs him to bring: his son Shear-jashub. The child's name is itself the message. Shear-jashub means 'a remnant shall return'—and in this moment of existential threat, when it seems as though everything will be destroyed, the very name of the prophet's son declares that something will survive. More than that: the verb yashuv ('return') in Hebrew carries dual meaning. It can mean physical return from exile, but it can also mean repentance, spiritual return to God. The name thus contains both threat and promise: yes, only a remnant will remain, but that remnant will return—both from exile and to God.

The location God specifies is highly deliberate. The aqueduct of the upper pool and the road to the fuller's field place Ahaz outside the city walls, in a vulnerable position—the very place where one would naturally be inspecting water supply in anticipation of siege. The fuller's field (sedeh koves) was an open area for washing and bleaching cloth, likely on the outskirts of Jerusalem. That this identical location will later become the staging ground for the Assyrian general's taunt (2 Kings 18:17) connects the two crises and shows how Ahaz's choice in this moment will have consequences in future trials.

God sends Isaiah to meet Ahaz at this intersection—this place of vulnerability and practical military concern. The meeting is not in the palace but outside, where the king is exposed to reality. And the presence of the prophet's son with the name meaning 'a remnant shall return' is itself a wordless prophecy: despite the immediate threat, God has already secured the future.

word_study.meaning: An imperative command ('go out') combined with the particle nā', which expresses urgency or entreaty ('please,' 'now,' 'I urge you'). The combination conveys both command and emotional weight—this is not a routine instruction but a matter of immediate importance.
word_study.significance: God's command to Isaiah is urgent and emphatic. The prophet does not deliberate; he does not question; he obeys. This immediate obedience stands in contrast to Ahaz's paralysis. The prophet will be the vessel of God's word, while the king will have to decide whether to receive it.

word_study.meaning: Composed of she'ar ('remnant,' 'what remains') and yashuv ('shall return,' or 'shall repent'). The name is a prophetic statement in the form of a name. She'ar appears throughout Isaiah (1:9, 10:20-22) to denote the survival remnant. Yashuv can mean both physical return and spiritual repentance, creating a name rich in covenantal meaning.
word_study.significance: Isaiah's children are living prophecies. His name (Isaiah = 'God is salvation') and his son's name together constitute a message: God will save through a remnant that returns. The Covenant Rendering notes that the boy's very presence beside his father is a prophetic sign to Ahaz. This combines sign theology (the child's existence and name are a sign) with covenantal promise (a remnant will remain and return to God).

word_study.meaning: A channel, conduit, or water-carrying structure. The upper pool and its conduit were crucial infrastructure for Jerusalem's water supply. The term is used in military contexts to describe vulnerable points in a city's defenses.
word_study.significance: The specific mention of the aqueduct places Ahaz in a location associated with both practical necessity (ensuring water during siege) and military vulnerability. It is the kind of place where a king would scout conditions for war. The same location appears in 2 Kings 18:17, where it becomes the site of the Assyrian threats that Ahaz's later decisions help to invite.

word_study.meaning: The upper pool or upper reservoir. Multiple aqueduct systems supplied Jerusalem; the 'upper pool' was one of several named water sources. The qualifier 'upper' (elyonah) distinguishes this from other pools in Jerusalem's water management system.
word_study.significance: The specific identification of this location suggests that Ahaz was conducting military reconnaissance—checking water supplies in preparation for a possible siege. The prophet meets the king at the point where the king is thinking militarily, practically, defensively. God does not call Ahaz into the palace for a comfortable conversation but meets him in his place of concern and fear.

word_study.meaning: The field of the fuller (koves = one who fulls cloth, i.e., washes and bleaches it). This was an open, exposed area outside the city walls. The Covenant Rendering's 'launderer's field' captures the sense of a place where industrial cloth work happened in the open air.
word_study.significance: The field location reinforces the sense of Ahaz being outside the city walls, vulnerable, exposed. The location will gain additional significance later: the same area becomes the setting for the Assyrian Rabshakeh's taunts (2 Kings 18:17), creating a connection between the two crises and showing how Ahaz's response in this moment shapes future catastrophes.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah later declares, 'Behold I and the children which God hath given me.' Isaiah's children—their names and their very existence—are signs and wonders to Israel, as prophetically constituted by God.
The same location (the fuller's field) appears as the setting for the Assyrian general's threats decades later, showing how Ahaz's choices have long-term consequences for future crises.

Isaiah opens his prophecies with the phrase 'except the Lord of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant' (she'ar ketsona'ah). Shear-jashub's name embodies this remnant theology central to Isaiah's entire message.

'O Israel, return unto the Lord thy God; for thou hast fallen by thine iniquity.' The verb yashuv ('return') in the prophetic tradition carries both meanings—physical return and spiritual repentance to God.

commentary.historical_context: The upper pool and the fuller's field are identifiable locations in ancient Jerusalem's topography. Archaeological study of Jerusalem's water systems confirms multiple pools and aqueduct systems. The upper pool is likely associated with what later became known as the Gihon Spring system, Jerusalem's primary water source. In times of siege, control of water access was literally a matter of life and death. The fact that Ahaz is inspecting these systems suggests he was actively preparing for a siege—a reasonable military response but one that would have kept him focused on human means rather than on God's promise. The fuller's field (a laundry and cloth-working area) would have been outside the city walls, an open area that would be unsafe in wartime. That God sends Isaiah to meet Ahaz in such a place indicates that the encounter is happening in the midst of Ahaz's practical military concern, not away from it.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The use of children's names as prophetic signs appears in the Book of Mormon as well. Alma names his sons—Helaman, Shiblon, Corianton—and their names carry meaning related to their roles in fulfilling God's purposes. The principle that God uses prophetic families to declare his word runs throughout Restoration scripture.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 21:4-6 teaches that the prophet's words will be God's words, and that the Church will hear his voice and obey it. Isaiah going to Ahaz represents the prophet's duty to deliver God's message, even when the recipient is in a state of fear and resistance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The water imagery—the aqueduct, the pool—carries temple significance in Isaiah's theology. Water and the temple are connected throughout Isaiah (e.g., Isaiah 12:3, 'therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation'). The meeting at the water source becomes a point of covenant renewal and a call to drink from spiritual waters rather than pursue earthly defenses.

commentary.christological_typology: The remnant theme—central to Shear-jashub's name—runs throughout Isaiah and points to the reality that God's purposes cannot be thwarted by human opposition. The remnant that survives ultimately includes the faithful in every generation, culminating in the Messiah himself as the ultimate remnant through whom God's purposes are fulfilled. Christ is the one in whom the remnant is preserved and through whom all restoration occurs.
commentary.application: For modern believers, the lesson is that God often meets us where we are, in the midst of our practical concerns and anxieties. Isaiah did not call Ahaz to abandon his military preparations but to add faith to them—to consider God's covenant while considering strategy. We are not called to blindness about real threats; we are called to trust God while taking prudent action. Additionally, the presence of Shear-jashub reminds us that God's word to us often comes wrapped in signs and symbols—in the people around us, in the names and roles that fill our lives. We are invited to read the providential meanings in our circumstances.

text_kjv: And say unto him, Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands, for the fierce anger of Rezin with Syria, and of the son of Remaliah.
text_kjv_alt: And say unto him, Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands, for the fierce anger of Rezin with Syria, and of the son of Remaliah.

commentary.narrative:
This verse contains the core message Isaiah is to deliver: a command to refuse fear. The opening imperative—'Take heed, and be quiet'—establishes the posture God demands. Heed means 'watch,' 'guard,' 'be careful,' and when combined with quiet (shaqat, 'be calm,' 'be peaceful'), it creates a paradox: Ahaz is to be watchful but not frantic, alert but calm, cautious but not consumed by anxiety. This is the posture of faith under threat—vigilance without panic.

Then comes the rhetorical device that reframes the entire crisis: the two threatening kings are reduced to 'two tails of these smoking firebrands.' The Hebrew phrase zanvot udim ashenim is deliberately contemptuous. A zanev is a tail—the remnant, the leftover. Udim means glowing coals or firebrands. Ashenim means smoldering. So the image is of two burnt-out stumps, still glowing faintly, still producing smoke, but essentially exhausted. Their fury—the 'fierce anger' (chorev af, literally 'heat of anger') of Rezin and the son of Remaliah—is real, but their capacity to effect it is spent. This is not denial of the threat but a theological reframing of it: yes, they are angry, but they are powerless. They are smoke, not fire.

The four imperatives stack up: 'Take heed,' 'be quiet,' 'fear not,' 'neither be fainthearted.' The latter two are directly reversed from verse 2, where Ahaz and his people were trembling (yanua'u). God is calling Ahaz to reverse the emotional trajectory he has begun. This is not a command to pretend there is no threat; it is a command to refuse to let fear determine his response. Faith here means trusting God's assessment of the situation over the assessment that panic suggests.

word_study.meaning: To guard, to watch, to be careful, to keep. The root conveys active vigilance and protective awareness. In covenant language, to shamar the Torah means to keep it, to guard it, to remain faithful to it.
word_study.significance: The command is not to relax but to guard—specifically, to guard one's heart and mind. The Covenant Rendering's 'be careful' captures this. Ahaz is not called to passivity but to active, intentional refusal of fear.

word_study.meaning: To be quiet, to be calm, to be peaceful, to rest. The word conveys not mere silence but an inner settledness and peace. It is the opposite of the trembling (nua') described in verse 2.
word_study.significance: Shaqat represents the state of the soul that trusts God. It is not passive resignation but active peace—a deliberate choosing of inner calm in the face of external threat. This is the antidote to the trembling described in verse 2.

word_study.term_english: fear not / do not be afraid
word_study.meaning: To fear, to be afraid, to dread. The root can also mean 'to revere,' to hold in awe. In this context, the command is not to fear the enemy but (implicitly) to fear God instead—to have awe-based trust in him rather than fear-based paralysis before the threat.
word_study.significance: The command is issued four times in Isaiah 7 (vv. 4, 4, 4, repeated in v. 5). The repetition emphasizes that fear is the central temptation Ahaz faces. The antidote to fear of the enemy is reverent fear of God.

word_study.term_english: fainthearted / let your heart grow faint
word_study.meaning: Soft, tender, weak, faint. When used of the heart (lebab rach), it means a heart that is weakened, discouraged, without courage. The Covenant Rendering's 'let your heart grow faint' captures the sense of internal collapse.
word_study.significance: This is the opposite of the 'strong heart' (lebab chazaq) that God demands. Ahaz's trembling heart is beginning to fail him. God calls him to resist this internal weakening—to maintain the vigor of his faith even as external threat increases.

word_study.meaning: A tail, the rear, the remnant, the end. The word carries connotations of inferiority and insignificance (the tail follows the body; it is not the head). To 'become a tail' is to become subservient; to be 'the tail and not the head' is to be reduced in status.
word_study.significance: By calling the kings 'tails,' Isaiah is using a word with deeper theological meaning. He is declaring that these human powers are in reality subordinate to God, trailing behind his purposes, not leading them. The dismissive image reinforces the theological point: human power is ultimately insignificant before God.

word_study.term_english: smoking firebrands / smoldering stubs of firewood
word_study.meaning: Ud = a firebrand, a glowing coal, a piece of burning wood. Ashen = smoking, smoldering, producing smoke but not active flame. Together, the phrase describes embers—fire that is expiring, producing smoke but no heat or expansion.
word_study.significance: The metaphor is contemptuous and theologically profound. Yes, Rezin and Pekah are still angry (hence 'smoking'), but their actual capacity to destroy is spent. Their 'fierce anger' (chorev af) is real, but it is the anger of a burnt-out coal, not a roaring flame. The image suggests that by the time these threats reach Ahaz, they are already spent forces.

word_study.term_original: חָרִי אַף (chorev af, literally 'heat of anger' or 'burning of nose')
word_study.meaning: An idiom for intense, burning anger. The 'heat of anger' or 'burning of nose' (in ancient thinking, the seat of emotion) represents fury at its fullest. Yet this fury is directed through the lens of the previous metaphor—it is the fury of exhausted coals.
word_study.significance: The acknowledgment that real anger exists (it is not imaginary) makes the reframing more powerful. God does not deny that Rezin and Pekah are furious; he reframes that fury as ultimately powerless. This is faith, not denial.

cross_references.connection: 'Be not afraid of sudden fear, neither of the desolation of the wicked when it cometh: For the LORD shall be thy confidence.' The same call to replace fear with God-based confidence.

'Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.' The pattern of command to courage in the face of threat, grounded in God's presence.

'Fear not to do good, my sons, for whatsoever ye sow, that shall ye also reap; therefore, if ye sow good ye shall also reap good for your reward.' The principle that trust in God's order displaces fear.

'I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded, for I know that the Lord giveth no commandments unto the children of men save he shall prepare a way for them that they may accomplish the thing which he commandeth them.' Faith as obedience despite perceived obstacle.

'Say to them that are of a fearful heart, Be strong, fear not: behold, your God will come with vengeance, even God with a recompence; he will come and save you.' The same pattern of calling people away from fear to faith.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern political rhetoric, the language of king's anger was serious—it could result in military action, tribute demands, or annexation. Yet Isaiah reduces this to smoke. The reframing is bold: what looks catastrophic from a human military perspective is, from God's perspective, merely expiring embers. The specific image of 'burning out' may reflect the actual historical trajectory: Pekah of Israel was soon overthrown (c. 732 BCE), and Rezin of Aram was defeated by Assyria. The prophecy's confidence in their imminent failure turned out to be accurate, though the mechanism (Assyrian intervention) came through complex political events rather than direct intervention.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma faces a similar reframing in Alma 57:26: he reports that the young Lamanite soldiers fought with 'exceedingly great courage' despite being 'young and inexperienced.' The principle that trust in God transcends military calculation runs throughout the Book of Mormon military narratives (e.g., Alma 2:26-31, where Alma's small force defeats a larger enemy through faith and strategic trust).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 64:2 teaches: 'Nevertheless, I, the Lord, forgave you, and say unto you, that in future you shall be more careful, that you shall not take up arms against one another.' The pattern in D&C is that God calls his people away from fear-based retaliation toward faith-based trust. D&C 50:41-42 similarly promises that light and truth flee not, but truth will eventually triumph.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The call to 'shaqat' (quiet, calm, peace) in verse 4 connects to the temple as a place of peace and receiving the presence of God. The psalms repeatedly link the temple with peace and divine presence (Psalm 122:6-7, 'Peace be within thy walls'). To be quiet before God is to position oneself to receive his peace, which surpasses understanding.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ exemplifies the response God calls for in verse 4. In the Garden of Gethsemane, facing genuine threat and suffering, Jesus achieves the balance of watchfulness (he prays) and peace ('not my will but thine'). He does not deny the threat; he places it within God's larger purpose. The Sermon on the Mount teaches 'be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves'—watchful yet at peace—a restatement of verse 4's dual imperative.
commentary.application: This verse addresses the most fundamental spiritual choice we face when threatened: whether to let fear dictate our decisions or to let faith direct our response. Modern examples abound: economic uncertainty, health crises, social hostility, relationship breakdown. In each case, the threat is real (not imaginary), but God calls us to assess the threat through the lens of his covenant rather than through the lens of the threat itself. The two kings seem mighty to Ahaz, but they are already spent. Similarly, the forces arrayed against faith in our time—secularism, materialism, ideological opposition—seem powerful, but from an eternal perspective, they are smoke from burning-out coals.
