This requires spiritual maturity: to acknowledge real difficulty while trusting God's ultimate sovereignty.

text_kjv: Because Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah, have taken evil counsel against thee, saying,

commentary.narrative:
This verse begins the elaboration of the threat—what exactly is the 'evil counsel' that has been taken against Ahaz? The verse introduces the content of the conspiracy, which will be fully revealed in verse 6. The use of the word 'evil' (ra'ah) to describe political strategy is theologically laden: what the coalition calls strategy and political necessity, God calls evil. This is not morally neutral diplomacy; this is an assault on God's covenant promises.

Notice that the verse refers to 'the son of Remaliah' rather than naming Pekah. This linguistic choice (repeated from verse 1 and appearing again in verse 9) is deliberate. Isaiah refuses to grant Pekah the dignity of his own name. By calling him 'the son of Remaliah,' Isaiah is denying him legitimacy. This matters because Pekah was indeed a usurper—he had seized the throne by assassination (2 Kings 15:25). To call him 'the son of Remaliah' is to underscore his illegitimacy in prophetic speech. By contrast, Ahaz, however unfaithful he may prove, is 'the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah'—he has genuine lineage from the Davidic dynasty.

The phrase 'taken evil counsel against thee' emphasizes that the conspiracy is actively directed toward Ahaz personally and toward his rule. It is not accidental enmity; it is deliberate plotting (yacats, 'to counsel,' 'to plan,' 'to plot'). The shift from describing the coalition in verses 1-2 to describing the specific nature of their plan in verse 5-6 narrows the focus: the reader now learns not just that there is a threat but what exactly the conspirators intend to do.

word_study.meaning: Evil, badness, harm, misfortune. When applied to counsel or counsel-taking, it means morally harmful or covenantally destructive planning. The root suggests something that breaks wholeness, that damages relationship.
word_study.significance: The use of 'evil' rather than 'hostile' or 'opposing' is significant. From Isaiah's perspective (and from God's perspective), the coalition's plan is not merely politically opposed to Ahaz—it is evil because it attempts to destroy God's covenant with David. Moral categories, not merely political ones, are at stake.

word_study.meaning: To counsel, to advise, to plan, to plot. The word can be neutral (giving good advice) or negative (plotting harm). In this context, with the object 'evil counsel,' it describes deliberate, intentional conspiracy.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes intention and deliberation. This is not an accident or a misunderstanding; the coalition has deliberately taken counsel—they have planned, schemed, and conspired. The active voice shows their agency in the plot.

word_study.meaning: The name of the dominant tribe of the northern kingdom of Israel. In Isaiah's time, 'Ephraim' had become a name for the entire northern kingdom. The use of Ephraim instead of 'Israel' emphasizes the northern kingdom's tribal identity and separateness from the covenant dynastic line (the house of David).
word_study.significance: By using 'Ephraim' rather than 'Israel,' Isaiah is making a theological point: the northern kingdom, which has broken from the Davidic line, is in rebellion against God's covenant structure. This usage foreshadows the later fall of Ephraim to Assyria (722 BCE, described in 2 Kings 17).

word_study.meaning: Aram, the kingdom of the Arameans to the north. The KJV renders this 'Syria,' which is the Greek term for the same region. Aram in this verse emphasizes the Aramean political identity, distinguishing it from Israel.
word_study.significance: The verse lists the three parties to the conspiracy: Aram, Ephraim, and Pekah (the son of Remaliah). The redundancy (Ephraim and Pekah are the same entity) emphasizes Pekah's personal agency in the conspiracy—he is not just the representative of a kingdom but an active plotter.

cross_references.connection: Pekah son of Remaliah came to the throne by assassinating Pekahiah. Isaiah's refusal to grant him his throne name reflects his status as a usurper without legitimate claim.
'A good man obtaineth favour of the LORD: but a man of wicked devices will he condemn.' The principle that God judges not merely actions but the counsel or plotting that precedes them.

'Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD.' The pattern of earthly power conspiring against God's covenantal order.
'How long can rolling waters remain impure? What power shall stay the heavens?' God's word will ultimately prevail against human plotting that opposes it.

commentary.historical_context: The Syro-Ephraimite coalition's plot was historically documented. The coalition aimed to remove Ahaz from power and replace him with a king who would join their anti-Assyrian alliance. The specific identity of 'the son of Tabeal' (v. 6) remains unknown, but he was clearly a non-Davidic figure whom the coalition intended to install. This was not merely a military threat but a coup plot. What was politically complex from a geopolitical standpoint—the logic of coalition-building against Assyrian expansion—is theologically unambiguous from Isaiah's perspective: it is an assault on God's covenant with David. The 'evil counsel' reflects not moral depravity in the usual sense but rebellion against the covenantal order that God had established.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon recounts numerous conspiracies against righteous rule: the conspiracy of Amalickiah (Alma 46-51), the Gadiantons' plots (Helaman, 3 Nephi). The pattern shows that rebellion against God's covenantal order is consistently labeled as 'evil' or 'wicked' in Restoration scripture, even when it appears politically rational. Alma 7:18-19 teaches that evil is defined ultimately by opposition to God's purposes, not by how it appears to human reasoning.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:38 states that God's words will stand whether by 'mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' This principle undergirds Isaiah's confidence: the conspiracy against the Davidic dynasty is ultimately a conspiracy against God's own declared purposes, which cannot ultimately prevail.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is built on the principle of God's covenantal order—the order that the Syro-Ephraimite coalition is attempting to overturn. The temple liturgy and ordinances depend on the continuation of the priesthood order that traces through the line of David. The coalition's plot is thus an assault on the very institutional structure that makes temple worship possible.

commentary.christological_typology: The conspiracy against the Davidic dynasty foreshadows the conspiracy against Jesus, David's ultimate descendant. The 'evil counsel' against Ahaz parallels the 'counsel together' of the Sanhedrin and rulers against Jesus (Acts 4:26-28, which quotes Psalm 2:1-2, the same passage invoked here). Yet just as God protected the Davidic line through the Syro-Ephraimite crisis, so God's purposes for the Messiah could not be thwarted by human conspiracy.
commentary.application: Verse 5 reminds us that opposition to God's covenantal order is not accidental or morally neutral—it is deliberate and, from God's perspective, evil. This applies to individuals and institutions that deliberately oppose God's revealed truth. However, we are also cautioned against seeing human opposition as ultimately determinative. The Syro-Ephraimite coalition took 'evil counsel,' but their counsel did not prevail. Similarly, opposition to the truth in our time, no matter how organized or powerful, is ultimately fighting against forces too great for human politics to overcome. Our response should be to stand firmly on covenantal principle, not to be moved by the winds of opposition.

text_kjv: Let us go up against Judah, and vex it, and let us make a breach therein for us, and set a king in the midst of it, even the son of Tabeal:

commentary.narrative:
Here is the explicit statement of the conspiracy: the coalition intends to invade Judah, terrorize it, breach its walls, and install a foreign puppet king. The directness of the plan shows why Ahaz's terror in verse 2 is understandable from a human perspective—this is a genuine existential threat to the Davidic dynasty. Yet it is precisely in the face of this concrete, articulated plot that Isaiah will call Ahaz to faith.

The sequence of verbs reveals the invasive strategy: 'go up' (military assault), 'terrorize it' (neqitsenah, convey psychological warfare and traumatic subjugation), 'make a breach' (break through the walls), and 'set a king' (replace the legitimate Davidic ruler). The escalation from military invasion to political replacement makes clear that the goal is not tribute or vassalship but dynastic change. The coalition wants to erase the Davidic rule and substitute their own appointed ruler.

The 'son of Tabeal' is otherwise unknown in the historical record. The name likely indicates an Aramaic-speaking figure, perhaps from the territories controlled by Aram. His obscurity itself is significant—he is not a figure with any claim to legitimacy or popular support; he is merely the tool the coalition would use to control Judah. This highlights the ultimate humiliation the coalition plans: not merely to defeat Ahaz but to replace him with a nonentity, a puppet with no independent standing. This complete erasure of the Davidic line is what God cannot permit, because it would contradict the covenant established in 2 Samuel 7.

Notice that this verse is framed as the content of the 'evil counsel' taken in verse 5. It is now explicit what the threat is. And in the very next verses (7-9), God will declare that this plot will not succeed. The oracle of assurance immediately follows the statement of the plot—showing that God's response is not delayed or uncertain.

word_study.meaning: To go up, to ascend, to invade. In military contexts, the verb regularly describes invasion or military advance. The verb often appears in the expression 'go up in battle' (alah ba-milchamah).
word_study.significance: The verb is direct and concrete. This is not diplomatic maneuvering but military invasion. The use of alah underscores the physical, military character of the threat. There is no ambiguity about what the coalition intends.

word_study.meaning: To harass, to disturb, to terrorize, to trouble greatly. The word conveys not merely military defeat but psychological trauma and distress. The Covenant Rendering's 'terrorize it' captures this sense of inducing terror and extreme suffering.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests that the coalition intends not just victory but subjugation through terror. They want to break not merely Judah's military resistance but its will to resist. This adds a note of brutality to the plan—it is not clean conquest but terroristic warfare.

word_study.meaning: To split, to break, to breach, to tear open. In military contexts, the verb describes breaching walls or defensive positions. The Covenant Rendering's 'break through' captures the sense of forcing entry.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes the forceful, violent penetration of Jerusalem's defenses. It is not a negotiated entry but a violent breach. The image is visceral—walls torn open, defenses shattered.

word_study.term_english: set a king / install a king
word_study.meaning: To reign, to rule, to make king. The verb in this form (causative) means to cause someone to reign, to install as king, to establish in rulership.
word_study.significance: The installation of a puppet king is the ultimate goal—not merely to damage Judah but to replace its legitimate government with a client regime. This transforms the invasion from a military operation into a political coup. The goal is control, not merely victory.

word_study.term_english: in the midst of it / in it
word_study.meaning: In the midst of, in the center of, within. The preposition emphasizes that the new king will rule from the heart of the kingdom—Jerusalem itself, the seat of the Davidic dynasty.
word_study.significance: The placement 'in the midst of' shows that the coalition intends complete political takeover. The puppet king will not be a tributary or vassal elsewhere; he will sit where the Davidic king should sit, rule from where Davidic authority should emanate. It is a complete replacement of the legitimate order.

word_study.meaning: The name 'Tabeal' (טָבְאַל) is otherwise unattested in biblical or extrabiblical sources. The name may be Aramaic or Arabic in origin, suggesting a non-Judean figure. The identitiy of this man is historically unknown.
word_study.significance: The obscurity of 'the son of Tabeal' emphasizes his status as a puppet. He has no claim to legitimacy, no popular support, no historical standing. He is merely the coalition's tool. This makes the threat particularly humiliating to Ahaz and the Davidic house—they would be replaced not by a rival with legitimate claim but by a nonentity. This also emphasizes God's role: God cannot allow his covenant to be undone by an unknown tool of foreign powers.

cross_references.connection: God's covenant with David: 'thy throne shall be established for ever.' The coalition's plan directly contradicts this promise; God's intervention through Isaiah protects the covenant against human assault.

'Nevertheless my lovingkindness will I not utterly take from him, nor suffer my faithfulness to fail. My covenant will I not break.' A psalm reaffirming the Davidic covenant in language suggesting divine protection against human threats.
The historical account showing that Ahaz ultimately seeks Assyrian help to counter the Syro-Ephraimite threat, a response very different from the faith God calls for in Isaiah 7.

Helaman's account of fortifying cities against threats: 'And thus he cut off all the strongholds of the Lamanites in the east wilderness.' The principle that human effort can be combined with faith, though Ahaz ultimately abandons faith for mere strategy.

commentary.historical_context: The historical evidence for the Syro-Ephraimite coalition comes from Assyrian records. Tiglath-Pileser III's annals record operations against both Aram and Israel during this period (c. 732 BCE). The specific plan to depose Ahaz and install a puppet ruler is recorded only in the biblical account; no extrabiblical source mentions 'the son of Tabeal.' However, the scenario (installing a puppet ruler loyal to the coalition) fits the standard Near Eastern political tactics of the era. The fact that the coalition needed a foreign puppet suggests that no existing Judean figure would agree to join their cause—all of Judah's legitimate nobility would resist. The coalition would have needed to govern through an outsider. The breaching of walls was the standard means of taking a city in ancient warfare; siege warfare often involved the sequential steps the coalition outlines: advance, terrorization through siege, breach of walls, occupation, and installation of new government.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains similar accounts of conspiracies to replace rightful rulers with foreign-backed puppets. The Amalickiah narrative (Alma 46-51) shows an internal traitor attempting to hand Zarahemla to the Lamanites, paralleling the Syro-Ephraimite plot to replace Ahaz with a foreign-backed puppet. In both cases, the legitimate ruler must choose between seeking military aid or trusting God's deliverance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 109:35-40 describes the dedication of the Kirtland Temple, invoking God's protection of Zion and his covenant people. The same principle—that God's covenants with his people override human plotting—underlies Isaiah's confidence in verses 7-9. D&C 121:33 teaches that all covenants, contracts, and agreements made not in God's name and bound by worldly power 'are of no efficacy when they are obtained in violation of my law.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple in Jerusalem was understood as the seat of God's presence and the center of covenantal worship. The installation of a foreign puppet king would represent the spiritual desecration of the temple order. God's protection of the Davidic dynasty is inseparable from protection of the temple and its priesthood structure.

commentary.christological_typology: The plot to replace the legitimate Davidic ruler with a puppet prefigures the historical attempt to replace Jesus with Barabbas. Both involve removing the true king and substituting a false one. Yet just as God protects the Davidic line through Isaiah's prophecy, so God's purposes for Christ cannot be thwarted by human conspiracy. The resurrection establishes that no plot against God's anointed can ultimately succeed.
commentary.application: Verse 6 makes the threat comprehensively real: this is not a vague or distant danger but a specific, articulated plan with concrete steps and a designated puppet ruler ready to be installed. It tests whether Ahaz (and by extension, whether we) will trust God when the threat is specific, real, and seemingly overwhelming. The 'son of Tabeal'—an unknown, powerless figure—paradoxically symbolizes both the humiliation that awaits if the plot succeeds and the confidence that God will not permit it. A nonentity cannot overthrow God's covenant. Similarly, modern threats to faith may feel overwhelming, but they are ultimately puppets—powerless except to the degree we consent to their power. Our response should be to stand on the covenantal ground God has given us, not to negotiate our way to compromise.

text_kjv: Thus saith the Lord GOD, It shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah delivers God's absolute veto against the military coalition threatening Judah. The Syrian-Ephraimite alliance, for all its military might and elaborate plotting, will not succeed. This is not a conditional warning or a tentative prediction—it is a divine pronouncement with the full authority of Adonai YHWH, the God who rules all nations and holds the Davidic covenant. The brevity and starkness of the statement are theologically significant: God does not argue his case or explain his reasoning. He simply negates the threat with two categorical phrases: "It will not stand" and "It will not come to pass." This economy of language reflects supreme confidence—the God who needs no debate, no elaboration, no justification.

The historical context makes this pronouncement remarkable. Ahaz sits on Judah's throne in genuine danger; Damascus and Samaria have formed a military alliance explicitly to remove him and replace him with a puppet king (Isaiah 7:6). From a purely political standpoint, Judah is outmatched and vulnerable. Yet God speaks with such finality that later history would prove him right: the coalition would fragment, Samaria would fall to Assyria within years, and Damascus would be conquered. This verse establishes the theological framework for everything that follows in chapter 7—God's sovereignty transcends military calculations.

word_study.meaning: Combines the sovereignty title (Adonai, 'Master/Lord') with the covenant name (YHWH, 'I AM'). Adonai emphasizes authority and rule; YHWH emphasizes eternal relationship and faithfulness. Together, the formula asserts both God's absolute authority over all nations and his binding commitment to Israel.
word_study.significance: This full titulation appears frequently in Isaiah and marks moments of supreme divine authority. In the Latter-day Saint tradition, YHWH is understood as the pre-mortal Jesus Christ (D&C 110:16), making this declaration a statement of Christ's authority over all earthly kingdoms. The use of both titles signals that this is not mere political prediction but a covenant word.

word_study.meaning: The root qum means 'to rise, stand, be established, endure.' The negation lo + future tense qum creates absolute negation: 'it will not stand, will not rise, will not be established.' In political language, a kingdom or coalition that 'stands' is one that endures and maintains power.
word_study.significance: The verb 'to stand' (qum) echoes through this entire passage—in verse 9, faith ('amunah) is what allows one to 'stand' (taqum). Here, the military coalition will not stand because it opposes God's will. The contrast prepares for the great reversal: only those who stand firm in faith will have a stable throne.

word_study.meaning: The root haya means 'to be, to happen, to come to pass.' The negation creates a flat denial of existence or occurrence. Where qum focuses on endurance and stability, haya focuses on actualization—the thing will not even happen.
word_study.significance: The pairing of these two negations—'will not stand' and 'will not come to pass'—is comprehensive. Even if something momentarily appears to happen, it will not ultimately endure or prove real. The Covenant Rendering captures this as two distinct dimensions of negation.

cross_references.connection: Celebrates God's authority over nations and their rulers, declaring 'The LORD shall have them in derision.' Isaiah 7:7 expresses this same principle in confrontation with specific historical threats.
Another proclamation of God's kingdom standing forever while human kingdoms crumble. Both passages affirm that ultimate political reality is determined by God, not human schemes.
The historical record of this very coalition's failure and Ahaz's mistaken appeal to Assyria instead of trusting God's word—the fulfillment of what Isaiah prophesies here.
God's statement about coercive power: 'All things are subject unto me, but powers that be are not orderly.' God overrules earthly power structures according to his own purposes.

Later in this same discourse, Isaiah reiterates the principle in different words: 'Counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand.' The coalition's counsel will fail.

commentary.historical_context: The Syrian-Ephraimite War (c. 735 BCE) was a regional military conflict in which the kingdoms of Aram (Syria) under Rezin and Israel (Ephraim) under Pekah attempted to force Judah to join an anti-Assyrian coalition. When Ahaz refused, they attacked Judah directly. The conflict occurred as Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria was expanding his empire westward, eventually absorbing all these regional kingdoms. From the perspective of ancient Near Eastern power politics, the outcome was determined by military and diplomatic calculation—Assyria was simply too large and too strong. But Isaiah's proclamation asserts that the true determination of events lies not in military might but in God's word. This verse would have sounded absurd to professional military strategists of the time, yet history vindicated it completely.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, Nephi receives a similar assurance that opposing kingdoms will not stand: 'Cursed are all those that shall rise up to fight against the work of the Lord' (2 Nephi 6:11). Both passages teach that opposition to God's covenant people ultimately fails because it opposes God himself.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:37-38 contains a parallel assertion of God's word's permanence: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled. What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken; I excuse not myself; and though the heavens and the earth pass away, my word shall not pass away.' Like Isaiah 7:7, this emphasizes the invincibility of God's word against all earthly opposition.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenant between God and the house of David (central to this entire passage) is renewed in temple worship. Ahaz's refusal to trust God in verse 12 represents a failure to honor the Davidic covenant. In Latter-day Saint theology, the Davidic covenant finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ, whose kingdom is eternal and whose word shall never fail.

commentary.christological_typology: While verse 7 itself does not explicitly mention the Messiah, it establishes the theological foundation for the Immanuel prophecy in verse 14. Jesus Christ is the ultimate guarantee that God's word stands against all opposition. His kingdom 'shall not be left to other people' (Daniel 2:44). The absolute confidence of verse 7—that no earthly power can thwart God's purposes—finds its ultimate vindication in the Resurrection and eternal reign of Christ.
commentary.application: This verse invites modern disciples to trust in God's word even when earthly circumstances appear threatening or uncertain. When personal, family, or institutional challenges seem to tower over us, verse 7 offers radical reassurance: God's word and purposes cannot be overthrown by opposition. The application requires distinguishing between God's revealed will (which stands invincibly) and our own preferences or calculations (which may fail). As Ahaz would learn to his cost, attempting to secure ourselves through alliances other than trust in God's covenant ultimately fails. The verse challenges us to ask: Are we consulting God's word or relying on worldly strategies that God has already declared will not stand?

text_kjv: For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. And within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah applies his sweeping negation to the specific threat at hand. The verse reduces each element of the coalition to its simplest, most powerless form: Aram's greatest city is merely Damascus; Damascus's ruler is merely Rezin—a mortal man. This reductive logic is a rhetorical strategy of Isaiah's genius. By stating facts that are technically true but deliberately minimizing, Isaiah shifts the mental frame from "overwhelming threat" to "limited human power." The implicit contrast is with verse 7's invocation of God—Rezin is a man; God is God.

The second part of the verse introduces a chronological puzzle that has generated centuries of scholarly debate. "Within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people." The northern kingdom of Israel (Ephraim) fell to Assyria in 722 BCE, roughly 13 years after this prophecy. Why would Isaiah give a 65-year timeframe? The most plausible explanation connects to Assyrian resettlement policy: when Tiglath-pileser III conquered Samaria, he immediately deported the Israelite population and repopulated the territory with foreign settlers. However, Assyrian policy allowed for gradual assimilation and return migration over decades. The complete dissolution of Ephraim as an identifiable people—the point at which they ceased to exist as a distinct ethnic and political entity—may have extended to around 670 BCE under Esarhaddon, which would place it roughly 65 years after Isaiah's prophecy. The Dead Sea Scroll 1QIsaᵃ confirms the "sixty-five" reading, demonstrating this was not a later textual corruption but part of the original prophecy.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'head,' but used idiomatically for leadership, the chief city, or the most important part. In political language, the 'head' of a kingdom is its capital or ruler—the command center. The word emphasizes centrality and authority.
word_study.significance: Isaiah's repeated use of ro'sh (head) in verses 8-9 creates a descending hierarchy: nation > city > ruler > mere man. Each repetition further reduces the coalition's power. This technique of rhetorical reduction—moving from large categories to smaller ones—prepares the listener to see through the illusion of overwhelming power to the reality of limited human capability.

word_study.meaning: From the root hata, meaning 'to break, be shattered, be crushed.' The prophetic perfect (speaking of future events in past tense for certainty) emphasizes the inevitability of this breaking. It is not conditional—Ephraim will be shattered.
word_study.significance: The term emphasizes violence and irreversibility. Ephraim's fate is not a gentle decline but a shattering—no piece can be reassembled. This aligns with the historical reality: the deportation under Tiglath-pileser was final; the northern kingdom never recovered as a political entity.

word_study.meaning: Me- means 'from' or 'away from'; am means 'people.' Together: literally 'away from people' or 'ceasing to be a people.' This describes the end of corporate identity and nationhood.
word_study.significance: To cease being a people (am) is the ultimate political death. It means losing not just territory or government but the basis of collective identity. The phrase echoes God's promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:2, where God promises to make him 'a great nation' (goy gadol). Here, that promise is reversed—Ephraim, once a people, will cease to be one. The irony is that this failure stems from their rejection of God's covenant.

cross_references.connection: Historical account of Pekah's reign over Israel and his aggressive policies that led to this war with Judah. Identifies the historical actors by name, making Isaiah's deliberate use of 'the son of Remaliah' more pointed.
Records the fall of Samaria in 722 BCE (roughly 13 years after this prophecy) when Tiglath-pileser deported the ten tribes. Confirms the beginning of the process Isaiah predicts.

Another prophecy of the northern kingdom's exile and end: 'Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall surely be led away captive.' Amos, Isaiah's contemporary, also prophesies Israel's dissolution.
God tells Hosea, 'Call his name Lo-ammi: for ye are not my people.' Hosea's symbolic action mirrors Isaiah's prophecy—Ephraim ceases to be 'am' (a people) because of covenant unfaithfulness.

The Book of Mormon records this very verse, confirming its significance for the Restoration. Nephi's inclusion of Isaiah 7 in his abridgment emphasizes the permanence of God's word even when nations fall.

commentary.historical_context: The verse reflects deep knowledge of Assyrian imperial policy and geography. Rezin of Damascus was a real historical figure who participated in anti-Assyrian coalitions; his city, Damascus, was indeed the capital of Aram and the seat of its power. The prophecy's specificity—naming Damascus and Rezin—authenticates Isaiah's prophetic claim. However, the 65-year timeframe is unusual. Some scholars argue it represents a later editorial insertion, but the Dead Sea Scrolls' confirmation of the number undermines this theory. The most likely explanation involves understanding what Isaiah means by Ephraim's end: not merely the political conquest in 722 BCE but the complete ethnic and cultural dissolution that followed decades of deportation and repopulation. Assyrian policy moved populations strategically, breaking ethnic continuity. By the time of Esarhaddon (681-669 BCE), the northern kingdom's territory had been so thoroughly resettled and absorbed into the Assyrian provincial system that 'Ephraim' no longer existed as a recognizable people. This aligns with the 65-year calculation from 735 BCE.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's use of Isaiah 7 in 2 Nephi 17 applies it to the larger pattern of nations that reject God's covenant. Nephi teaches that the same principle applies to the Americas: faithfulness preserves a people; unfaithfulness leads to their dissolution. The Book of Mormon's own narrative shows this pattern repeatedly—the Nephites' and Lamanites' rise and fall follow the spiritual law Isaiah articulates.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:14 states, 'And the arm of the Lord shall be revealed; and the day cometh when they who have not known me shall see me and know that I am the Lord.' Isaiah 7:8's prophecy of Ephraim's dissolution is part of this revelation—God's arm is revealed through the fulfillment of prophecy.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenant that preserves Judah (while Ephraim falls) is the Davidic covenant, the most significant monarchy covenant in scripture. In Latter-day Saint understanding, this covenant is renewed in the temple, and the ordinances of the temple represent the way individuals and families 'stand firm' (verse 9) in covenant. Those who break covenant, like the northern kingdom, are scattered; those who keep covenant, like the southern kingdom under its faithful kings, are preserved.

commentary.christological_typology: The contrast between Ephraim (the northern kingdom that falls away and ceases to be a people) and Judah (the southern kingdom that is preserved) points forward to the division between those who accept and those who reject Jesus Christ. In John 10:16, Christ says, 'Other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring.' Throughout history, the question is not whether a 'people' will endure but whether they will remain faithful to God's covenant. Christ's kingdom, unlike Ephraim's, will 'never be left to other people' (Daniel 2:44).
commentary.application: Verse 8 contains a hard truth for modern believers: faithlessness to God's covenant carries real consequences at the societal level, not merely the individual. A people who turn from God's covenant—whether through outright rebellion or slow spiritual drift—eventually cease to exist as a coherent covenant community. This does not mean physical annihilation but the loss of collective identity, purpose, and spiritual cohesion. For members of the Latter-day Saint tradition, this verse serves as a warning against complacency about covenant life and institutional faithfulness. The phrase "no longer a people" should sobering us to consider what keeps a covenant people unified: shared adherence to God's word, shared ordinances, shared expectations of faithfulness. When these erode, the people itself erodes. Conversely, this verse also offers hope: Judah, despite its flaws, was preserved because the Davidic covenant remained in effect. God's covenant commitments are more powerful than the dissolution that overtakes the unfaithful.

text_kjv: And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is Remaliah's son. If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah completes his reduction of the coalition to its minimalist terms—Ephraim's greatest city is Samaria; its ruler is merely "the son of Remaliah" (a patronymic, denying Pekah even the honor of his own name). But the verse's structure shifts fundamentally at its center. The first two clauses continue the pattern of diminishment: national threat > city > man > mere patronymic. Then Isaiah drives the theological point home with the conditional: "If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established."

This is the hinge-verse of Isaiah 7:1-9. Everything pivots here from external analysis of the threat to internal examination of trust. Isaiah is telling Ahaz (and by extension, the entire house of David) that the real question is not whether Rezin or Pekah can conquer Judah—the answer is no. The real question is whether Ahaz and his people can trust God's word enough to stand firm without seeking alternative security (like appealing to Assyria). The verse contains one of Isaiah's most famous wordplays, preserved identically in the Dead Sea Scrolls: "If you do not stand firm in faith (ta'aminu), you will not stand at all (te'amenu)." Both Hebrew words derive from the root 'aman, which carries the profound meaning of 'to be firm, reliable, trustworthy'—the same root as 'Amen' and 'emunah' (faith/faithfulness) and 'emet' (truth). Faith and stability share a common root. Without trust in God, there is no firm ground. This is not poetry for its own sake; it is theology inscribed into the very structure of language. Isaiah is not offering Ahaz a rational argument but a reality principle: the firmness of your kingdom depends on the firmness of your faith.

Crucially, the address shifts from singular 'you' (Ahaz) to plural 'you' (ta'aminu). Isaiah is now addressing not just the king but the entire covenant people of Judah. The challenge of faith is corporate as well as personal. The stability of the kingdom rises or falls on the collective faithfulness of the people and their leadership.

word_study.meaning: A patronymic, using the father's name instead of the son's personal name (Pekah). In ancient Near Eastern convention, patronymics were sometimes used respectfully (to establish lineage) but could also be used dismissively when stripping someone of personal honor.
word_study.significance: Isaiah deliberately denies Pekah his own name, reducing him to a genealogical reference. This rhetorical degradation is Isaiah's way of expressing God's judgment: Pekah is not worthy of royal designation. He is no one. Only 'the son of Remaliah.'

word_study.meaning: Root meaning 'to be firm, sure, reliable, trustworthy.' In the Hiphil stem (used here in the negative form ta'aminu, 'you do not believe'), it means 'to trust, have faith in, affirm as reliable.' The Covenant Rendering notes that this root underlies 'Amen' (so be it), 'emunah' (faith, faithfulness), and 'emet' (truth). To believe is to recognize something as firm and true.
word_study.significance: The root connects faith to firmness, belief to ontological stability. This is not mere intellectual assent but a relational trust that creates a foundation for existence. In Isaiah's theology, believing in God is not opposed to practical wisdom; it IS the deepest practical wisdom because it aligns you with the firm, true reality that God establishes.

word_study.meaning: From the same root 'aman, but in the Niphal passive stem, meaning 'to be made firm, be established, be stable, endure.' The passive voice indicates that one's stability comes from outside oneself—from God, not from one's own efforts or fortifications.
word_study.significance: This is the theological climax of the wordplay: you cannot establish yourself through military alliances or political maneuvering. Stability comes only through trusting the One who can truly make things firm. The passive voice is crucial: Ahaz cannot secure his kingdom; only God can.

word_study.meaning: The Hebrew conditional particle. In this context, it introduces a conditional statement with a real consequence: 'If X happens, then Y will result.' This is not a mere hypothetical; it states a binding logical or spiritual law.
word_study.significance: The use of 'if' emphasizes that the outcome is not automatic but dependent on Israel's choice. God will preserve them—but only if they trust. This preserves both divine sovereignty (God establishes) and human responsibility (you must believe). The conditional creates theological tension: both are true.

cross_references.connection: Prohibits testing the LORD: 'Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God.' Ahaz will later cite this verse (7:12) to refuse God's offer of a sign, ironically misusing the principle of faith as a justification for faithlessness.
Echoes this principle: 'Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him.' True stability comes through trust in God, not through activist maneuvering. Like Isaiah, Psalm 37 equates faith with firmness.
Quotes Isaiah 2:4 (via Habakkuk 2:4) about the righteous living by faith and not shrinking back. The New Testament authors recognized in Isaiah the principle that faith and endurance are inseparable.

Nephi applies the principle: 'O Lord, I have trusted in thee, and I will trust in thee forever. I will not put my trust in the arm of flesh.' This is the direct corollary of Isaiah's teaching: trusting God rather than human military strength.

In a context of persecution, God promises that 'thy confidence wax strong in the presence of God' when you are 'made strong' through righteousness. The Restoration teaches the same principle as Isaiah: stability comes through alignment with God's truth, not through external security.

commentary.historical_context: The verse reflects the political crisis of 735 BCE with clarity. Ahaz has received the warning from Isaiah and faces a genuine military threat. His options appear to be: (1) trust God's promise and fortify Judah's defenses spiritually while standing firm, or (2) seek protection from Assyria through tribute and vassalage. Historically, Ahaz chose option 2—within a short time, he appealed to Tiglath-pileser III for military support, which Assyria provided by attacking Damascus and Israel. This military assistance "worked" in the short term, but it committed Judah to vassalage and initiated a long process of spiritual and political decline. The 2 Kings 16:7-8 account shows that Ahaz sent the treasures of the temple to Assyria as payment. He traded long-term spiritual stability for short-term political security. Isaiah's verse 9 predicts exactly this dilemma and its resolution: those who trust God will be established; those who trust in the arm of flesh will not. Ahaz's historical choice to appeal to Assyria (the opposite of belief) led not to security but to increasing dependence and ultimately contributed to Judah's own later vassalage and exile. The verse is not abstract theology but concrete political wisdom forged in real crisis.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly applies this principle. Helaman teaches his sons (Helaman 5:12): 'Remember that it is upon the rock of our Redeemer, who is Christ, the Son of God, that ye must build your foundation; that when the devil shall send forth his mighty winds, yea, his shafts in the whirlwind, yea, when all his hail and his mighty storm shall beat upon you, it shall have no power over you to drag you down to the gulf of misery and endless wo, because of the rock upon which ye are built, which is a sure foundation.' This is Isaiah 7:9 embodied in narrative form: those who build on the rock of faith will be established; those who build on the shifting sand of political alliances will fall.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:37-38 contains the very principle: 'What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken; I excuse not myself; and though the heavens and the earth pass away, my word shall not pass away.' The Restoration teaches that God's word is the most reliable, most firm thing in existence. To believe that word is to place oneself on the only stable foundation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Davidic covenant—the covenant between God and the house of David (central to Isaiah 7)—is renewed in modern temple ordinances. The covenants made in the temple represent the commitment to trust God rather than rely on worldly power. Temple language and symbolism repeatedly emphasize building on a sure foundation (the Cornerstone, who is Christ). Ahaz's failure to trust God contrasts with the covenant path of those who receive temple ordinances and commit to stand firm in faith.

commentary.christological_typology: The verse points toward Christ as the foundation of stable faith. Just as Isaiah tells Ahaz that stability comes through trusting God's firm word, the New Testament teaches that Christ is 'the Way, the Truth, and the Life' (John 14:6)—the embodiment of truth ('emet' in Hebrew) and firmness ('aman'). In 1 Peter 2:6, Christ is identified as 'a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation' (quoting Isaiah 28:16, another Isaiah passage about foundational stability). Those who build their lives on Christ, the Resurrection says, will not fall when storms come. The ultimate fulfillment of verse 9 is not merely political endurance but eternal salvation—being established forever in God's presence.
commentary.application: Modern disciples face the same choice as Ahaz: Do we trust God's covenant promises, or do we seek security through worldly alliances and strategies? The verse challenges us to examine our actual faith—not our stated beliefs but our real trust. When facing uncertainty about finances, health, relationships, or career, do we instinctively turn to worldly counsel (lawyers, therapists, financial advisors, political allies) before or instead of trusting God? None of these resources are inherently wrong, but verse 9 asks us to examine the order and primacy of our trust. The wordplay on 'aman (believe/be established) invites us to consider: My stability—my peace, my security, my sense of firm ground beneath me—depends on the firmness of my faith. Am I truly believing, or am I merely giving intellectual assent while practically relying on the arm of flesh? For families and communities, the verse speaks to corporate faithfulness. A Latter-day Saint community that stands firm in covenant will weather crises that would destroy a community built on shared cultural convenience or social conformity. The application is both personal and collective: 'If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established.'

text_kjv: Moreover the LORD spake again unto Ahaz, saying,

commentary.narrative:
This brief transitional verse carries enormous theological weight in its apparent simplicity. After delivering the initial message (verses 7-9), God does not abandon the unresponsive king to his fears. Instead, the LORD speaks again. The Hebrew word 'yachaph' (yoseph yochaph, 'moreover' or 'yet again') emphasizes repetition and persistence. God is not done with Ahaz. In fact, what follows is the most gracious offer in the entire passage: an unconditional invitation to ask for a sign of any magnitude—a literal blank check to test God's faithfulness.

This verse marks a theological pivot. The first message (verses 7-9) was declarative: God asserts his sovereignty and the condition for Judah's stability. Now comes the invitation to relationship—God explicitly offers Ahaz personal assurance. The repetition of God's word to Ahaz shows what theologians call 'the patience of God' or 'the persistence of grace.' Ahaz has already heard God's word through Isaiah; he has already heard the condition for stability (faith). Rather than leaving him with that demand, God extends one more gesture: 'Ask for yourself. Test me. Let me prove to you that I am worthy of your trust.' The offer presupposes that Ahaz has been paralyzed by fear and doubt. God is not callous about that fear; he is inviting Ahaz into personal reassurance.

word_study.meaning: Yoseph means 'to add, continue, do again.' Combined with dabar ('to speak'), it means 'to add a word' or 'to speak yet again.' The construction emphasizes continuation and repetition—God is not done speaking.
word_study.significance: The phrase reveals God's pedagogical patience. He repeats his message, not because Ahaz will automatically understand but because God's commitment to reaching Ahaz persists. This reflects the Latter-day Saint doctrine of line upon line, precept upon precept—God's instruction is patient and cumulative.

word_study.meaning: The covenant name of God, emphasizing his eternal existence, his fidelity to his word, and his binding relationship with his people. The use of YHWH (not the more distant 'Elohim') personalizes the address.
word_study.significance: By using YHWH rather than a more generic term for 'God,' the narrator emphasizes that this is the same God who made the Davidic covenant, the same God who has bound himself to David's house. The use of the covenant name makes the offer a covenant act.

word_study.meaning: Root meaning 'to speak, say, declare.' In prophetic contexts, dabar is the vehicle through which God's word becomes reality—to speak is to create, to establish, to make real.
word_study.significance: The biblical worldview sees speech (especially God's speech) as performative. When God speaks, things happen. The repetition of dabar here (God speaks again) emphasizes that the second word carries the same weight and reality as the first.

cross_references.connection: Balaam's acknowledgment: 'God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do?' God's repeated speech demonstrates his consistency and reliability.

The New Testament principle of God's patience: 'The Lord is not slack concerning his promise... not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.' God's repeated speaking to Ahaz exemplifies this patience.

Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.' God's pattern is to repeat his message through his prophets until it is understood or definitively rejected.

God's statement to Joseph Smith: 'And I have sent forth the fulness of my gospel by the hand of my servant Joseph; and in weakness have I blessed him.' God's repeated communication through chosen vessels demonstrates his commitment to his people.

commentary.historical_context: Verse 10 functions as a narrative hinge in Isaiah's account of the Syrian-Ephraimite crisis. From a historical standpoint, Ahaz would have been in extreme distress when receiving this message. The military threat was real, the siege was ongoing (2 Kings 16:5), and the political pressure to either fight or submit was immense. A second word from God would have been welcome—but only if Ahaz was actually listening. The verse suggests that Ahaz was not yet ready for the first message; God extends grace by offering him a second opportunity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of God speaking again appears throughout the Book of Mormon. Nephi hears God's voice, then hears it again when he needs reassurance (1 Nephi 2:16-19). The pattern reflects a God who is persistently engaged with his people, not distant or dismissive. The principle teaches that God's instruction is not a one-time event but an ongoing relationship.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:63 teaches: 'If thou lovest me thou shalt serve me and keep all my commandments.' God's repeated speaking to Ahaz demonstrates this love—God is not content to give one warning; he speaks again to invite relationship and assurance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the place where God speaks to his people repeatedly. Through ordinances and personal revelation, God continues to teach, guide, and reassure. Just as God speaks to Ahaz multiple times, the temple provides ongoing opportunities for divine communication.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's ministry embodies this principle of God speaking again and again. Matthew 23:37 records Christ's lament: 'O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!' Christ's repeated invitation represents the persistence of God's grace toward those who resist. Like Ahaz, Jerusalem was offered signs and invited into relationship, yet repeatedly refused.
commentary.application: This verse offers comfort to modern disciples who fear they have already missed God's message or blown their chance. The principle of 'God spoke again' suggests that God does not give up on us after one missed opportunity. If we have heard God's word and not responded, this verse invites us to expect God to speak again—in new circumstances, through new messengers, with new invitations. However, the verse also carries warning: repeated offers of grace eventually reach a point of closure. Ahaz will refuse this second offer (verse 12), and that refusal will have permanent consequences. The pattern suggests that God's patience is real but not infinite. For modern believers, verse 10 invites us to maintain openness to God's continued speaking and not to assume that one moment of unresponsiveness ends the matter. But it also urges us not to indefinitely defer our response to God's word—grace persists, but not eternally.

text_kjv: Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above.

commentary.narrative:
God's second word to Ahaz contains the most extraordinary offer in the passage: an unconditional invitation to request any sign Ahaz desires, with no limitation on scope or magnitude. The phrase 'Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God' (sheal-lecha 'ot) uses the imperative, commanding Ahaz to ask. This is not a timid suggestion but an authoritative invitation. God is telling the king to name his terms, to test the divine reliability. The phrase 'thy God' (Eloheka) is remarkably personal—God is not positioning himself as a distant authority but as Ahaz's own God, bound to him in relationship. This personalizing language is crucial: it emphasizes the relational nature of covenant.

The second part of the verse defines the unlimited scope: "Ask it either in the depth, or in the height above." The phrase encompasses the entire vertical axis of the cosmos—from Sheol (the depths, the underworld) to the highest heaven. 'In the depth' (ha'amek) recalls Sheol, the realm of death and the bottom of cosmic reality. 'In the height above' (hagbeh lemalah) reaches upward to the highest heaven. Together, these spatial extremes suggest that whatever sign Ahaz requests—whether it touches death itself or the highest reaches of heaven—God can provide it. This is not a minor reassurance; it is a declaration that God transcends all cosmic boundaries and can work anywhere in creation. The offer is breathtaking in its generosity. Ahaz could ask for Rezin's death, for the enemy army's destruction, for an angel to appear, for the sun to stand still—anything at all. God is essentially saying: 'Your faith is paralyzed by fear. Let me remove that barrier. Ask for whatever would convince you to trust me. I will provide it.'

Yet Ahaz will refuse this offer (verse 12), and that refusal will carry permanent consequences. The tragedy is that God's grace is extended but not accepted. This verse represents the divine will to communicate, to reassure, to break through the king's paralysis—and the crushing reality that grace can be refused.

word_study.meaning: Generally means 'sign, mark, token, portent.' An ot is something that points beyond itself—a mark that confirms, verifies, or indicates something else. In biblical usage, an ot can be a natural phenomenon given divine timing or meaning, a miracle, or even a symbolic action. The key is that it confirms God's word or covenant.
word_study.significance: An ot is not necessarily a violation of natural law but anything that serves as confirmation of God's word. Throughout scripture, signs are tokens of covenant—the rainbow is an ot (Genesis 9:12-13), circumcision is an ot (Genesis 17:11). God is offering Ahaz something that will confirm his reliability and trustworthiness.

word_study.meaning: From the root amaq, meaning 'deep, deep place.' In cosmic geography, the depth represents the lower realms—Sheol, the underworld, the bottom of reality. Ancient cosmology conceived of a three-tiered universe: heaven above, earth in the middle, Sheol below.
word_study.significance: By offering to provide a sign 'as deep as Sheol,' God is claiming authority over death itself, over the realm beyond life. This is cosmic language asserting that God's power extends to every level of creation, including the most fearful—the realm of death.

word_study.meaning: Hagbeh means 'high, lofty place'; lemalah means 'upward, above.' Together, they describe the upper reaches of the cosmos—heaven itself, the realm of God's throne. Isaiah 6:1 opens with 'In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up' (using related language).
word_study.significance: The offer encompasses heaven and earth and the underworld—the totality of creation. God is asserting that his power and resources are not limited to any particular realm but transcend all boundaries. This universal scope emphasizes divine omnipotence.

word_study.meaning: The combination of YHWH (the covenant name, emphasizing eternal relationship) and Eloheka ('your God,' second person singular possessive). Together, this is the most intimate divine address possible in Hebrew—the God of the cosmos is YOUR God, bound to you personally.
word_study.significance: This phrasing appears in covenant contexts throughout scripture. By calling himself 'thy God,' the LORD is invoking the personal relationship of covenant. He is not positioning himself as a universal deity distant from Ahaz but as bound specifically to this king and his dynasty.

cross_references.connection: Prohibits testing the LORD: 'Thou shalt not tempt the LORD thy God.' Ironically, Ahaz will cite this verse (verse 12) to refuse God's own command to test him—misusing the principle to avoid faith.

Elijah's challenge to the prophets of Baal: 'Call ye on the name of your gods... and I will call on the name of the LORD: and the God that answereth by fire, let him be God.' Like Isaiah offering Ahaz a sign, Elijah offers a test of which god is real.

The Pharisees ask Jesus for a sign, and Jesus responds by declining their request (while offering the sign of Jonah). Jesus' refusal contrasts sharply with God's offer to Ahaz—God actively invites the sign; the Pharisees arrogantly demand it.

God's instruction to seek signs: 'And it shall come to pass that he that asketh in Spirit shall receive in Spirit.' The Restoration teaches that appropriate seeking for signs (through proper spiritual channels) is valid, unlike the mere carnal demand for proofs.

Later in Isaiah: 'Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the LORD revealed?' Despite signs and invitations, people often refuse to believe. Isaiah's narrative arc traces God's repeated offers of signs (chapter 7) and their rejection by subsequent generations (chapter 53).

commentary.historical_context: The offer of a sign in verse 11 must be understood in its ancient Near Eastern and biblical context. Signs were understood as confirmations of prophetic word and marks of covenant relationship. When God offers Ahaz a sign, he is offering the ancient equivalent of 'Let me prove myself to you.' In the ancient world, establishing trust between ruler and deity involved visible demonstrations of power and favor. The offer would have been extraordinary—a king receiving an invitation to request direct divine intervention. Yet Ahaz, we learn in verse 12, will refuse this offer. His refusal may seem pious (he cites Deuteronomy 6:16 against 'testing' God), but in context it is deeply problematic: God himself is inviting the test. To refuse God's own invitation to seek confirmation is a rejection of covenant relationship. The historical irony is profound: Ahaz refused God's offer of a sign but would soon receive the sign of Immanuel (verse 14) anyway—not as reassurance to him but as judgment and promise for his house beyond his lifetime.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly offers signs to those who believe. Nephi performs miracles to convince Laman and Lemuel (1 Nephi 7:10-16). The Savior appears in the Americas and offers the people direct experience of his reality (3 Nephi 11). The pattern suggests that faith and signs are not opposed; rather, God offers signs to those who seek him in sincerity. Ahaz's refusal of the sign contrasts sharply with the Book of Mormon's pattern of faith deepened through experience.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 46:14 teaches: 'To some it is given by the Holy Ghost to know the diversities of operations... to another, to work a miracle; to another, prophecy.' The Restoration acknowledges that signs, wonders, and spiritual gifts are part of God's ongoing relationship with his people. Verse 11's offer of a sign is consistent with the Restoration principle that God provides witnesses to faith.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is itself a place of signs and covenants. Temple ordinances function as signs—visible, physical, repeated actions that confirm and seal God's promises. The offer of a sign in verse 11 parallels the temple's function: providing tangible evidence of God's reality and commitment to those who enter covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodies the ultimate sign offered by God to humanity. In John 2:18-22, Jesus offers the sign of his own resurrection: 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.' The Resurrection is the cosmic sign that confirms Jesus's identity, God's power, and the redemption of all creation. It encompasses both the depth (death and Sheol) and the height (resurrection to eternal life). Like the offer to Ahaz, Christ's offer of the sign of resurrection is an invitation to faith—but many refuse to believe even in the face of the greatest sign of all.
commentary.application: Verse 11 invites modern disciples to examine their own relationship with divine signs. Do we recognize signs when God offers them? Are we alert to the ways God confirms his reality and covenant through experience—both miraculous and providential? The verse also challenges us to consider what might prevent us from accepting signs God offers. Like Ahaz, we might have reasons to refuse: pride, fear, prior commitments that conflict with trusting God, or misguided piety that uses scriptural principle ('don't test God') to avoid engagement. The verse invites us to ask: What sign would convince me that God is real? And am I open to receiving it if God provides it? More broadly, the verse teaches that God is not hostile to our seeking, not distant from our doubts. Like Ahaz, we are invited to bring our questions, our fears, our need for confirmation directly to God. The tragedy is not in asking; the tragedy is in refusing the answer when it comes.

text_kjv: But Ahaz said, I will not ask, neither will I tempt the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
The tragedy of Isaiah 7 crystallizes in this single verse. God has offered Ahaz everything—a divine guarantee of protection (verse 7), the reduction of the enemy threat to its powerless components (verses 8-9), a reiteration of the condition for stability (verse 9), a second word of reassurance (verse 10), and an unprecedented blank check to request any sign at any cosmic scale (verse 11). And Ahaz refuses. The Hebrew is emphatic with doubled negatives: "Lo esh'al velo anasseh et-YHWH"—"I will not ask. I will not test the LORD." The doubling suggests Ahaz is not merely declining politely; he is digging in, closing himself off completely.

The refusal sounds pious on its surface. Ahaz cites Deuteronomy 6:16, the commandment against "tempting" (testing) the LORD. This is technically correct scripture—it is indeed a violation of covenant to test God's faithfulness through trials or presumption. But Ahaz's piety is a catastrophic misreading of the situation. God himself has commanded Ahaz to ask; to refuse a divine command in the name of obedience to divine law is the deepest form of disobedience. It is like a child saying, "My father told me to come inside, but I'm going to stay outside to obey his rule about not making noise indoors." The logic is absurd because it privileges a general principle over a specific divine directive. More fundamentally, Ahaz's refusal reveals his real problem: not excessive faith but faithlessness masked as piety. He has already decided to seek help from Assyria (2 Kings 16:7-8 records this happening almost immediately). Accepting a sign from God would have obligated him to trust God's protection instead of Tiglath-pileser's military might. Ahaz's evasion—his misuse of scripture to avoid engagement with God—is a choice for political pragmatism over covenant fidelity.

The tragic irony is that Ahaz will receive a sign anyway, but not the one offered to him (verse 14). The sign of Immanuel is now reframed as judgment: God will give a sign, but not to reassure Ahaz—to fulfill his own purposes and judge the faithlessness of the king. Ahaz's refusal does not prevent prophecy; it only prevents him from benefiting from it personally.

word_study.meaning: Negation (lo) + first person singular future of sha'al (to ask, request, inquire). The future tense with negation creates absolute refusal: 'I will not ask, I refuse to ask.'
word_study.significance: The refusal is volitional and complete. Ahaz is not hesitant or uncertain; he is choosing not to engage with God's invitation. The personal pronouns throughout this verse emphasize Ahaz's individual agency in rejecting grace.

word_study.meaning: Negation (lo) + first person singular future of nasah (to test, try, tempt, put to the test). The preposition et marks the direct object: 'I will not test the LORD.' Nasah carries the sense of attempting to prove something by trial—it can mean either legitimate testing or presumptuous challenging.
word_study.significance: The term nasah is crucial because it invokes Deuteronomy 6:16. Ahaz is citing scripture to justify his refusal of God's command. However, there is a fundamental difference between spontaneously testing God (the prohibition in Deuteronomy) and responding to God's invitation to test him (what God offers in verse 11). Ahaz conflates the two, using the prohibition to refuse the invitation. This is a textbook example of how scripture can be misused to avoid obedience.

word_study.meaning: The covenant name of God. By naming YHWH, Ahaz acknowledges the God to whom he is bound by Davidic covenant, yet refuses to trust him.
word_study.significance: The use of YHWH in the context of refusal makes the disobedience especially sharp. Ahaz is literally refusing the God of the covenant that sustains his throne. He is rejecting relationship with the God who has bound himself to his dynasty.

cross_references.connection: The law Ahaz cites to refuse the sign: 'Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God.' Ahaz misapplies this prohibition by using it to refuse God's explicit command to seek a sign.

He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.' Ahaz's covering of his faithlessness with pious language exemplifies the very problem Proverbs warns against.

Jesus cites Deuteronomy 6:16 when refusing Satan's temptation to jump from the temple. But Jesus distinguishes between testing God out of presumption versus seeking God's will—Ahaz conflates these wrongly.

The historical record of Ahaz's actual response: 'So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me out of the hand of the king of Syria.' His refusal to trust God leads him directly to vassalage.

Now the just shall live by faith: but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him.' The New Testament echoes Isaiah's principle: refusal to believe draws God's displeasure. Ahaz's withdrawal from faith has permanent consequences.

He that will not hear my voice... shall not receive the token of my covenant.' God's warning in the Restoration directly parallels Ahaz's situation: refusal to hear God's word means forfeiture of covenant protection.

commentary.historical_context: The historical record (2 Kings 16:5-9) shows exactly what happened after Ahaz's refusal. Rather than wait for God's promised deliverance, Ahaz immediately sent envoys to Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria, offering tribute in exchange for military support against the coalition. Assyria responded by attacking Damascus and Israel, temporarily relieving the pressure on Judah. However, this decision initiated a long process of Judean vassalage and spiritual decline. Ahaz became a vassal of Assyria, lost Judean autonomy, and eventually imported pagan religious practices into Judah (2 Kings 16:10-18 records his installation of an Assyrian altar in the Jerusalem temple). The decision that seemed politically pragmatic—seeking security through the great power of the day—ultimately led to Judah's erosion and, eventually, to exile. Ahaz's refusal of God's sign was not a victorious stand against manipulation but a closing-off of the only genuine security available. The irony is profound: Ahaz thought he was choosing wisdom, but he was actually choosing the slow dissolution of his kingdom.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows the consequences of refusing prophetic signs. Laman and Lemuel refuse Nephi's miraculous works (1 Nephi 7, 18). Korhor refuses all evidence of God's reality and faces divine judgment (Alma 30:43-52). The pattern is consistent: those who refuse signs seal their own spiritual fate. Unlike Ahaz, who receives the Immanuel prophecy as distant promise rather than personal reassurance, the Book of Mormon shows that closed hearts miss not only security but salvation itself.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 63:9-10 teaches: 'But wo unto them who see these things and believe not in the Son of Man. Neither will the Father have compassion upon them; for they are vessels of wrath.' The Restoration warns that seeing evidence of God's reality and refusing to believe carries cosmic consequences. Ahaz saw God's word through Isaiah and refused to respond; he became a vessel of judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the place where one enters covenant with God and receives signs and seals of that covenant. Ahaz's refusal to ask for a sign reflects a broader spiritual resistance to covenant engagement. In contrast, those who enter the temple and receive its ordinances are accepting God's invitation to signs and confirmations of faith.

commentary.christological_typology: Ahaz's refusal of the sign prefigures the broader rejection of Jesus Christ by the religious establishment of first-century Israel. In John 6:30-31, the Jews ask Jesus: 'What sign shewest thou then, that we may see, and believe thee?' They demand a sign (like Ahaz's refusal suggests they refused signs in his day), and when signs are given, they refuse to believe. Matthew 12:38-42 records the Pharisees demanding a sign, and Jesus responds with disappointment: 'An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign.' The paradox is that those who refuse God's invitation to faith are often the same people who arrogantly demand signs on their own terms. Ahaz is caught in this paradox: he refuses the sign God offers and relies instead on human power (Assyria). Israel's religious leaders repeat this pattern: they refuse Jesus's signs and rely instead on their own righteousness and political alliances.
commentary.application: Verse 12 contains sobering implications for modern believers. It warns against the misuse of religious principle to avoid uncomfortable engagement with God. Like Ahaz citing Deuteronomy 6:16 to avoid faith, we might cite other scriptures (or our own constructed doctrines) to justify faithlessness. 'Don't be too zealous.' 'Don't expect miracles; that's not how God works.' 'Real faith doesn't need signs.' These can be sophisticated forms of spiritual avoidance, ways of using correct doctrine to shield ourselves from the risk of trusting God. The verse also cautions against 'pragmatic spirituality'—the tendency to make decisions based on worldly calculation (Ahaz's appeal to Assyria) while giving the appearance of piety. The modern equivalent might be: making career choices based purely on financial return while claiming God's leading; pursuing relationships based on worldly status while calling it faith; entering into alliances or allegiances that compromise our covenants while telling ourselves we're being realistic. The application cuts deeply: When have I refused God's invitation to faith by hiding behind religious language? What does it look like in my specific circumstances to accept God's sign rather than run to worldly solutions? The tragedy of Ahaz is that his refusal did not protect him from the future; it only prevented him from standing firm in faith to meet it. The same pattern threatens modern disciples: refusal to engage with God does not provide security; it surrenders the only genuine foundation for endurance.

text_kjv: And he said, Hear ye now, O house of David; Is it a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also?

commentary.narrative: Isaiah's patience has reached its breaking point. After offering Ahaz a sign—any sign—and watching the king refuse, the prophet now shifts his address from Ahaz individually to the 'house of David' collectively. This plural indictment expands the accountability: it is not merely one faithless king, but the entire dynasty that stands accused. The language of 'wearying' is visceral and anthropomorphic. The verb halal (לאה) means to exhaust or tire, as one grows weary from prolonged labor. Isaiah uses this term twice in quick succession—first applied to men (whom Ahaz has already exhausted), then applied to God himself. The implication is staggering: God's patience, like human patience, can be worn thin. This is not a statement about God's power (which is infinite), but about his willingness to endure continued faithlessness. The prophet is saying: you have exhausted human advisors and courtiers with your indecision and fear; now you presume to exhaust God's forbearance.
commentary.narrative_2: The possessive shift is theologically pregnant. Isaiah says 'my God' (Elohay), not 'your God.' This is a painful marker of relational distance. Isaiah maintains covenant relationship with the divine; Ahaz's relationship to God is now in question. The phrase 'Is it a small thing for you' echoes a rhetorical formula used elsewhere in scripture to denote grave offense (cf. 1 Samuel 15:17). In the Ancient Near Eastern context, such language would be understood as a formal indictment—the kind a suzerain might level at a vassal who repeatedly violates treaty obligations. Ahaz is not merely personally faithless; he is dragging the entire Davidic house toward judgment. The warning carries an implicit ultimatum: God will act, whether Ahaz cooperates or not.

word_study.meaning: to be weary, exhausted, worn out; to tire someone through prolonged effort or endurance
word_study.significance: This verb appears only sparingly in the Hebrew Bible and carries the weight of human limitation. When applied to God, it anthropomorphizes divine patience rather than divine power. The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'weary' (rather than KJV's 'weary') preserves the exhaustion motif. Isaiah 43:24 and Malachi 2:17 apply the same verb to God's weariness with sacrifice and complaint, establishing that God's patience—not his strength—can be tried by unfaithful people.

word_study.meaning: the royal household; the Davidic dynasty; all who belong to the line and covenant promises of David
word_study.significance: This phrase identifies not just one king but an entire lineage. By addressing the 'house of David' rather than 'Ahaz,' Isaiah invokes the Davidic covenant itself—the promise in 2 Samuel 7 that David's throne would be established forever. The irony cuts deep: the very dynasty promised eternal stability is now on the brink of forfeit through its own faithlessness. The plural 'you' (atem, אתם) in the phrase 'for you to weary men' extends culpability to the whole house, not Ahaz alone.

word_study.meaning: my God; the possessive form indicating personal covenant relationship
word_study.significance: Isaiah's use of 'my God' rather than 'your God' or 'the God' is the critical interpretive hinge of this verse. It asserts Isaiah's own fidelity in sharp contrast to Ahaz's apostasy. In the Prophetic Literature, such a possessive claim often signals the speaker's standing as a true servant of the covenant, qualified to speak God's judgment on those who have broken faith.

cross_references.connection: God says 'thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities'—using the same verb halal, confirming that God's patience can be exhausted by persistent unfaithfulness.
The people weary the Lord by saying 'Everyone that doeth evil is good in the sight of the LORD'—again applying halal to God, establishing the theme of divine patience worn thin.
The Davidic Covenant promises David's house eternal stability; Isaiah's invocation of 'house of David' implicitly recalls this covenant promise now at risk through unfaithfulness.
God says 'your appointed feasts my soul hateth: they are a trouble unto me'—establishing Isaiah's consistent theme that ritualistic unfaithfulness exhausts God's patience.
Samuel confronts Saul: 'It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king'—another moment when God's patience with a faithless king reaches its limit.

commentary.historical_context: Ahaz reigns during the height of the Syro-Ephraimite crisis (735–732 BCE). The northern kingdom of Israel (under Pekah) and the Syrian state of Damascus (under Rezin) have formed an anti-Assyrian coalition and are pressuring Judah to join. Ahaz, terrified, has already sent envoys to Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria, seeking military protection and vassalage. From Isaiah's perspective, this represents a catastrophic lapse of faith. The Davidic king should trust in God's protection; instead, he is court-shopping for human military alliances and simultaneously rejecting divine signs. The 'house of David' language would resonate powerfully for Isaiah's audience: they would recall their national mythology, the glory of David and Solomon, the Temple, the Davidic Covenant. To hear that this line has become an exhaustion to God would have registered as profound scandal. In the royal court, such language might also have been politically dangerous—this is Isaiah speaking truth to power in a way that could be heard as seditious.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi receives a parallel experience of exasperation when his own brothers reject divine signs and counsel (1 Nephi 2:12-14). Like Isaiah, Nephi must confront the reality that faithful remonstrance can be met with hardened hearts. The Book of Mormon frames such moments as trials of faith for the messenger, not mere condemnation of the hearer.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:37-38 reflects a similar dynamic: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the covenants which I have made with my people are not to be broken... Whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' The Lord will speak—through Isaiah or through other servants—but the house of David (or any people) cannot indefinitely reject that voice without consequence.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The 'house of David' evokes not only the royal line but the Temple that David's son Solomon built. Ahaz's faithlessness represents a break in the sacral connection between the Davidic king and the Temple cult. Later in Isaiah (chapter 8), the prophet will use Temple imagery (the stone of stumbling) to describe how covenant rejection leads to stumbling and captivity.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah's role as a faithful messenger, enduring rejection and weary with his people's refusal to believe, prefigures the suffering servant of Isaiah 50 and 53. The servant of the Lord, too, will be 'despised and rejected' (53:3), wearied by a people unwilling to receive the word. In the Latter-day Saint understanding, Christ himself embodies perfect faithfulness where the Davidic house failed; the Messianic King who was promised in 2 Samuel 7 arrives as one who perfectly trusts in the Father and never wears out in his mission.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members face a parallel dynamic. We receive signs—the still, small voice; the witness of the Spirit; the written word; the counsel of living prophets. The temptation is to weary God with our repeated demand for 'just one more sign' or our insistence on walking our own path despite clear guidance.
