The New Testament vision of a redeemed creation where God 'shall wipe away all tears' and there is no more death or sorrow echoes Isaiah's vision of creatures at peace, free from fear and harm.
Modern revelation affirms that when the celestial law is established, 'the lion and the lamb shall lie down together, and all things shall be at peace' on an earth made new.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern literature occasionally depicted paradoxical animal relationships, but never with Isaiah's theological weight. In Mesopotamian texts, predator-prey peace appears as fantasy or allegory, not eschatology. Isaiah transforms animal symbolism into cosmic theology. The cow and bear, the lion and ox—these were creatures the ancient audience knew intimately. Farmers feared the bear's predation on livestock; shepherds knew the lion as a constant threat. The pastoral communities of Judah would have understood Isaiah not as describing a quaint nature reserve, but as announcing a complete reversal of the hierarchy that governed survival itself. The predator-prey relationship was not merely a physical reality but a fundamental ordering principle of the ancient world. To envision its reversal was to announce a new creation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 30:12-15 describes the future when 'the wolf also shall dwell with the lamb' and 'a little child shall lead them,' echoing Isaiah's vision. The Book of Mormon places these promises specifically in the context of the conversion of Lamanites and the building of the Church in the latter days.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:24-31 describes the order of the New Jerusalem, including verse 26's affirmation that the lion and lamb shall lie down together. Section 29:22-24 describes how in the regeneration, the earth itself will be renewed and all things will return to 'their proper and perfect frame.' This connects Isaiah's individual animal pairs to a doctrine of complete cosmic restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The peaceable kingdom represents the ultimate temple state—a condition of holiness where all creation dwells in the presence of God. The temple in the messianic age (Isaiah 2:2-3) becomes the center of a fully redeemed creation, and the creatures within it reflect the harmony of God's direct presence.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah's peaceable kingdom is Christological in its center: Jesus Christ is the one in whom all hostile forces—natural and spiritual—are reconciled. Colossians 1:20 speaks of Christ 'reconciling all things unto himself.' The lion and lamb lying together is not primarily about animal behavior but about the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6) bringing all creation into harmony. The Lion of Judah (Revelation 5:5) becomes docile as a lamb—Christ's own self-emptying and sacrifice make possible the peace of all creatures.
commentary.application: For modern disciples, this verse challenges us to imagine what it means to live in a reconciled creation. Do we live as if peace is possible only when the dangerous are eliminated or contained? Or do we trust that genuine transformation of nature—starting with human nature—is the messianic promise? We are invited to become, in our limited sphere, agents of this transformation: speaking truth to power, refusing to accept predatory systems as inevitable, and embodying the reality that reconciliation, not domination, is the final order. The vision of the peaceable kingdom should make us restless with the violence, competition, and fear that characterize this present world.

text_kjv: And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah reaches the theological culmination of the peaceable kingdom vision with the most loaded image in Scripture: a nursing child playing safely over the cobra's hole, a weaned child reaching into the viper's den. This is not a cute picture of children petting snakes. According to The Covenant Rendering's translator notes, this directly addresses the oldest enmity in creation: Genesis 3:15's curse that the serpent and the woman's seed would be enemies. The child reaches into the den not because the serpent has been declawed or removed, but because the curse has been reversed. The enmity that has shaped all of human and cosmic history is undone. A child—the most vulnerable human—becomes the most safe. The asp and the viper, which kill through stealth and venom, are rendered harmless not by physical constraint but by transformed nature.
commentary.narrative_continued: The progression from nursing child (yoneq) to weaned child (gamul) suggests increasing independence and vulnerability as the child grows. Yet the danger increases only in appearance: the nursing infant plays at the cobra's hole from outside; the weaned child actively reaches his hand into the viper's den. Both actions would result in death in any actual circumstance. Yet both are described with the same assurance of safety. This is the eschatological reversal at its most radical point: the deepest curse of creation—the enmity between humanity and the serpent—becomes the deepest peace. The children are safe not because they are wise or careful, but because the nature of the serpent itself has changed. This verse answers the question that has haunted human experience since Eden: will the curse ever truly be reversed, or only managed, contained, and endured?

word_study.meaning: to delight, play, amuse; implies childlike joy without fear or constraint. The root suggests playful engagement, not fearful interaction.
word_study.significance: The word choice is deliberate: the child is not carefully approaching or cautiously touching, but playing—engaged in joyful activity. This is peace expressed as delight.

word_study.meaning: nursing child, infant still at the breast; represents utter dependence and vulnerability, incapable of defense or self-protection.
word_study.significance: The yoneq cannot flee, cannot defend itself, cannot reason or negotiate. Yet it is safe. This emphasizes that the safety of the messianic age depends not on human capability but on transformed creation.

word_study.meaning: weaned child, child separated from the mother's protection but still a young child; represents growing awareness and independence without yet having adult strength.
word_study.significance: The gamul has begun to act independently, reaching out actively into danger. Yet this increased vulnerability does not threaten safety—the transformed creation protects even the child who actively engages with threat.

word_study.meaning: asp or cobra; a venomous snake of the Middle East, deadly to humans. Paten appears elsewhere in Isaiah as a symbol of danger and curse.
word_study.significance: These are real threats, not harmless garden snakes. The Hebrew distinguishes between different types of serpents, but all represent genuine danger. The child's safety is not illusory.

word_study.meaning: viper; another deadly serpent, often used symbolically for evil and treachery (Matthew 23:33, 'generation of vipers').
word_study.significance: By using three different serpent terms (asp, cobra, viper), Isaiah emphasizes the completeness of the reversal: all types of serpent threat—all expressions of the curse—are overcome.

word_study.meaning: den, lair, habitation; refers to the serpent's dwelling place, its domain of power and hiding.
word_study.significance: The child reaches into the serpent's territory, its place of concealment and power, without harm. The messianic peace includes the reversal of threat even in the predator's own space.

cross_references.connection: The curse placed on the serpent ('thou shalt bruise his heel, and he shall bruise thy head') is directly reversed. No bruising occurs; the child and serpent coexist in peace. The enmity is dissolved.

The psalmist declares 'thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder; the young lion and the serpent shalt thou trample under feet.' Isaiah universalizes this promise: in the messianic age, all creatures—including children—will be safe from serpents and predators.

Paul affirms 'the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly.' The serpent's defeat through Christ connects to Isaiah's vision of the serpent rendered harmless through the messianic peace.

Jesus instructs disciples to be 'as harmless as doves' (akeraios, innocent, without mixture). While requiring wisdom with serpents, the ultimate vision is of harmlessness prevailing—echoing Isaiah's innocence of the child and transformed nature of the serpent.
The serpent is identified with Satan himself. Revelation's vision of Satan being bound (20:2-3) is the fulfillment of the reversal Isaiah describes: the ancient enemy is rendered powerless.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, the serpent was a symbol of cosmic threat and chaos. Mesopotamian mythology depicted serpents as harbingers of plague and death. In Egyptian tradition, the serpent (particularly Apophis) represented disorder that must be constantly defeated. Isaiah stands this entire ancient worldview on its head: the serpent is not to be eternally battled but transformed. The child-and-serpent image would have been shocking to Isaiah's audience: children died of snakebite. This was not theoretical; it was a realistic fear of any parent in the Levantine climate. To promise that even infants would be safe from serpents was to promise not merely improved protection but a reversal of the fundamental order of nature and threat. The ancient world understood the serpent as unkillable symbol of danger; Isaiah promises it will be defanged—not destroyed, but transformed. This challenged the entire ancient assumption that threat and predation are permanent features of creation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 30:12-15 preserves Isaiah's vision with particular emphasis on the role of the Messiah: 'And it shall come to pass that the wolf shall not hunt the lamb; and the lion shall not devour the kid.' The Book of Mormon adds that this occurs in the 'time of his coming,' tying the peaceable kingdom explicitly to Christ's messianic work.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:26-31 extends the vision to include the earth itself being renewed and 'the enmities of all flesh being done away.' This connects Isaiah's promise of reversed enmity (the serpent and child) to a comprehensive doctrine of cosmic reconciliation through Christ. D&C 29:22-25 speaks of the 'regeneration' when all things return to their 'proper and perfect frame'—a frame in which the curse of Genesis 3 is undone.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The child's safety in the serpent's den represents ultimate security in God's presence. The temple is the place where God's protective presence is most concentrated. The messianic temple (Isaiah 2:2-3) represents a creation where that safety extends everywhere: the whole earth becomes temple, and all creatures—including the most vulnerable—dwell in the security of God's presence.

commentary.christological_typology: The child reaching into the serpent's den is a type of Christ's redemptive work. Christ enters into the domain of the serpent (Satan) and emerges victorious, transforming the nature of evil's power. The 'seed of the woman' (Genesis 3:15) comes in human form as an infant child (Luke 1:26-35), and through His life, death, and resurrection, He bruises the serpent's head. The child's safety is ultimately Christ's victory. Additionally, every child made safe in the redeemed creation participates in the fruit of Christ's atonement: the curse is broken, the enmity is ended, and created beings—from the most powerful predator to the most vulnerable infant—exist in reconciled peace.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern disciples with the radical nature of the gospel promise. We live in a world of genuine danger—physical, spiritual, social. Isaiah does not promise we will escape all difficulty in this life. But he does promise that the ultimate resolution of all threat, all enmity, all predatory hierarchy is real. We are invited to live as if the child's safety in the serpent's den is not fantasy but our destiny. How would our faith change if we truly believed that the deepest enmities of our world—between races, genders, classes, nations—are subject to the same reversal that transforms the serpent? Practically, we are called to be agents of that transformation: to refuse to accept enmity as permanent, to seek reconciliation where the world sees only threat, to trust that peace is not weakness but the ultimate order that Christ restores.

text_kjv: They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.

commentary.narrative: Verse 9 provides the theological explanation for the entire vision of the peaceable kingdom. The reason why predators and prey, serpents and children, can coexist in perfect peace is stated with startling clarity: it is because of knowledge. The earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD, and when this knowledge saturates creation as completely as water covers the sea, harm and destruction become impossible. This is not primarily about information or doctrine, but about de'ah et-YHWH—intimate, relational knowing of God as He truly is. It is the same knowledge (da'at) bestowed on the Messiah in verse 2 ('the spirit of knowledge') now extended to all creation. The theological vision is stunning: universal peace flows not from external enforcement or constraint, but from universal transformation of consciousness. When every creature knows God truly, violence ceases not because it is forbidden but because it becomes unthinkable.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'my holy mountain' (har qodshi) refers primarily to Zion/Jerusalem, the seat of God's throne and the center of His kingdom. But the scope of the verse expands this immediately: 'the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD.' The holiness of the mountain spreads until the entire planet is hallowed. This echoes Isaiah 6:3's trisagion—'the whole earth is full of his glory'—and presents its eschatological fulfillment. What is true now in the heavenly throne room (Isaiah 6:1-4) will one day become true throughout creation: the entire earth filled with the knowledge and glory of God. The two verses form a bracket around Isaiah's entire vision: the present reality in heaven (6:3) becomes the future reality on earth (11:9). This is not escapism or disembodied spirituality; it is the most concrete and material promise of transformation: the physical earth, filled not with ignorance but with the intimate knowledge of the Living God.

word_study.meaning: to hurt, harm, do evil, cause suffering. The word covers both active malice and passive indifference to others' suffering.
word_study.significance: The prohibition of harm (lo' yare'u) is not merely external control but flows from transformed will. In the messianic age, the impulse to harm is no longer present in any creature.

word_study.meaning: to destroy, ruin, corrupt, bring to ruin. Often used of destruction in judgment (e.g., Sodom) but also of natural decay and harm.
word_study.significance: The word encompasses not only violence but all forms of ruin and deterioration. The messianic peace includes cessation of all destructive activity—predatory, environmental, social.

word_study.meaning: knowledge, knowing; from the verb yada, which means far more than intellectual understanding. Yada is the verb for deepest human relationships, for God's intimate knowing of His people, for experiential, transformative understanding. De'ah is not cognitive data but lived relationship.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes emphasize this: 'De'ah is not cognitive data but lived, relational knowledge—the kind of knowing that transforms the knower. When this knowledge of God saturates creation, the conditions for violence simply cease to exist.' This is knowledge that changes the heart, not merely the mind.

word_study.meaning: to be full, to fill, to be complete, to be satisfied. The word implies totality and sufficiency.
word_study.significance: The earth is not partially or gradually filled with God's knowledge; it is completely, thoroughly filled. Every space, every creature, every moment is saturated with this knowing.

word_study.meaning: to cover, to hide beneath, to overwhelm; the sense is of complete submersion and saturation.
word_study.significance: As waters cover the sea entirely—so completely that you cannot see beneath to the bottom—the knowledge of God covers all creation. There is no part of the created order beyond the reach of this knowledge.

cross_references.connection: The trisagion ('Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory') describes the heavenly reality. Isaiah 11:9 promises the eschatological fulfillment when earth mirrors heaven: the whole earth filled with the knowledge of the LORD.

Habakkuk uses identical language: 'For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.' The connection is explicit and deliberate, confirming the eschatological promise.

Jeremiah prophesies that in the new covenant, 'they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them' and God will 'remember their sin no more.' The universal knowledge Isaiah describes is the foundation of this new covenant reality.

John affirms 'ye have an unction from the Holy One, and ye know all things.' The anointing (chrisma) that John describes as universal in the redeemed community echoes Isaiah's vision of all creatures filled with God's knowledge.

Modern revelation teaches that 'the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehendeth it not; nevertheless, the day shall come when you shall comprehend even God.' This affirms that knowledge of God is transformative and total in the redeemed state.

commentary.historical_context: In Isaiah's time, knowledge of God was mediated through the temple, the priesthood, and the prophetic word. Most of the common people had limited access to Scripture (which did not yet exist in written form for most) and relied on oral tradition and priestly instruction. Isaiah's vision of all the earth filled with God's knowledge would have seemed not merely future but almost impossible: knowledge of God was rare, costly, mediated through proper channels. For Isaiah to promise that it would saturate the entire earth 'as the waters cover the sea' was to promise not merely better communication or broader availability, but transformation of the fundamental human (and cosmic) condition. In ancient Near Eastern religion, knowledge of the gods was dangerous, esoteric, and jealously guarded. Isaiah's vision of universal, accessible, transformative knowledge would have been revolutionary.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 3 Nephi 21:26-27 references Isaiah 11:9 in the context of the gathering of Israel and the establishment of Zion: 'And behold, they will crucify him; and after he is crucified, they will scatter my people, save these who shall be taken away even now I declare unto my people, who have believed, both of the house of Israel and of the Gentiles, and that know the covenants of the Lord, and will repent of their sins.' The Book of Mormon connects the knowledge that Isaiah promises to covenantal knowledge—the intimate knowing of God through the restored gospel.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 93:1 teaches 'Every soul who forsaketh his sins and cometh unto me, and calleth on my name, and obeyeth my voice, and keepeth my commandments, shall see my face and know that I am.' Modern revelation affirms that the knowledge of God Isaiah describes is available now to those who enter the covenant, and will be universal in the messianic age. D&C 76:10 describes those in the celestial kingdom as knowing 'even as they are known'—the mutual, intimate knowledge that Isaiah associates with the peaceable kingdom.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Isaiah 11:9 describes the eschatological fulfillment of what the temple represents now: the place where human beings come to know God through ordinances, instruction, and spiritual experience. The entire earth becoming 'holy mountain' means the entire creation becomes temple—every place a place of intimate encounter with God.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the 'knowledge of the LORD' that Isaiah promises. John 1:14 declares 'the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us'—God's knowledge becomes incarnate, relational, accessible. The gift of the Holy Ghost in the messianic age (promised in Joel 2:28-29 and fulfilled at Pentecost) is the means by which this knowledge spreads: through the testimony of Christ, all are invited into intimate knowing of God. The fulfillment of Isaiah 11:9 in Christ involves both His incarnation (God made knowable) and His extension through the Holy Ghost (knowledge made universal and transformative).
commentary.application: For modern disciples, Isaiah 11:9 invites us to consider what it means to be filled with the knowledge of God. Personally, it challenges us: Am I cultivating intimate, transformative knowledge of God, or merely accumulating information about God? Corporately, it asks: How do we work toward a Zion community where the knowledge of God saturates every relationship, every institution, every interaction? Practically, this verse teaches that genuine peace is not achieved through force, law enforcement, or external control, but through transformation of hearts through knowledge of God. We are invited to be instruments of that transformation—teaching, testifying, inviting others into the intimate knowledge of Christ that changes everything. When we approach Scripture, prayer, temple worship, or any spiritual practice with the understanding that we are seeking de'ah, relational knowing of God, it transforms those practices from routine to revolutionary.

text_kjv: And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah shifts focus from the cosmic vision of the peaceable kingdom to the central figure who makes it possible. The botanical metaphor that began in verse 1 reaches a paradoxical culmination: the one who grew from Jesse's root (the Branch from the stump) is now called the 'root of Jesse' himself. The Covenant Rendering translator notes emphasize this paradox: 'The one who grew from Jesse's root now becomes the root itself—the foundation, the source, the anchor.' He is simultaneously the fruit of David's line and its ultimate foundation. This Messianic figure stands as a nes ('signal, banner, rallying point')—not hidden or localized but raised high, visible, a gathering point for the peoples. The scope has expanded dramatically: the promise began with the spirit-endowed ruler (v. 2), developed through the peaceable kingdom (v. 6-9), and now reveals that all nations—not merely Israel—seek this figure and find in him their rest.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'in that day' (ba-yom ha-hu) marks this as part of the one comprehensive vision of the messianic age. But verse 10 provides the hinge point: the peaceable kingdom and the international gathering are not separate events but expressions of a single reality centered in the Messiah. The nations ('goyim') seek him not through conquest or coercion but through attraction. They stream toward him as a banner streams from a high point. His 'rest' (menucha) echoes the rest God gives His people in the promised land (Deuteronomy 12:9) and the Sabbath rest (Hebrews 4:9). But here it is explicitly connected to his glory (kavod): his reign is characterized by the weight, honor, and presence of God. The rest he offers is glorious because it is rest in the presence of God, the ultimate security and satisfaction.

word_study.meaning: root, foundation, source; the part of a plant that anchors it in earth and draws up sustenance. Metaphorically, the root is the foundational source of identity and life.
word_study.significance: By calling the Messiah both branch (v. 1) and root (v. 10), Isaiah presents a paradox: He is both descended from Jesse and the source of Jesse's ultimate meaning. All history flows to this figure and from this figure. In The Covenant Rendering note, this is explained: 'He is both the product of the line and its foundation—the one in whom the entire Davidic purpose finds its source and meaning.'

word_study.meaning: to stand, to take one's position, to endure. Often used of taking a stance of authority or bearing witness.
word_study.significance: The Messiah is not hidden or passive but actively stands—takes his position—as the gathering point for the nations.

word_study.meaning: signal, banner, standard, pole raised for signaling. In military contexts, a nes rallied troops; more broadly, it was a visible marker that drew people together.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes: 'A nes was a pole or flag raised on a hill to rally troops or signal a gathering point. The root of Jesse becomes the visible marker around which the nations assemble—not by conquest but by attraction.' This is not domination but magnetic draw.

word_study.meaning: to seek, search for, inquire; often implies not merely seeking information but seeking a person or relationship with intention and desire.
word_study.significance: The nations actively seek the Messiah. This is not passive discovery but intentional quest, suggesting the deep human hunger for the salvation He offers.

word_study.meaning: rest, resting place, repose; often used of the land of Israel as God's gift of rest to the people. Also implies peace, security, and cessation from toil.
word_study.significance: The rest of the Messiah is not idleness but secure, stable peace. Hebrews 4:3-11 interprets this as the true Sabbath rest that remains for God's people—rest in the presence of God.

word_study.meaning: glory, honor, weight, heaviness; the manifested presence and majesty of God. Kavod is God's visible, tangible manifestation of His nature and power.
word_study.significance: The Messiah's rest is not merely comfortable or peaceful; it is glorious—saturated with the divine presence and majesty. His rest is God's rest, characterized by the fullness of God's kavod.

cross_references.connection: Paul quotes Isaiah 11:10 directly ('There shall be a root of Jesse, and he that shall rise to reign over the Gentiles; in him shall the Gentiles trust'), affirming that Jesus is the Messianic root to whom all nations are drawn.

Both passages envision all nations gathering to the Lord's house/mountain in the latter days. Isaiah 11:10 identifies Jesus as the center of this gathering; Isaiah 2:2-4 shows the result: nations learning war no more.

Moses uses menucha ('rest') to describe the place where God will establish His name and worship. Jesus offers the ultimate 'rest' that Deuteronomy foreshadows—not merely a geographical location but a covenantal relationship.
The epistle interprets the 'rest' that remains for God's people as entering into Christ's rest—ceasing from works and trusting in His completed redemption. This fulfills Isaiah's promise.
Modern revelation affirms that Christ will be 'raised up as a standard among the people' and that 'the glory of the Lord shall rest upon Zion, and he shall come and visit all the people of Zion.'

commentary.historical_context: In Isaiah's day, 'root of Jesse' would have been immediately recognized as Messianic language. Jesse was David's father, so any 'root of Jesse' was inherently connected to the Davidic covenant and the promise of an eternal king (2 Samuel 7:12-16). But Isaiah's paradox—calling the Messiah both the 'shoot from the stump' (v. 1, the fruit of the line) and the 'root of Jesse' (v. 10, the source)—transcends the normal succession of kings. Kings inherit the throne from their fathers; they do not typically become the foundation of the dynasty itself. This suggests a figure who transcends normal historical causation. In ancient Near Eastern vassal states and tribute relationships, a signal or banner raised by the great king would summon the smaller nations to gather. Isaiah appropriates this language: the Messiah is not merely a regional king but one whose signal draws all nations. The universalism of Isaiah 11:10 would have been striking to Isaiah's 8th-century audience: the Messiah's appeal extends beyond Israel to goyim (Gentiles), 'to the uttermost parts of the earth' (Romans 15:12 interpretation).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 21:10 preserves Isaiah 11:10 exactly. Nephi frames the entire prophecy within his own experience of seeing Christ in vision (2 Nephi 11:2-3), making clear that the Messiah Isaiah describes is Jesus Christ, the God of Israel. The Book of Mormon repeatedly interprets Isaiah through Christ (e.g., 1 Nephi 19:23-24), establishing that all Isaiah's messianic language finds fulfillment in Jesus.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:58-59 promises 'I will raise up as a standard... Jesus Christ my Son, and he shall stand as a standard among the people.' This is a direct modern revelation parallel to Isaiah 11:10's nes ('standard/signal'). D&C 49:22-23 describes how the Messiah will 'make all things new' and bring about the peaceable kingdom—fulfilling the entire vision of Isaiah 11:1-10.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Messiah is the embodiment of the temple's function: the place where heaven and earth meet, where God's glory (kavod) is manifest, where all peoples come to seek God. Jesus identifies Himself as the temple (John 2:19-21), and His exaltation makes Him the spiritual center toward which all creation is drawn—the true 'signal' that gathers the nations.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is explicitly the 'root of Jesse' to whom Isaiah points. The paradox of being both root and branch is resolved in Christ: He is the offspring of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3) but also the 'Lord' of David (Matthew 22:43-45), the one in whom the entire Davidic purpose finds both its fulfillment and its source. He is the banner/signal before whom all nations bow (Philippians 2:9-11). His 'rest' is the peace He gives (John 14:27), the Sabbath rest in the presence of God that characterizes the redeemed (Revelation 21:1-4). His glory (kavod) is revealed in His incarnation (John 1:14), crucifixion (1 Peter 1:10-11), and exaltation (Acts 7:55-56).
commentary.application: Isaiah 11:10 invites modern disciples to recognize Jesus Christ as the 'signal/banner' that draws us and holds us together. In a fragmented world of competing loyalties and signals, we are called to look to Jesus as the one supreme standard. Personally, this means making Christ the center of our life's orientation—not merely one value among many but the North Star by which all other decisions are evaluated. The rest He offers is not escape from difficulty but secure peace in covenantal relationship with God. Practically, we are invited to become 'banners' ourselves (Isaiah 49:22, 'He will lift up an ensign to the nations')—visible witnesses whose lives point others toward Christ. Corporately, the Zion community Isaiah envisions is gathered around this signal; the Church's purpose is to raise Christ's standard and invite all nations to seek Him. The promise is not that all will immediately respond, but that the signal is clear, visible, and continuously raised for those who have eyes to see.

text_kjv: And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah transitions from the Messiah as the 'signal' to which all nations are drawn (v. 10) to the specific work of gathering: God will reach out His hand 'a second time' to reclaim the scattered remnant of His people. The 'first time' refers to the exodus from Egypt—the foundational act of redemption in Israel's memory. But Isaiah announces a second exodus, greater in scope and more comprehensive than the first. The Dead Sea Scrolls variant noted that shenit ('second time') reads identically in 1QIsaᵃ, confirming that this 'second exodus' theology was understood consistently across centuries. The verb liqnot ('to acquire, reclaim, redeem') carries the sense of purchasing back what was lost—a redemptive act involving cost and deliberate action. The Lord does not simply allow the scattered to return; He actively reaches out His hand in redemptive gesture.
commentary.narrative_continued: The geographical list is comprehensive: Assyria (the northeastern superpower that had exiled the northern kingdom), Egypt (the southern power that threatened Judah), Pathros (Upper Egypt), Cush (Ethiopia/Sudan, representing the far south), Elam (east, modern Iran), Shinar (Babylon, another great eastern power), Hamath (northern Syria), and the 'islands of the sea' (the Mediterranean diaspora to the west). This is not merely a return from Babylon (which happened in 538 BCE under Persian decree). This is a vision of gathering from every corner of the known world. The list traces a full compass—no exile is too distant, no scattered group beyond God's reach. The remnant theme that dominates Isaiah (1:9, 10:20-22, 11:11, etc.) reaches its climax: judgment had reduced Israel to a remnant; grace gathers that remnant from the uttermost parts of the earth.

word_study.meaning: a second time, again; the word implies both the precedent of a first occasion and the anticipation of a repeated or renewed action.
word_study.significance: The 'second time' anchors Isaiah's vision to the exodus narrative: just as God reached out His hand the first time in Egypt, so He will do it again. This is not invention of new theology but renewal and completion of God's redemptive purpose.

word_study.meaning: to acquire, buy, purchase, create; when used in the context of redemption, it means to reclaim or redeem by payment or ransom. It carries the sense of deliberate, costly acquisition.
word_study.significance: The word suggests that gathering the remnant is not a passive process but an act requiring divine power and resources. God purchases or redeems the scattered people, buying them back from exile.

word_study.meaning: remainder, remnant, what is left; when applied to God's people, it refers to the survivors who will inherit God's promises. The remnant concept pervades Isaiah: judgment reduces the people to a remnant; grace works through that remnant.
word_study.significance: The 'remnant' is not a consolation prize but the vessel of God's purpose. Throughout Isaiah, from the present judgment (1:9) through the servant figure (53:10-11), it is the remnant that carries forward God's redemptive work. This verse promises that even the scattered fragments of that remnant will be gathered.

word_study.term_original: יִשָּׁאֵר (yisshaer, 'that shall be left'; related to she'ar)
word_study.meaning: that shall be left, remain, survive; implies those who are separated or dispersed.
word_study.significance: The construction emphasizes that the gathering will include not merely the core remnant but even those who have been left behind in diaspora—all the scattered pieces of the people.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah earlier promises that 'a remnant shall return, even the remnant of Jacob' and describes this remnant's return as an act of salvation. Chapter 11:11 is the eschatological expansion of this promise: a universal gathering rather than merely the return from Babylon.

Jeremiah explicitly echoes Isaiah's 'second exodus' language: 'Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that it shall no more be said, The LORD liveth that brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt; But, The LORD liveth that brought up the children of Israel from the land of the north.' The 'second exodus' becomes a common prophetic theme.

Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones rising includes the gathering of the 'two sticks' (Israel and Judah) and their union into one nation. This echoes Isaiah 11:11-12's theme of gathering the scattered remnant and reuniting the divided kingdoms.

Nephi declares that Isaiah's words 'shall all be fulfilled' and specifically emphasizes Isaiah's prophecy about 'the gathering of the house of Israel' in the last days. The Book of Mormon treats Isaiah 11:11-12 as a key prophecy of the Restoration.

Modern revelation describes Christ gathering the faithful from 'the four quarters of the earth' and emphasizes that this gathering is the work of the Restoration—the return of scattered Israel in the latter days.

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah lived in the 8th century BCE, during the period when the Assyrian Empire was at its height. The northern kingdom of Israel had been conquered and exiled in 722 BCE; Judah stood in danger of the same fate. When Isaiah speaks of gathering from Assyria, he speaks from a context of fresh trauma: whole populations had been deported by Sargon and Sennacherib to distant lands. The promise that God would reach out again, a second time, to gather from Assyria would have been radical hope in an age of despair. Later, in the 6th century, Babylon conquered Judah and exiled the leadership. But even this return under Cyrus (539-538 BCE) was limited: most Jews remained in the diaspora. The later Jewish experience of widespread diaspora—reaching across the Mediterranean, into Persia, and eventually throughout the Roman world—lent new urgency to Isaiah's 'second exodus' language. The geographical sweep of verse 11 (from Assyria to Egypt, from Sudan to Iran to the Mediterranean islands) reflects not the world of Isaiah's 8th century but the full extent of Jewish diaspora in the Roman period.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 21:11-12 preserves Isaiah 11:11-12. Nephi frames these verses in the context of the Book of Mormon's own purposes: the record is given to 'convince both Jew and Gentile that Jesus is the Christ' (Title Page), and it witnesses to the gathering of Israel in the latter days. The Book of Mormon uses Isaiah's 'second exodus' language throughout (e.g., 3 Nephi 16:4-5, where Christ promises the Father's work with 'this people' will continue after His earthly ministry).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:1-2 speaks of Christ 'gathering together the faithful from the four quarters of the earth.' D&C 45:42-46 describes the gathering of the faithful before the Second Coming. D&C 110 records that the keys of the gathering of Israel were restored through Elijah, explicitly tying the Restoration to Isaiah's promise of a second exodus. Joseph Smith declared that 'the building up of Zion is a cause that has interested the people of God in every age' (D&C 64:26), making clear that the gathering Isaiah describes is central to the Restoration's purpose.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The gathering of the scattered remnant is preparatory to building Zion and establishing the Lord's house. The temple ordinances make possible the covenantal relationships through which the scattered are bound together. In LDS theology, the sealing power restored through Joseph Smith (D&C 110:16) enables the gathering spoken of in Isaiah: families and individuals scattered across time and space are sealed together through the temple covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the one who reaches out His hand 'the second time' to gather the remnant. The first exodus was typological, prefiguring Christ's redemptive work. The second exodus is the eschatological gathering into the kingdom of God, made possible by Christ's atonement and the Holy Ghost's power. Christ identifies Himself as the Shepherd who gathers His flock (John 10:14-16, 'other sheep I have, which are not of this fold'). The universality of His gathering—from every corner of the earth—reflects the universal scope of His redemption.
commentary.application: For modern disciples, Isaiah 11:11-12 speaks powerfully to the central work of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints: the gathering of Israel. We live in the dispensation when this prophecy is being fulfilled. Those who join the Church from every nation, kindred, tongue, and people are literally participating in the fulfillment of Isaiah's vision. The 'second exodus' is not primarily physical relocation to Utah (as it was historically for some) but rather spiritual gathering into covenantal community. Personally, joining the Church represents answering God's call to come home—to be gathered into Zion despite the scattering of human history and circumstance. Practically, we are invited to see missionary work not as winning a theological argument but as participating in the greatest gathering of the human family: inviting the scattered children of Israel to return to the Father through the Messiah. The remnant theme also comforts us in small things: our individual branches and wards are not insignificant; they are part of the remnant gathering. We are invited to bear testimony that the gathering spoken of in Isaiah is not future wishful thinking but present reality.

text_kjv: And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah's prophecy culminates with a vision of comprehensive gathering and reunion. The 'ensign/signal' (nes) reappears from verse 10, now actively raised to summon the dispersed. The verse explicitly names both kingdoms: nidchei Yisra'el ('the outcasts of Israel,' the exiled northern kingdom) and nefutsot Yehudah ('the scattered of Judah,' the dispersed southern kingdom). This is not merely the return of Judah from Babylon; it is the reunion of the two kingdoms that had been divided since the split after Solomon. The phrase 'from the four corners of the earth' emphasizes universality and comprehensiveness—no exile is too remote, no diaspora too permanent. The regathering leaves no scattered group unaddressed. This verse forms the conclusion of the entire Chapter 11 vision: from the Spirit-endowed Messiah (v. 2) through the peaceable kingdom (v. 6-9), through the Messiah as signal (v. 10), through the second exodus (v. 11), all flows toward this final image of the banner raised, the two kingdoms reunited, the scattered gathered from every compass point.
commentary.narrative_continued: The distinction between Israel (the northern kingdom) and Judah (the southern kingdom) is crucial. After Solomon's death (c. 930 BCE), the kingdom divided: Israel in the north was conquered by Assyria in 722 BCE and its population scattered into the Assyrian Empire; Judah in the south was exiled to Babylon in 586 BCE. By Isaiah's time or shortly after, the northern kingdom had ceased to exist as a political entity—its people were absorbed into diaspora communities. When verse 12 promises to gather 'the outcasts of Israel' and 'the scattered of Judah,' it is promising something that seemed impossible in any historical sense: the reunion of kingdoms that had not existed together for centuries, peoples who had lost ethnic and linguistic continuity. Yet this is precisely what the Restoration promises: through the gospel of Jesus Christ, all covenant Israel—from every tribe and kingdom and diaspora—will be gathered as one people. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve nidchei and nefutsot identically, confirming that the distinction between the two kingdoms and their separate dispersion was central to the prophetic vision even in antiquity.

word_study.meaning: signal, banner, standard, ensign; a pole or flag raised to rally, summon, or identify. In military contexts, the nes gathered troops; metaphorically, it represents a focal point or gathering point.
word_study.significance: This is the same nes ('signal') from verse 10, now raised explicitly to gather the nations. The Messiah is both the signal itself (v. 10) and the power that raises the signal for the gathering. The parallelism shows that gathering around Christ and gathering of the scattered remnant are expressions of the same reality.

word_study.meaning: to gather, collect, assemble; often used of ingathering, harvest, or gathering people into a community.
word_study.significance: The word implies not merely scattered individuals finding each other but active collection and assembly into community. This is not passive return but purposeful gathering into covenantal unity.

word_study.meaning: outcasts, banished ones, driven out; those separated or expelled from community. The root nadach means 'to thrust away, drive out.'
word_study.significance: The term emphasizes the painful separation of exile: these are not merely distant, but explicitly separated, cast out. The gathering of the nidchei is redemption of the rejected and separated.

word_study.meaning: scattered, dispersed, scattered abroad; the state of being spread out, no longer cohesive.
word_study.significance: Where nidchei emphasizes the act of being driven out (Israel's explicit exile), nefutsot emphasizes the state of dispersion (Judah's broader diaspora). Both forms of separation—forced and dispersed—are reversed.

word_study.meaning: to gather, collect, bring together into one place or group; similar to asaf but emphasizing the bringing together of dispersed elements.
word_study.significance: The use of three different verbs for gathering (asaf, qabatz, and earlier qanah and nassa—'raise up') emphasizes the complete and comprehensive nature of the ingathering: every verb choice reinforces the totality of the gathering.

word_study.meaning: the four corners/wings of the earth; a poetic expression for all directions, all regions, the complete earth.
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes the universality and completeness of the gathering. From every direction, every distance, every region—there will be no remainder left scattered. The geographic scope is total.

cross_references.connection: Verse 10's 'root of Jesse' standing as 'an ensign of the people' reappears here as He actively 'sets up an ensign for the nations.' The Messiah and His signal are one: He is simultaneously the rallying point and the power that gathers.

This historical passage describes the actual conquest of northern Israel by Assyria and the deportation of Israel. Isaiah's promise in 11:12 is precisely that these exiled 'outcasts of Israel' would be gathered—a promise that seemed impossible from a historical perspective.

King Hezekiah's passover extended an invitation to the remnant of Israel (the northern kingdom) to return and participate in the feast at Jerusalem. This is a historical foreshadowing of Isaiah's promise of reunited kingdoms.

Jeremiah echoes Isaiah's language: 'and his name whereby he shall be called, The LORD Our Righteousness. Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that they shall no more say, The LORD liveth, which brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt; But, The LORD liveth, which brought up and which led the seed of the house of Israel.' Both prophets envision a second exodus as the ultimate redemptive work.

Mormon testifies that the Book of Mormon is written for the 'remnant of the house of Israel' and speaks of their future gathering. Moroni's words at the end of the Book of Mormon (Moroni 10:27-34) invite 'all the ends of the earth' to come unto Christ—the literal fulfillment of Isaiah's vision.

Modern revelation explicitly applies Isaiah 11:11-12 to the gathering in the Restoration: 'Hearken and hear, O ye inhabitants of the earth. Listen, ye elders of my church together, and hear the voice of the Lord; for he calleth upon all men, and commandeth all men everywhere to repent. For behold, the Lord hath shown forth his wisdom in giving unto all who ask him, that ask in faith...that they may gather together unto the place which I have appointed.' The gathering is God's central work in the last days.

commentary.historical_context: By the Second Temple period (515 BCE onward), the historical reality was that the northern kingdom had never been 'returned' in any organized way. The exiles deported by Assyria to Mesopotamia had not marched back to Canaan; their descendants were absorbed into local populations or formed diaspora communities. When Isaiah spoke of gathering the 'outcasts of Israel' (the northern kingdom) and the 'scattered of Judah' (the diaspora of the southern kingdom), he was making a promise that transcended historical probability. The Return under Cyrus in 538 BCE primarily involved Judah and Jerusalem. The 'ten lost tribes' became a mystery, a theological problem: where were they? Some rabbinical tradition suggested they were 'on the other side of the river Sambatyon.' The promise of their gathering remained a future hope rather than an accomplished fact. In the Christian era, Jewish diaspora communities spread from the Mediterranean throughout the Roman Empire, into Persia, North Africa, and eventually across Europe and the world. The promise of reunion seemed more impossible with each passing century. Yet this is precisely why the Restoration of the gospel and the establishment of gathering places became so theologically significant: they provided a mechanism through which Isaiah's impossible promise could become realized.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 21:12 preserves Isaiah 11:12 exactly, and immediately follows with commentary in 2 Nephi 21:13-16 regarding the remnant of the house of Israel. The Book of Mormon frames Isaiah's prophecy as foundational to understanding the Restoration: Joseph Smith and his followers are understood as instruments of the gathering. 1 Nephi 22:3-8 has Nephi explain to his brothers that the prophecies concern 'the remnant of the house of Israel' which 'shall be scattered, and shall be smitten by other people, and shall be driven to and fro, and shall be hunted, and shall be smitten and scattered abroad' but ultimately gathered. The Book of Mormon's entire narrative is wrapped within Isaiah's framework.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:1-2 identifies the gathering of Israel as Christ's work: 'I am Jesus Christ, the Son of God. I came into the world to do the will of my Father...And as I said unto the apostles, so I say unto you—Hearken and hear the voice of the Lord your God.' D&C 45:42-46 promises that in 'that day' the faithful will be gathered in 'one place upon the face of this land, to prepare their hearts and be prepared in all things against the day when tribulation and desolation are sent forth upon the wicked.' D&C 110:11 records that Moses appeared to Joseph Smith and restored 'the keys of the gathering of Israel from the four parts of the earth.' The keys of the gathering—specifically identified with the prophecy of Isaiah—are central to the Restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the center of gathering. In the Salt Lake Temple, the gathering room and the various ordinances (particularly the sealing ordinances) are designed to unite families, stakes, and nations into one people. The work of baptism for the dead (D&C 124:29-30) extends the gathering across time: those who lived in ages past are vicariously gathered into the covenant. In prophetic vision, the celestial kingdom represents the ultimate gathering—all covenant Israel, from every age and nation, sealed together by the sealing power restored through Joseph Smith.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the 'ensign' raised for all nations, whose signal draws both Israel and the Gentiles. The gathering of Israel and the conversion of the Gentiles are both expressions of His redemptive work. Ephesians 2:14-16 describes Christ breaking down the 'middle wall of partition' between Jew and Gentile, making them 'one new man' in Himself. The reunion of divided Israel and the gathering of all peoples around Christ is the ultimate reconciliation. The cross is the supreme nes—the signal pole on which Christ was lifted up, drawing all peoples to Him (John 12:32, 'I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me'). Every act of gathering, every conversion, every family sealed by covenantal power is an expression of the drawing power of Christ.
commentary.application: Isaiah 11:12 speaks directly to the fundamental work of The Latter-day Saint Church: the gathering of Israel. For individual members, this verse invites several applications: (1) Recognize that you are part of the fulfilled prophecy. By joining the Church, you have literally answered the call to be gathered. This is not coincidence; it is the working out of Isaiah's vision. (2) Understand your conversion as part of a larger cosmic narrative. You are not simply joining an organization; you are being gathered into the covenant of Israel. (3) Participate in the ongoing work of gathering by sharing the gospel. Every person you help come to Christ is part of Isaiah's vision being fulfilled. (4) Extend the gathering through temple work. By performing ordinances for those who lived in ages past, you extend the signal to all generations. (5) Recognize that the division and scattering we see in the world today—between nations, races, religions, families—is not God's final word. Isaiah's prophecy of complete gathering proclaims that these divisions will ultimately be healed through Christ. This should make us hopeful about the possibility of reconciliation and peaceful unity, even when the world seems fractured. (6) Be prepared for the reality that gathering is difficult and often incomplete in our experience. Though Isaiah promises total gathering, we live in a time when the work is partial, ongoing, and often thwarted by human resistance. Yet we work toward the vision, trusting that Christ will complete what we can only begin.

text_kjv: The envy also of Ephraim shall depart, and the adversaries of Judah shall be cut off: Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 11:13 stands as one of the most politically charged verses in the entire chapter—and perhaps in all of Isaiah's messianic prophecy. The verse addresses a wound that has bled through Israel's entire history: the bitter division between the northern kingdom (Ephraim, representing the ten northern tribes) and the southern kingdom (Judah) that began under Rehoboam around 930 BCE and never healed. This division was not merely political; it was fratricidal. The two kingdoms fought each other, formed competing alliances, and viewed each other with deep suspicion and hostility. The "Syro-Ephraimite crisis" of Isaiah 7—when northern Israel and Syria threatened Judah—shows how acute this hatred had become. Isaiah's audience would have understood this verse as politically astonishing: the promise is not merely that Ephraim and Judah would stop fighting, but that the psychological root of their conflict—the envy (qin'ah), the jealousy, the mutual contempt—would be surgically removed.

The structure of the verse reinforces its message through parallel negation: "Ephraim will not be jealous of Judah, and Judah will not harass Ephraim." This is not compromise or détente; it is genuine reconciliation rooted in a complete transformation of the human heart. The Covenant Rendering's translation of qin'ah as "jealousy" rather than merely "envy" captures the deeper Hebrew sense of competitive obsession—the kind of jealousy that consumes the jealous person from within. When Isaiah says this will "depart," he uses a verb (sarah) that means to turn away, to separate, to withdraw. The healing is total and internal, not merely behavioral.

This verse also contains an implicit Christological promise. The reunification of Ephraim and Judah under a single messianic ruler (the Branch of Jesse, described in verses 1-5) represents the healing of the primary division within God's covenant people. Later in history, when the northern kingdom was exiled by Assyria in 722 BCE, the ten tribes seemed lost to history. But Isaiah's prophecy insists they are not lost to God's purpose—they will be gathered again, their jealousy healed, their mutual hostility erased. This becomes a powerful type of how the Atonement heals all divisions: between Jews and Gentiles (Ephesians 2), between male and female, bond and free (Galatians 3:28), between all who covenant with Christ.

word_study.meaning: Jealousy, rivalry, envious burning. The root קנא (qn') carries the sense of competitive intensity, the kind of jealousy that eats from within. Unlike simple envy (coveting what another has), qin'ah implies active rivalry and burning zeal. It can be righteous (God's jealousy for His covenant) or destructive (tribal rivalry). Here, it is the destructive kind—the two kingdoms' obsessive comparison and competitive hatred.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's use of 'jealousy' over 'envy' preserves the emotional intensity of the Hebrew. This is not a cool disagreement; it is a burning, consuming mutual suspicion that has shaped Ephraim and Judah's entire relationship. The promise is that this inner fire will be extinguished—a work only God can accomplish in human hearts.

word_study.meaning: To turn aside, to depart, to withdraw. The verb סור (sur) denotes a complete turning away or separation. It can mean physical departure (turning away in space) or psychological/spiritual withdrawal (turning one's attention or affection away from something).
word_study.significance: The jealousy does not merely become dormant or suppressed; it actively departs, turns away, withdraws from the relationship between Ephraim and Judah. This suggests not a management of conflict but a fundamental transformation in how the two kingdoms relate to each other.

word_study.meaning: Those who trouble, harass, oppress, form against. The root צור (tzur) means to form, shape, or press against. Tzorrei are not merely opponents but those who actively press against, create enmity, and form plots. They are adversaries in an active, ongoing sense.
word_study.significance: The verse promises not only the removal of Judah's internal jealousy but also the 'cutting off' of those who oppose Judah from outside. This may refer to Edom, Ammon, and other regional enemies who have exploited Ephraim-Judah division to weaken them both. The messianic age brings both internal reconciliation and external security.

word_study.meaning: Will be cut off, will be destroyed. The root כרת (krt) means to cut, sever, or destroy. In covenant language, 'to cut off' often means to sever from the covenant people or from existence. Here it means complete removal or destruction.
word_study.significance: The adversaries are not merely defeated or pushed back; they are 'cut off'—removed entirely. Combined with verse 14, this suggests that the messianic era brings not only reconciliation between Ephraim and Judah but also definitive victory over those who have opposed both.

word_study.meaning: To form against, press against, harass, trouble. The root צור (tzur, same as in 'tzorrei') means to shape or form. When used of one person against another, it means to press, to harass, to trouble actively.
word_study.significance: Judah's old habit of pressing against, troubling, harassing Ephraim will cease. The parallelism between Ephraim not being jealous of Judah and Judah not harassing Ephraim suggests mutual responsibility—both must change. Both the emotion (jealousy) and the action (harassment) must end.

cross_references.connection: Chronicles the brutal conflict between Judah (David's forces) and Israel (Saul's house), showing the fratricidal warfare that Isaiah 11:13 promises will end in the messianic age.
Records the original split between Ephraim (northern ten tribes) and Judah under Rehoboam, the wound that Isaiah 11:13 prophesies will be healed in the age of the Branch of Jesse.
Describes the Syro-Ephraimite crisis, when northern Israel and Syria united against Judah, illustrating the depth of the jealousy and hostility that verse 13 promises will depart.

Also prophesies the reunion of Judah and Ephraim: 'In those days the house of Judah shall walk with the house of Israel, and they shall come together out of the land of the north to the land that I have given for an inheritance unto your fathers.'
In NT typology, Christ breaks down the wall between Jew and Gentile as the messianic king breaks down Ephraim-Judah division, making one new humanity through the Atonement.

commentary.historical_context: The division of the united monarchy into northern Israel (Ephraim, with its capital at Samaria) and southern Judah (with capital at Jerusalem) occurred around 930 BCE, just after Solomon's death. This was not merely a political divorce; it was rooted in tribal grievances, control of trade routes, and the economic resentment of the northern tribes who felt they bore the burdens of Solomon's building projects and military conscription. For nearly two centuries, until the northern kingdom's exile in 722 BCE, Ephraim and Judah were rivals, sometimes allies, sometimes enemies. The "Syro-Ephraimite crisis" (c. 734 BCE) was particularly acute: northern Israel and Syria allied to pressure Judah into joining a coalition against Assyria. Isaiah lived through this period and saw firsthand how the division of God's covenant people weakened them all. His prophecy of reunification under a messianic king would have sounded politically revolutionary—a promise that what human politics had torn apart, God's coming king would restore. The very fact that the northern kingdom was later exiled and "lost" to history made this promise even more profound: Isaiah insisted that these lost tribes would be found again, gathered together, and healed. The phrase "the remnant of his people" (verse 16) becomes crucial—even exile cannot erase God's purposes for His covenant people.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes the gathering of both Judah and Ephraim as a sign of the last days. Alma 46:24 promises that 'whosoever believeth in Christ' will be 'reckoned unto the house of Ephraim.' 3 Nephi 16:1-3 records Christ telling the Nephites that He has other sheep 'of the house of Israel' who will hear His voice. The reconciliation of Ephraim and Judah prophesied here is a key component of the Restoration's understanding of the gathering of Israel—not merely the return of the Jews, but the reunification of all the tribes under Christ.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 133:26-34 describes the gathering in the last days: 'Let them fall upon the lofty mountains and the mountains shall be thrown down, and the valleys shall not be found... And the streams shall be turned from their course, and the rivers shall cease to flow... And behold, there is none other place appointed than that which I have appointed; neither shall there be any other place appointed than that which I have appointed, for the work of the gathering of my people.' The highway (mesillah) of Isaiah 11:16 becomes the literal gathering of the remnant of Jacob in the latter days, a central theme of D&C revelation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The healing of Ephraim-Judah division is foundational to understanding the temple as a gathering place. The temple is where all the tribes—whether literally descended from the old kingdom lines or spiritually grafted in through covenant—come into unity before God. The vicarious work for the dead in the temple fulfills in a spiritual sense what Isaiah prophesies politically: the gathering and reconciliation of all God's covenant people, transcending all earthly divisions.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 11:13 points to the messianic king (the Branch of Jesse, verses 1-5) as the one who heals the deepest divisions within God's covenant people. Just as Christ in His ministry and atoning work broke down the wall between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14-15), the messianic king prophesied here heals the division between Ephraim and Judah. The removal of 'jealousy' and 'hostility' is a work of the Spirit—the same Spirit that 'rests upon' the Branch (verse 2) and gives Him the ability to judge with righteousness (verses 3-5). This is not political unification achieved through military conquest, but spiritual transformation achieved through covenant renewal and the work of the Holy Ghost. The type is radical: the king heals not by force but by changing hearts, making 'the jealousy depart' from within the people themselves.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, this verse speaks directly to the work of reconciliation and unity that the restored Church is called to accomplish. Just as Ephraim and Judah were divided by jealousy and mutual suspicion, the modern world is fractured by tribalism, national rivalries, and competitive identity politics. The verse invites us to examine where we harbor 'jealousy' toward others—whether of other nations, other faiths, or other political communities—and to recognize that such jealousy is antithetical to the messianic vision Isaiah articulates. More specifically, for Latter-day Saints, this verse reminds us of the unique role of Ephraim in the latter-day gathering. Members of the Church often discover in their lineage blessings that they are 'of Ephraim' (the tribe that was scattered among all nations and therefore is primary in the latter-day gathering) or 'of Judah' (the Jewish remnant). The verse promises that these ancient tribal distinctions will not divide us but will be healed in our common covenant with Christ. In our own families and communities, we are called to be peacemakers who heal jealousy, who turn away from harboring grudges, and who actively reconcile rather than press against one another. The messianic vision begins in our own hearts and relationships—the jealousy departs when we choose to let it go.

text_kjv: But they shall fly upon the shoulders of the Philistines toward the west; they shall spoil them of the east together: they shall lay their hand upon Edom and Moab; and the children of Ammon shall obey them.

commentary.narrative:
If verse 13 speaks of internal healing, verse 14 pivots to external conquest. The reunited Ephraim-Judah, no longer divided against itself, now turns outward to subdue the enemies that have surrounded and oppressed them. The imagery is striking and violent: they 'fly upon the shoulders' (literally, 'upon the shoulder,' singular, of the Philistines) like birds of prey, moving westward toward the Mediterranean coast where Philistine power has always been concentrated. The verb 'swoop down' (afu in Hebrew) paints a picture of a predatory bird diving on its target—swift, overwhelming, irresistible. This is not negotiation or gradual expansion; it is a sudden, comprehensive military domination.

The verse then expands the scope of this conquest: they will 'spoil them of the east'—plunder the eastern peoples (likely the desert tribes and Arabian kingdoms) together, as a unified force. Then they turn south and southeast, laying their hand upon Edom (south of Judah, the homeland of Esau's descendants) and Moab (east of the Dead Sea). Finally, the Ammonites (further north and east) will 'obey them.' The Covenant Rendering's translation of 'submit to them' (mishlach yadah) captures the sense of not merely military defeat but political subordination—the Ammonites become vassals. The verse paints a comprehensive picture: the messianic-age Israel conquers all the nations that surround it, from west (Philistia) to east (Ammon), from north to south, establishing hegemony over the entire region.

It is crucial to understand that this verse is not describing contemporary political history—there is no moment in Israel's actual history when they conquered the Philistines, Edom, Moab, and Ammon simultaneously. Rather, this is eschatological vision, spoken of a future age under the messianic king. The ancient Israelite audience, living in a geopolitical context where they were often threatened by these very nations (Philistines from the west, Edomites from the south, Moabites and Ammonites from the east), would have understood this as a promise of vindication, security, and the restoration of the blessed dominion that Israel (in their idealized memory) had enjoyed under David and Solomon. The verse asserts that the messianic age will not only heal internal divisions but also establish Israel's security through the defeat of external enemies.

word_study.meaning: Will fly, will swoop. The root עוף (uf) means to fly. In military contexts, it often carries the sense of swift, predatory descent—like a bird of prey diving on its target. The verb suggests speed, inevitability, and overwhelming force.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'swoop down' captures the aggressive, predatory quality of the Hebrew. This is not gradual military advance but sudden, overwhelming conquest. The imagery draws on the association between flying birds and swift military strikes throughout ancient Near Eastern warfare metaphors.

word_study.meaning: Shoulder, slope, side. The singular 'shoulder' here likely refers to a geographic feature—the Philistine coastal region or hills, literally the 'shoulder' or slope of the land. It may also carry the sense of 'flank' or 'side' in a military sense.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's translation of 'the Philistine slope' clarifies the geographic sense—the messianic Israel will swoop down upon the western coastal region (where Philistia is located), treating it as a slope or flank to be overwhelmed. The singular 'shoulder' suggests a unified, focused strike.

word_study.meaning: Will plunder, will despoil, will rob. The root בזז (bzz) means to plunder, to strip of goods, to rob. It denotes not merely military victory but the taking of treasure, resources, and wealth from the defeated enemy.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes that the conquest is comprehensive—not only military but economic. The vanquished nations lose not just political autonomy but their material wealth. This is the ancient Near Eastern practice of total conquest: submission means loss of resources to the victor.

word_study.meaning: To stretch out, extend their hand. Mishloch means 'send forth' or 'extend.' Yad (hand) in Hebrew often symbolizes power, authority, agency. 'Stretching out one's hand' against someone means to exert power over them, to seize control.
word_study.significance: This phrase moves beyond mere plunder to active political domination. To 'lay hand upon' Edom and Moab means to seize control, to assert authority, to bring under one's power. The Covenant Rendering's language ('stretch out their hand against') preserves this sense of forceful assertion of dominance.

word_study.meaning: From their obedience, their listening, their submission. The root שׁמע (sma) means to hear, to listen, to obey. Mishmaatem is a construct phrase meaning 'from the obedience of' or 'from the submission of.' The Ammonites are brought into a state of listening obedience to the messianic Israel.
word_study.significance: The verb 'obey' or 'submit' (mishmaatem) suggests a less violent mode of subjugation than the plundering of other nations. The Ammonites 'submit' rather than being 'spoiled.' This may indicate that not all enemies will be dealt with through plunder and slaughter; some will be brought into vassal status through political surrender. The variety of verbs suggests a nuanced picture of messianic conquest: some enemies are devastated, some are subjugated, all are brought into submission.

cross_references.connection: Chronicles David's actual conquests of Philistines, Edom, Moab, and Ammon—historical precedent for the messianic conquests Isaiah 11:14 prophesies, suggesting a 'second David' will restore these dominions.
Celebrates David's victories over Edom, Moab, and Philistia: 'Moab is my washpot; over Edom will I cast out my shoe,' language of dominion echoed in Isaiah 11:14's promise of messianic conquest.
Describes the judgment and destruction of Edom in the messianic age, aligning with Isaiah 11:14's promise that messianic Israel will lay its hand upon Edom.

Prophesies that 'the house of Jacob shall possess their possessions' and 'saviours shall come up on mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau'—direct parallel to Isaiah 11:14's vision of messianic conquest.
In NT eschatology, the kingdoms of the world become the kingdom of Christ; Isaiah 11:14's vision of messianic dominion over surrounding nations is fulfilled in Christ's ultimate kingship.

commentary.historical_context: The four enemy nations mentioned in verse 14 represent the major threats Israel faced throughout its history. The Philistines, who occupied the Mediterranean coast west of Judah, were Israel's most formidable western enemy—they appear throughout the judges period and into the monarchy (Samson, Saul, David all fought them). Edom, south of Judah (occupying the territory of Esau's descendants), was a frequent rival and often a vassal of Judah depending on the era. Moab, east of the Dead Sea, was a buffer state between Judah and the Arabian desert, sometimes hostile, sometimes allied. Ammon, northeast of the Dead Sea, was another Transjordanian kingdom that frequently clashed with Israel and Judah. Under David (c. 1000 BCE), Israel did indeed conquer or bring under tribute many of these nations—this period represents the 'golden age' of Israelite dominion. However, by Isaiah's time (8th century BCE), Israel's power had eroded significantly. The northern kingdom was under increasing Assyrian pressure, and the southern kingdom's security was constantly threatened. Isaiah's prophecy thus echoed a memory of Davidic greatness and promised its restoration under the messianic king. The specific mention of these four nations also likely reflects the geopolitical reality of Isaiah's era: these were the primary threats to Judah, and the promise of their subjugation would have been deeply reassuring to Isaiah's audience living in constant geopolitical anxiety.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon does not directly parallel this conquest language, but Nephi's throne vision (1 Nephi 13-14) describes the future glory of Zion and the dominion of the Lamb—which includes the spiritual conquest of all peoples and nations. The metaphor shifts from military conquest to spiritual dominion, but the eschatological vision of universal submission to God's kingdom remains central.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 87-88 describe the last days in terms of wars and judgments among nations—a period when the kingdoms of the earth will be subdued before the kingdom of God. D&C 101:80-101 prophesies of a New Jerusalem and the establishment of God's kingdom during the millennium. The 'conquest' of Isaiah 11:14 is reframed in Restoration thought as the spiritual conquest of all nations by the power of the gospel—not through military means but through covenant and truth.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the geographic center from which God's dominion radiates outward. Isaiah 2:2-3 prophesies that 'the mountain of the LORD's house shall be established in the top of the mountains... and all nations shall flow unto it.' This verse's vision of messianic conquest is ultimately a vision of all nations coming willingly to covenant with God at His holy temple, not through force but through the irresistible attraction of truth and divine authority.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ, the Branch of Jesse, fulfills the messianic-king imagery of Isaiah 11:14 in a way that transcends military conquest. Rather than subjugating the Philistines, Edomites, Moabites, and Ammonites through force, Christ conquers all nations spiritually through the power of the Atonement and His gospel. The 'hand laid upon' the nations becomes His hand extended in mercy and redemption. The prophecy's fulfillment in Christ reveals that the true conquest is not of territory but of hearts and souls—all nations and peoples brought into submission to Him not through fear but through love and truth. This is the 'second exodus' that Isaiah will describe in Chapter 40: not a military reconquest of the promised land but a spiritual homecoming of all God's covenant people.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 14 invites reflection on what 'conquest' means in the context of the gospel. We are not called to military dominion over other peoples, but we are called to 'go forth... proclaiming the gospel' (D&C 80:1) with the same spirit of inevitability and urgency that Isaiah describes. The 'hand laid upon' the nations in verse 14 becomes our hand extended in missionary work, service, and covenant-making. Just as the messianic Israel brings surrounding nations into submission through the assertion of true power, the Church brings individuals and families into covenant through the assertion of truth and the power of the Holy Ghost. The verse also challenges us not to view other nations or peoples as enemies to be conquered and plundered, but as brothers and sisters to be brought into the family of God through invitation and testimony. The ultimate vision of 'all nations flowing unto the mountain of the LORD's house' (Isaiah 2:2-3) is fulfilled when we extend our hands in genuine invitation, not domination, to all the world's peoples to come and know the God of Israel through Christ.

text_kjv: And the LORD shall utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian sea; and with his mighty wind shall he shake his hand over the river, and shall smite it in the seven streams, and make men go over dryshod.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah now moves into one of the most explicit 'second exodus' passages in the entire Hebrew Bible. Verse 15 is not merely a continuation of the messianic conquest imagery; it represents a fundamental shift in metaphor and theology. The prophet is no longer speaking of Israel subjugating surrounding nations but of God miraculously removing the physical obstacles that separated Israel from the diaspora. The 'tongue of the Egyptian sea' refers to the narrow inlet or gulf—most likely the Gulf of Suez at the northern tip of the Red Sea, the same body of water that God parted in the Exodus under Moses. That original parting was the foundational miracle of Israel's history, the event that proved God's power and made Israel a covenant people. Now, Isaiah prophesies a second parting—at both ends of the ancient world, so to speak. The Euphrates (the 'river' in ancient Near Eastern geographical consciousness, often simply called 'the river') would be parted as well.

The imagery is almost violent in its grandeur: the LORD will 'utterly destroy' (literally, 'devote to destruction,' using the word cherem—the same word for herem as in the conquest of Canaan) the tongue of the Egyptian sea. He will 'wave His hand' (literally, 'shake His hand' or 'brandish') over the Euphrates with a 'scorching wind' (as the Covenant Rendering translates it)—echoing God's use of the east wind to dry the Red Sea in Exodus 14. He will 'split it into seven channels' so that people can cross 'dryshod' (literally, 'in sandals,' a detail recalling the haste and preparedness of the original exodus, when Israel left Egypt with shoes on their feet).
